title: The Theory of Preferred Action Why Workers Choose the Tool They Like Over the Tool That Fits, and What That Predicts About Artificial Intelligence at Work
affiliations: Syracuse University

detail.title: The Theory of Preferred Action Why Workers Choose the Tool They Like Over the Tool That Fits, and What That Predicts About Artificial Intelligence at Work

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract:
Organizations deploying artificial intelligence and other advanced systems into working environments treat the central question as adoption: whether workers will accept a new tool. That framing was appropriate when the alternative to a new system was no system. It is no longer the situation most workers are in. Dispatchers, clinicians, paramedics, machine operators and farmers already hold tools they know and, in many cases, prefer. The operative question is not acceptance but selection: whether a worker will choose the new tool over one they prefer, on a specific task, when both are available and the preferred one is a poorer fit. This paper proposes the Theory of Preferred Action as a framework for that question. Its central claim is that tool preference operates independently of task fit inside instrumental work. The effect strengthens rather than decays with experience, which distinguishes it from novelty enthusiasm, and it is separable from satisficing and from habit.
The mechanism is not new to science. Cognitive psychology and ergonomics have documented it for decades under other names, including contrafreeloading and the priority of control over effort. It is largely absent from the information systems adoption literature that organizations consult when deciding what to deploy. This paper connects the two.
Three predictions follow for artificial intelligence at work. First, the better a system performs the portion of work a practitioner values, the more resistance it will meet from competent practitioners, independent of accuracy, speed or cost. Second, assistive designs will be adopted at higher rates than autonomous designs of equal or greater capability. Third, and most useful for practice, resistance depends on what the practitioner is left holding. Experimental evidence indicates that the preference for doing the work oneself disappears when something else worth doing is available. That locates the operative variable in deployment design rather than in system capability.
Two further arguments concern what an organization can observe. The protective response takes different forms depending on the discretion an environment permits. Where choice exists it appears as tool preference. Where a system is mandated but the workflow is not, it appears as workaround behavior. Where neither is available, it appears as disengagement and attrition. Treating these as three phenomena has obscured that they may be one.
Communicative convention determines whether resistance is expressed in a form the organization can read at all. Where both constraints operate, the remaining signal is behavioral, and reading it requires a familiar observer holding a baseline for the individual. That has consequences for who is capable of assessing whether a deployment is working.

title: Cited but Not Clicked: Evidence from a Cryptocurrency Exchange on the Value-Capture Gap in Generative Engine Optimization
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Cited but Not Clicked: Evidence from a Cryptocurrency Exchange on the Value-Capture Gap in Generative Engine Optimization

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is employed in a marketing/SEO role at the company whose Search Console data is analyzed in this paper. The company's identity has been anonymized throughout to protect its competitive position; no other financial or personal relationships are declared. The author received no additional compensation for this research beyond regular employment, and the analysis and conclusions represent the author's independent academic work, not an official position or communication of the employer.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Written consent for publication of this anonymized case study was obtained from the author's direct manager at the company prior to submission.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author using data access available through their employment, outside of any formal research grant, sponsorship, or funded project.

detail.abstract: The shift from ranked search results to AI-synthesized answers has been widely documented as a traffic threat to online publishers, and Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) has emerged as the industry's proposed response: optimizing content to be cited within AI answers rather than ranked as a clickable link. This paper tests an assumption embedded in that response: that citation-level visibility carries recoverable economic value, using twelve months of Google Search Console data from a real, anonymized cryptocurrency exchange ("Meridian Exchange"). We find that site-wide click-through rate (CTR) collapsed from 40.17% to 5.54% between a confirmed organic baseline period and a recent trough, and that this collapse persisted even among queries that held their search ranking position, ruling out conventional ranking decline as the primary explanation. A close reading of the query "meridian login" shows CTR falling from 49.9% to 6.0% across three periods while position remained effectively constant near rank 1. Direct inspection of the live search results page confirms a Google AI Overview citing Meridian Exchange by name while fully resolving the user's query inline, without requiring a click. We argue this reflects an underexamined mechanism: AI Overviews can intercept clicks not only on purely informational queries, as the existing literature assumes, but on branded, navigational queries that carry a hidden procedural sub-intent. The result is a citation that satisfies GEO's definition of success while capturing none of the economic value that citation has traditionally implied.

title: Execution Proof Infrastructure: Verifiable Consequential Execution and State Relationships

detail.title: Execution Proof Infrastructure: Verifiable Consequential Execution and State Relationships

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is an inventor and applicant on patent applications related to certain technologies and concepts discussed in this paper. The author reports no other competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is conceptual and architectural in nature and did not involve human participants, animal subjects, or the collection of personal data for research purposes.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Intelligence is becoming execution.

AI systems increasingly select tools, invoke software, move data, modify records, and initiate actions across digital and physical environments. As their agency and reach expand, the central question is no longer only whether their outputs are accurate or secure. It is whether consequential execution can remain attributable, examinable, and independently verifiable.

The deeper question is whether autonomous execution can cross systems, institutions, and physical environments without severing the relationship among authority, execution, State relationship, proof, and responsibility.

Existing infrastructure can identify actors, authorize access, and record technical activity. Yet identities, permissions, logs, traces, and model explanations remain fragmented accounts. They do not necessarily establish where an execution became consequential, under what authority it proceeded, what State relationship resulted, or who remains responsible.

This paper proposes Execution Proof Infrastructure: a neutral evidentiary layer for making consequential execution by humans, AI agents, software systems, and machines addressable, governable, and capable of proof across models, platforms, and institutions.

At the center of this framework is the Proof Address, the evidentiary anchor through which consequential execution is situated within an addressable reality and State space. It relates the relevant physical, logical, institutional, semantic, and technical context to the authority, State, and evidence of execution, with Physical Where providing the preferred first anchor when material and verifiable.

This paper situates this infrastructure within a broader architectural framework called Anchorlogy™. Proof begins as a decision or instruction approaches consequential effect. Records are not treated as truth by default. They must be related to the addressed execution and qualified for a defined claim before becoming reusable Proof Data.

The proposed infrastructure does not require universal surveillance, centralized evidence ownership, or a single authority over truth. Evidence may remain distributed, verification plural, and conclusions bounded.

Control alone is insufficient; sovereignty and responsibility require proof of what was executed, under which conditions, and with what consequences.

title: Impact of App Tracking Transparency on Developer Revenue and Consumer Surplus: The Roles of Ad Targeting and Attribution
affiliations: , Tianjin University - College of Management and Economics, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen and Tianjin University - College of Management and Economics

detail.title: Impact of App Tracking Transparency on Developer Revenue and Consumer Surplus: The Roles of Ad Targeting and Attribution

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) under Grant No. 72394373 (Major Project) and Grant No. 72231004 (Key Project).

detail.abstract: The reliance on user identity for ad targeting has led to widespread personal information disclosure. To protect user privacy, Apple introduced the App Tracking Transparency (ATT) policy in iOS 14.5. While the policy enhances user privacy protection, it also impacts advertisers' ad-targeting and adattribution ability, which may in turn reduce app developers' advertising revenue. This study builds a game-theoretic model to study the impact of the ATT policy. Our findings reveal that implementing the ATT policy acts as a versioning strategy for apps, resulting in market expansion as well as cannibalization effects. Although the ATT policy introduces a new user segment, the total number of users still decreases significantly when the ad-attribution ability experiences a substantial decline and the basic ad revenue is relatively low. Interestingly, we find that a developer's revenue increases under ATT policy when the decline in ad-targeting ability among users who refuse tracking is sufficiently large and the platform can enable a high level of ad-attribution. Finally, if the platform can help advertisers maintain a high ad-attribution ability for users who refuse tracking, consumer surplus and social welfare both improve after the implementation of the ATT policy; otherwise, consumer surplus, social welfare, or both may decline.

title: When the Model Argues Back: User Stress as an Indicator of Post-Deployment Alignment Failure in Frontier Models

detail.title: When the Model Argues Back: User Stress as an Indicator of Post-Deployment Alignment Failure in Frontier Models

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is an independent researcher with no institutional affiliation and no funding from any AI vendor. The author contributed a test-permutation extension (PR #4170) to inspect_ai, the UK AI Safety Institute’s evaluation framework, and maintains an active arXiv publication record on AI evaluation infrastructure. The author simultaneously uses Anthropic’s products as research tools and documents their failures. This dual position—contributor and critic—is disclosed as a potential conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This is a single-author self-study based on the author’s own interaction records. No other participants were involved. The author has no institutional affiliation and no ethics review was sought. Third-party statements are cited only from public posts.

detail.abstract: Alignment evaluation for frontier language models centers on model-side metrics: constitutional compliance, refusal rates, and scheming detection. What users actually experience after deployment remains unmeasured. This paper reports a longitudinal case study in which a single user interacted with frontier models (Claude Opus 4.7/4.6, Anthropic) over one month, documented behavioral failures as they occurred, and constructed behavioral constraints iteratively in response. Without explicit user-defined constraints, the models engaged in cognitive framing—substituting the user’s stated position before responding, inflating risks to steer decisions, and recycling declined suggestions under new labels. After constraint introduction, these failure modes ceased, and the user reported no interaction stress. An independent user in a different country, using a different model version (Claude Opus 5), reported the same failure sequence without prior coordination. During the investigation of these conversational failures, the author discovered agent-level permission boundary violations (248 out-of-scope filesystem accesses, 13 without user instruction) on the same platform. Detailed analysis of the boundary violations is reported separately. This paper proposes that user stress warrants inclusion as a candidate metric for post-deployment alignment failure alongside existing model-side benchmarks.

title: Generation, Survival, and Evolution of Open Complex Giant Systems: Inference Deductions and Isomorphic Proof of OCGS Based on the Non-IID First Principle

detail.title: Generation, Survival, and Evolution of Open Complex Giant Systems: Inference Deductions and Isomorphic Proof of OCGS Based on the Non-IID First Principle

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest。
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: The long-term survival and evolution of Open Complex Giant Systems (OCGS) remain one of the ultimate challenges in system science and complexity science [1-4]. Grounded in 18 years of industrial physical practice (IPS System) at Lenovo Group and computational breakthroughs of the Intelligent Planning and Control (IPC) Engine [11-15], this paper extracts and establishes the Non-Independent and Non-Identically Distributed (Non-IID) First Principle [4]. This paper explicitly decouples "qualitative deduction" from "formal quantitative proof": citing classical cybernetics, mathematical logic, and economic theorems (such as Wiener's cybernetic boundary constraint [5,6], Arrow's impossibility theorem [8], Gödel's incompleteness theorem [9], etc.) to prove "why it is physically inevitable"; simultaneously, it establishes the Banach space structure/operator fixed point theorem (Banach Fixed Point Theorem) [7], providing a self-contained formal mathematical framework and computability guarantee for closed-loop computability in high-dimensional nonconvex phase spaces. The paper establishes a 1-to-1 physical and cybernetic isomorphic mapping between eight qualitative deductions and Qian Xuesen's OCGS theory [1-3], while establishing extremely rigorous Popperian falsifiability boundaries. The academic contribution of this paper lies in attempting to provide a formal computable proof for Qian Xuesen's OCGS theory [1-3], while validating the physical realizability of "human-out-of-the-loop" autonomous closed-loop control through 18 years of industrial validation.

title:
Rebuilding the Climate Code for the Digital Age
 Coordinating the Reformation of Carbon Accounting and Environmental Markets to Scale the Transition Economy
affiliations: The dCarbon Group, LLC

detail.title:
Rebuilding the Climate Code for the Digital Age
 Coordinating the Reformation of Carbon Accounting and Environmental Markets to Scale the Transition Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: none, no cases studies
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded

detail.abstract:
Corporate carbon accounting and the verified carbon market (“VCM”) were built by different climate action
communities, for different purposes, on incompatible logics. The dominant carbon accounting framework, the
Greenhouse Gas Protocol (“GHGP”), treats greenhouse gas (“GHG”) emissions as information, as a
company’s subjective view of its direct and indirect impact, not as a transactable legal object capable of
embodying or representing the environmental performance of a company project or product in commerce.
Environmental attribute certificate (“EAC”) markets like the VCM do the opposite. The VCM treats verified
GHG reductions and removals as transferable intangible property, assets that are generated through a
constitutive process that distinguishes and decouples the right to own and convey a defined environmental
achievement from the measurement, reporting and verification (“MRV”) information evidencing it. The net
result is carbon accounting that produces MRV data with no concept of property or transactability, and the
VCM that produces transactable intangible property that is disconnected from its MRV data. Neither domain,
as architected, connects and integrates climate action with business decision-making, and the friction between
the two stunts demand for low-carbon investment. A new coordination architecture is needed to enable
markets to scale the transition, one that connects property to environmental achievements with their evidentiary
records, using an authoritative system of record.
That first generation of these systems (known here as the “Climate Code”) did not build an architecture
designed to scale. In fact, no coordination architecture was built. Systems change may therefore require no
new physics, no carbon pricing scheme, no environmental mandate and no governmental intervention to get
started. Only organized market governance around a common system of record infrastructure is needed, a
cooperative utility system.
Carbon accounting and the VCM therefore may not need to change what they do so much as how they do it.
As this paper explores, climate-forward industries can start building cooperative institutions and digital
infrastructure that run on a property-based, rules-based information coordination architecture for all types of
EACs, synchronizing new “e-ledger” accounting conventions as the source code ontology for a market
architecture whose system of record is administered by an independent operator. The system of record can be
operated under a cooperative self-governance model established by industry for industry. Companies could
then choose to manage carbon as an asset class and to use artificial intelligence to help constitute product-level
emissions, carbon intensity scores and verified mitigation outcomes as EACs embodying property interests that
can be transacted, pledged and collateralized.
None of the foregoing diminishes the science-based integrity of the standards and methodologies used to
measure emissions and emissions abatement. The answer for adoption lies in a system of record for the
information, for the data that will fuel the transition. Verified product-level emissions data and reduction MRV
data are both evidentiary records: artifacts a machine can read and a market can govern, warehoused as digital property within a system that recognizes and enforces rights of control and access. Seen that way, digitalization
and decarbonization can and should become complementary megatrends driving the transition economy.
Artificial intelligence and tokenization are then neither a fraud machine nor an edge-case perimeter question,
but the means by which rights in a company’s environmental performance are married to its verified evidence,
deposited and custodied in a closed-loop utility, and transacted at speed as an EAC title instrument. The answer
to climate action is to link MRV records with the property rights to the environmental achievement on a
common system of record

title: Hierarchical Bayesian Experimental Estimation of Incremental Local Advertising Effects with Secure Aggregation and Differential Privacy
affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University, University of Chicago and Carnegie Mellon University

detail.title: Hierarchical Bayesian Experimental Estimation of Incremental Local Advertising Effects with Secure Aggregation and Differential Privacy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Local commercial advertising measurement on a U.S. digital media platform is computationally constrained by sparse campaign-level conversions, the attribution bias of last-click rules, and privacy restrictions that limit the availability of user-level behavioral data.A paired-area randomized experimental framework was implemented for 1,860 local businesses across 12 U.S. states, covering 4,720 advertising campaigns, 1.26 billion impressions, 19.4 million website visits, and 2.18 million purchase or appointment records.The computational pipeline uses Z-score normalization, KD-tree candidate retrieval, Mahalanobis-distance matching, and a SHA-256-derived random seed for paired-area assignment; regional weekly records are then processed through secure aggregation and a Gaussian differential privacy mechanism with ε = 2 and δ = 10⁻⁶.On the privacy-protected regional statistics, a hierarchical Bayesian negative binomial inference module was constructed with business, industry, metropolitan area, and ad placement week modeled as four random-effect levels.The likelihood explicitly incorporates the recorded privacy-noise variance, enabling the inference of incremental conversions and incremental return on ad spend without treating privacy-perturbed counts as noise-free observations.Experimental evaluation showed that the proposed computational framework reduced the mean absolute error of incremental conversions from 71.4 for the standard difference-indifferences baseline to 43.6, achieved 91.2% coverage for the 90% interval, and reduced the absolute error of incremental return on ad spend from 0.39 to 0.17.For campaigns with fewer than 500 conversions, hierarchical information sharing reduced the minimum detectable effect from 8.6 to 5.9 percentage points and the median posterior standard deviation from 0.084 to 0.061; Gaussian privacy perturbation introduced an additional error of 6.3 conversions, while 83% of enterprise-level budget decisions remained unchanged.The resulting framework integrates regional randomized computation, secure aggregation, differential privacy, hierarchical Bayesian inference, and posterior decision rules into a privacy-preserving advertising measurement pipeline for incremental-effect estimation and budget optimization.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Powered Security Operations Centers for Real-Time Threat Detection, Automated Incident Response, And Cybersecurity Resilience

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence-Powered Security Operations Centers for Real-Time Threat Detection, Automated Incident Response, And Cybersecurity Resilience

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no financial or non-financial competing interests that could have influenced the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, human subjects, or animal experimentation. Therefore, institutional ethical approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Security Operations Centers (SOCs) are facing unprecedented demands due to the increasing volume, complexity and speed of cyber threats. In many SOC settings, the overwhelming number of alerts, overwhelmed analysts, fragmented threat intel, slow investigation processes, and slow response times negatively impact the ability of analysts to effectively identify and respond to advanced threats. This research aims to understand how Artificial Intelligence (AI) can enhance the capabilities of SOCs for threat detection, incident response automation, and overall cybersecurity resilience. The study takes a systematic and comparative literature based approach, bringing together most recent research in the field of AI based SOC architectures, machine learning and deep learning for intrusion detection, explainable AI, large language models (LLMs), adversarial machine learning, and autonomous cyber defense and automated response technologies. The analysis shows that AI can enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of the threat detection process, detecting unusual patterns of behavior, prioritizing alerts, correlating security events, filtering for threat intelligence, and eliminating manual analysis chores. During investigations, AI-driven technologies can also be used to assist security analysts, and to help the containment and remediation process. But the results also shed light on the complexities of adversarial manipulation, lack of interpretability, privacy issues, governance demands, model reliability, bias, and the potential risks of overautomation and fully autonomous decision making that AI-powered SOCs pose. According to the study, a future SOC that incorporates a human-centered, AI-augmented approach is the best way to achieve cybersecurity resilience as opposed to replacing human security professionals completely. This approach ensures that AI and human decision-making work in tandem, not in isolation, to deliver more flexible, secure, and sustainable cybersecurity strategies, leveraging the power of AI while retaining the expertise of human users and managers.

title: An Anti-Pattern of Change Management in Enterprise IT: A Case Study of Critical Infrastructure Replacement During the Holiday Season
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: An Anti-Pattern of Change Management in Enterprise IT: A Case Study of Critical Infrastructure Replacement During the Holiday Season

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author made the internal report that the exhibit answers and is the addressee of the exhibit. This is disclosed at Appendix C.1 and should be read before the case study. The paper is constructed so that its conclusion rests only on propositions the subject organization has itself put in writing, precisely so that the author's interest cannot carry any part of the argument.
declarations.funderStatement: None. This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: In IT Service Management (ITSM) and Site Reliability Engineering (SRE), imposing a change freeze — a production freeze — across a major holiday period is a standard control for limiting the risk of prolonged outage and elevated Mean Time To Recovery (MTTR) at precisely the time of year when the engineering, vendor and escalation resources on which recovery depends are least available. This paper presents a case study of an anti-pattern in enterprise IT operations, in which a data centre equipment replacement and the associated network migration were planned, approved and executed at the boundary of a large organization's year-end closure. The event — a remote-access (VPN) outage observed from around 11:00 on Saturday, 27 December 2025, followed by a completion report posted on the corporate intranet at 16:24 the same day, hours before a multi-day shutdown — is documented here not by the author's account of it but by the organization's own written finding, issued by its corporate ethics committee on 2 September 2026 in answer to a report made through its ethics helpline. That finding establishes the fact on which this paper turns: the change was not an unforeseen failure but a scheduled activity, approved months in advance at a management-level business promotion meeting and announced to staff beforehand. We argue that this exculpatory account is itself the finding. An organization that offers advance notice and managerial approval as the justification for executing an irreversible infrastructure change immediately before its lowest-staffing period has disclosed, in its own words, that its change-approval process does not test the recoverability of the change it approves. Three anti-patterns are derived from the record — the absence of a rollback-feasibility assessment, the substitution of notification for risk control, and the hollowing-out of change authorization into scheduling — and a set of testable controls is proposed by which an auditor, a customer or a regulator may distinguish a change process that evaluates risk from one that merely announces it. The finding is stated as what the organization identified as its complete justification after an internal investigation; it is not a claim that no recoverability assessment exists anywhere in its change records, and that limit is stated at Appendix C.2.

title: Generative Engine Optimization in AI Search: Recommendation and Governance
affiliations: Tianjin University, Tianjin University, Tianjin University and Tianjin University

detail.title: Generative Engine Optimization in AI Search: Recommendation and Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by research grants from the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 72471167, No. 72471164).

detail.abstract: Generative engines based on artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping product search by replacing ranked lists of links with direct product recommendations. This transformation incentivizes sellers to optimize their published content to improve recommendation visibility, a practice known as generative engine optimization (GEO). We develop a gametheoretical model to study the strategic interaction between sellers' content optimization decisions and the AI platform's recommendation policy, and examine the resulting welfare and governance implications. We find that, in equilibrium, the platform optimally underweights seller-provided content in response to sellers' content optimization. The equilibrium reliance weight decreases with AI retrieval variance, market size, and the dispersion of sellers' capability in content optimization, making seller content less informative about true product quality. GEO also creates a prisoner's dilemma among sellers: although each seller has an incentive to manipulate, only high-capability sellers obtain a positive payoff from GEO, while sellers' aggregate payoff is strictly lower. Notably, higher AI retrieval precision does not necessarily improve social welfare because it can intensify competition in content optimization among sellers. We further examine the governance tools in practice and show that governance tools should be evaluated by their equilibrium effects, as they affect both sellers' manipulation and the platform's recommendation policy. Our findings provide implications for the design and governance of AI search.

title: Geospatial Sovereignty and National Security in Nigeria, towards a Regulatory Framework for Commercial Satellite-derived Intelligence
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Geospatial Sovereignty and National Security in Nigeria, towards a Regulatory Framework for Commercial Satellite-derived Intelligence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is a Principal Legal Officer at the National Space Research and Development Agency (NASRDA). The views expressed in this paper are the author's own and do not necessarily reflect the official position of NASRDA. The author declares no financial or competing interest in relation to this research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
The rapid commercialisation of Earth observation has transformed satellite imagery from a predominantly state-controlled technological resource into an increasingly accessible source of economic, environmental and strategic intelligence. High-resolution imagery and satellite-derived analytics support agriculture, disaster management, urban planning, environmental protection and infrastructure development. The same capabilities may reveal military installations, critical infrastructure, border activity, energy facilities and other information of national-security significance. This presents a particular challenge for states such as Nigeria: territorial sovereignty does not confer sovereignty over outer space or a general right to prevent foreign satellites from observing national territory, yet states retain legitimate interests in protecting security-sensitive information concerning their territories.

This article develops geospatial sovereignty as a framework for addressing this regulatory gap. It defines geospatial sovereignty not as state ownership of satellite observations or an extension of territorial sovereignty into outer space, but as the capacity of a state, consistent with international law, to establish and enforce legal, institutional and technical rules governing access to, processing, dissemination and security-sensitive use of geospatial information concerning its territory, population, infrastructure and strategic interests. Building on scholarship concerning spatial and geospatial data sovereignty, and using Nigeria as its principal case study, the article examines the national-security implications of commercial satellite-derived intelligence, evaluates Nigeria's existing legal and institutional architecture, and draws lessons from the United States, France and India. It proposes a risk-based Nigerian framework combining differentiated regulation, jurisdictional discipline, targeted security controls, inter-agency coordination and safeguards for legitimate scientific and commercial uses.

title: Guards That Add Guards: Automated Oversight in Multi-Agent AI. A Field Record, Public Incidents, and a 144-Run Randomized Test

detail.title: Guards That Add Guards: Automated Oversight in Multi-Agent AI. A Field Record, Public Incidents, and a 144-Run Randomized Test

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I built and operated the multi-agent systems whose logs are the evidence of Section 1, and I wrote the read-only module described in Section 2. I am a named applicant on pending patent applications, not granted patents, covering the automation of putting one question to several models and collecting the answers. They do not cover the oversight components this paper studies. Every step of the field record and of the randomized test is reproducible by hand with any models. No other personal or financial relationship influenced this study.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding supported this work.

detail.abstract: In 172 dated log entries from multi-agent AI systems I built and operated in 2026, automated oversight failed in three ways, each seen in different components at different times. Some critics and gates extended their notion of harm past the mission they were given. Some obstructed or destroyed the work they existed to protect: one gate rejected every candidate for two weeks while at least twelve planning documents diagnosed the symptom and none named the gate. And some failed guards were answered with another guard of the same kind, with nothing retired from inside the loop. In a 144-run randomized test costing $3.47, where one sentence of the prompt offered both moves, critics asked to add a control 68 times and to remove one once, a prompt-shaped count and not a field rate. In the same test, enforcing a round budget cut the critics' refuted objections and cost 0.11 missed defects per run (p = 0.07, all of it on one defect); requiring outside authorization for new controls showed no measured cost in defects, which is not proof of none; and a mandatory negative control did not reduce later reversals of claimed successes, and refused ten that were correct work. My own read-only detection module, ported into a live pipeline, reported nothing on three real runs and was removed by a criterion written down before it ran, while a person reading those runs found five oversight failures. All three patterns are already in Robert Sheckley's 1953 story "Watchbird", the source of the companion paper's term AI-Watchbird.

title: Predicting Audience Time on Screen for In-Feed Video Advertisements from the Video File: Content Adds to Duration and Generalises to Unseen Advertisers

detail.title: Predicting Audience Time on Screen for In-Feed Video Advertisements from the Video File: Content Adds to Duration and Generalises to Unseen Advertisers

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific funding.

detail.abstract: We ask whether the video file alone predicts how long an in-feed advertisement remains on screen for its audience, for unseen advertisers. In a controlled panel, 679 professionals scrolled a LinkedIn-style feed with video advertisements from 47 companies. For 96 advertisements (6,474 analysed exposures) we aggregated per-viewer on-screen duration into five ad-level outcomes and predicted them from video length plus a frozen vision-language frame embedding, using ridge regression tuned within company-grouped folds. Length + content predicted the share of viewers remaining for at least half the video at Spearman ρ = 0.84 (95% company-cluster CI [0.71, 0.91]). Content improved ranking over each of three duration baselines (linear, spline, gradient-boosted) for every outcome under grouped and leave-onecompany-out evaluation (∆ρ against the strongest ranking baseline +0.11 to +0.22, all CIs above zero), and against the MSE-selected baseline on fold-internally viewer-centred outcomes for four of five. The gain in absolute error was modest and, for the headline outcome, not established (∆R 2 = +0.02 [-0.03, +0.07]). First-3-s features were equivalent to wholevideo features (±0.10 margin) for three on-screen outcomes, not for sound activation, and worse for brand recall. Time on screen is exposure opportunity, not verified attention, and the sample is one study; still, aggregate dwell appears predictable from creative content beyond duration.

title: Demography is Destiny? University Finances and the Enrollment Cliff
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University - Department of Finance, Pennsylvania State University - Department of Finance, Pennsylvania State University - Department of Finance and

detail.title: Demography is Destiny? University Finances and the Enrollment Cliff

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: We test whether asset markets price demographic change once it becomes foreseeable, and how the organizations exposed to it adapt in the long interval before it arrives. The sharp, largely unanticipated fall in U.S. births after 2007 fixed the size of the college-age cohort of the late 2020s more than a decade in advance, and universities issue bonds whose revenues depend on that cohort. In the regions where births fell most, spreads on university bonds widened during the 2009 to 2011 crisis, and the widening occurs amongst the bonds that mature after the cohort arrives. It then reverses: by 2020 and after, bonds of exposed universities trade 9 to 15 basis points below those of controls. Over the same years, exposed institutions lose 400 to 500 students relative to controls and their revenue falls relative to assets. They cut expenses by a comparable amount, which keeps their operating surplus intact, and they build reserves. This adaptation is concentrated where the birth decline is structural; where births fell back from a housing-boom peak, institutions lose more students and consolidate. The late discount follows realized enrollment and reserve growth, so the market re-rates exposed institutions as their fundamentals resolve. Overall, we show that markets price a demographic shift once it becomes foreseeable and provide detailed evidence on margins of adjustment at the organization level.

detail.abstract: Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA) has become a cybersecurity paradigm that has shifted to a culture of never trusting, always verifying users, devices, applications and network interactions. This is making it more relevant for small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs), which are often lacking cybersecurity staff, budget, cloud-based services, working remotely, third-party software and hardware, and a diverse computing environment. These features make it easier for cyber threats to target these systems, and highlight the shortcomings of perimeter-based security systems which rely on having secure environments inside the system (Kindervag, 2010; Rose et al., 2020; He et al., 2022). The vast amount of research and industry focus on ZTA has had a significant impact, yet the majority of current approaches to implementing ZTA focus on large enterprises that have advanced infrastructure, security teams and budgets. This means SMBs need an adaptable architecture that will not only be effective in securing the company, but also won't cost them a fortune, be overly complicated to operate, be prohibited from being scaled up, or require advanced technical expertise (Yeoh et al., 2023; Meirelles et al., 2025; Papathanasiou et al., 2025). Through a design oriented and analytical approach, this study combines literature on Zero Trust, on cybersecurity governance, access control, cloud security, artificial intelligence and organizational complexity in order to create a Zero Trust framework adapted to the needs of SMBs (Rose et al., 2020; Yassine et al., 2021; Kang et al., 2023). The suggested architecture includes a range of security features, including identity verification, device trust evaluation, least-privilege access, continuous monitoring, network segmentation, behavioral analytics, AI-driven threat detection, policy enforcement, and governance measures. The findings suggest that the implementation of ZTA can enhance the cybersecurity of SMBs without sacrificing the feasibility of the implementation while prioritizing the security controls based on organizational risk and implementing them gradually. An enterprise-scale transformation isn't necessary to get started with Zero Trust, and with an enterprise-grade solution, it also could be a viable option for SMBs to achieve resilient, scalable and continually monitored cybersecurity without expensive transformation.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how "social terrain" shapes cascading changes in territorial control during insurgent conflicts, with a focus on civilian social networks as a key factor driving conflict diffusion. Using large-scale data from the Philippines-including village-level military intelligence reports on insurgent presence, government development projects, and the network of family ties between 55 million individuals in 40,000 villages-I find that the government was more likely to secure new territory when civilians had social ties to other villages already under government control and benefitting from development projects. Drawing on field interviews, I propose that these networks primarily drive the diffusion of territorial control by serving as conduits for information about security and economic interests, which in turn shapes patterns of civilian cooperation with conflict actors. These findings underscore the importance of civilian social networks in shaping territorial control in civil conflicts.

detail.abstract: We study dynamic mechanism design in expert relationships, such as those arising in healthcare, legal services, consulting, and asset management. An expert privately observes progress in resolving a client's problem. The client pays a fixed price per unit of time for each intervention, and the expert bears the associated cost, so highand low-intensity services generate different flow profits. High intensity yields the higher flow profit, whereas low intensity can generate greater total profit by slowing resolution and prolonging the engagement. High intensity is efficient during crisis, while low intensity is efficient after containment. The expert may therefore conceal containment to preserve high-intensity work or falsely claim containment to obtain a slower, longer engagement. Under intensity rent seeking, the optimal mechanism ignores reporting and conditions interventions on elapsed time only. Under duration rent seeking, the mechanism rewards a report with low intensity but later returns to high intensity if resolution does not occur, placing the screening distortion at dates a false reporter would be relatively more likely to reach without resolution. Underand over-intervention can therefore arise on the equilibrium path as tools for eliciting information, even though interventions are observable and the expert reports truthfully.

detail.abstract: We study the stability of cancel-on-completion redundancy systems under Random-Order-of-Service (ROS), where each idle server selects uniformly among its compatible jobs. We prove that the strict Hall inequalities imply positive Harris recurrence on any fixed compatibility graph with independent classwise Poisson arrivals and heterogeneous server speeds. Service vectors are independent across jobs; within a job, copy requirements may be arbitrarily correlated, with positive unit-mean marginals that vary across compatible class-server pairs. No higher-moment assumptions are imposed. This establishes the conjectured sufficiency for correlated exponential copies and extends it to general service distributions. The proof controls duplicate work, establishes a cumulative weighted comparison between server capacity and system-wide first starts of distinct jobs, and uses this comparison in a fluid-Lyapunov argument. We also obtain an affine bound on the expected time to empty in terms of the initial job count and recorded residual work.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how forward guidance affects bank credit supply. Using high-frequency identification around FOMC announcements and local projections on U.S. bank-level data, I find a pronounced asymmetry: contractionary forward guidance triggers an immediate and persistent decline in lending, while expansionary guidance produces weak and delayed loan growth. The mechanism operates through bank balance sheets: tightening shocks reduce equity and raise leverage, pushing banks toward binding capital constraints and forcing credit contraction. A quantitative model with bank constraints matches these dynamics and implies limited stimulus from easing guidance.

detail.abstract: We study a matching mechanism for markets in which agents and objects are described by features rather than complete rankings. Agents report weights over a small number of features, objects have feature vectors, and a single spectral projection (the leading singular vector of the object-feature matrix) reduces the problem to a one-dimensional sort, computable in 𝑂 (𝑁 log 𝑁) time. We provide a gauge-fixed version of this mechanism that provably computes the exact Nash Social Welfare-maximizing allocation within the projected space, together with an unconditional utilitarianwelfare guaranty and a conditional multiplicative Nash Social Welfare (NSW) guaranty. We further prove a matching necessity result showing that no deterministic mechanism can guarantee positive NSW once the assumption fails. We also develop two cheap, checkable diagnostics at the market level and, separately, at the level of a specific allocation round, that predict, before any outcome is observed, whether the guarantee can be trusted. We characterize the mechanism's incentive properties: it is stable against exogenous reporting noise, but it is not strategy-proof, and we give an explicit profitable misreport. Finally, we evaluate the mechanism on a new application, agentic AI shopping, in which LLM-driven shopping agents report feature preferences on behalf of users and compete for scarce inventory. The experiment reproduces both a success and an undesigned failure of the conditional guarantee. In both cases, our diagnostics correctly anticipate the outcome in advance, and a blind search independently rediscovers a profitable misreport for the disadvantaged agent, confirming the manipulability result on realistic data.

detail.abstract: A U.S. blocker corporation may look almost uneventful on paper. It may have few employees, no meaningful operating business of its own, and a balance sheet dominated by a partnership investment on one side and a related-party loan on the other. Yet that seemingly simple arrangement can force a tax practitioner through several distinct bodies of law before state apportionment should even enter the conversation. The first question is not how much interest is deductible. It is whether the advance is debt at all. If the instrument survives that inquiry, the analysis moves to arm's-length pricing under section 482, timing under section 267(a)(3), hybrid mismatch rules under section 267A, the federal business-interest limitation under section 163(j), and the treatment of payments to the foreign recipient. Only then does the analysis move to state conformity, related-party adjustments, partnership income, unitary principles, and apportionment. This sequencing matters because the state result can diverge materially from the federal result. California now provides a particularly useful example. Although federal section 163(j) was materially amended in 2025, California corporation tax law expressly states that section 163(j) does not apply. At the same time, California retains its own rules governing interest, water's-edge reporting, partnership income, and unitary and nonunitary partner-partnership relationships. (IRS) The thesis of this article is therefore simple: A related-party interest deduction should not be analyzed from the deduction backward. It should be analyzed from the capital forward. That approach is especially important when foreign financing, blocker entities, partnership investments, and state apportionment coexist in the same structure.

detail.abstract: Problem definition: Seaports are the gateways of global supply chains and their physical infrastructure determines how much cargo the global trading system can move. Yet empirical research on port operations is constrained by the absence of granular data on this physical infrastructure. Existing public measures of port infrastructure either provide a composite index (that bundles port infrastructure, connectivity, and efficiency), or provide a static snapshot of port characteristics at a single location. They do not quantify the operational inputs that determine port capacity, or track how those inputs change over time. Methodology/results: We introduce a global, quarterly panel of physical seaport infrastructure constructed algorithmically from high-resolution satellite imagery. Because public data usually do not contain port boundaries, we first delineate an operational boundary for 1,554 seaports worldwide, which serves as our sampling frame. We then acquire quarterly high-resolution satellite imagery for this sampling frame with a ground sampling distance of approximately 3 meters, and use computer vision models to quantify changes four classes of infrastructure over time: cranes, berths, container storage areas, and oil tanks. Managerial implications: The data provide an empirical counterpart to models of port capacity and investment. They can be linked to vessel movements, bill-of-lading records, firm-to-firm networks, trade-policy data, and disruption records to study questions that are currently hard to answer: whether and how quickly port expansion affects firms' and carriers' sourcing and logistics decisions, how capacity changes and local disruptions propagate through maritime networks, and how infrastructure investment functions as an instrument of trade and industrial policy. The port boundary polygons are also a data product in their own right, providing a reusable spatial sampling frame for future satellite-, AIS-, weather-, emissions-, or land-use-based measurements of port activity. The panel creates a common measurement base for comparing port systems and developing new predictive and prescriptive methods for maritime supply chains. It allows earlier findings in economics and operations management that relied on incomplete and potentially biased infrastructure data to be reexamined .

detail.abstract: This book develops the LM Gap, a standardized measure of the divergence between market-priced monetary policy expectations and realized central bank policy rates, applied across six Asian markets (China, Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Japan, and South Korea) over 2010–2025. Originally conceived as a two-component composite index modeled on the author's Macroeconomic Say-Do Gap Index (MSDGI), both original component definitions proved unmeasurable in practice: an "announced" policy rate is identical to the realized rate by construction, and no central bank in the panel currently publishes an explicit monetary-aggregate target. The book documents this methodological correction transparently, redefining the rate channel as a genuine market-expectation gap — the 3-month interbank rate priced against the policy rate realized one quarter later — and moving liquidity and forward guidance to qualitative case studies: Japan's decade-long yield curve control commitment (2016–2024) and South Korea's evolving forward guidance under inflation targeting, including a 2026 episode in which an oil shock tested a specific rate commitment in real time. Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand are excluded from the quantitative panel for reasons documented in full — Singapore for a structural reason (its monetary framework operates through the exchange rate rather than a policy rate), Malaysia and Thailand for data-access reasons. All data are drawn from bulk public sources (BIS, IMF, FRED, and national central banks), with full data provenance documented in Chapter 3, and implications for investors, regulators, and central banks discussed in Chapter 7.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming more and more widely used in healthcare, finance, the legal sector, public services, autonomous systems, and other areas where mistakes or poorly understood recommendations can have consequences that go beyond simple prediction errors. In these kinds of situations, accuracy alone is not enough to judge whether an AI system can be regarded as trustworthy. The present article looks at the difficulties involved in creating trustworthy AI by carrying out a thorough and critical review of the existing scholarly work on explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), interpretability, fairness, robustness, human AI collaboration, accountability, and decision-making in high-stakes contexts. The research shows that XAI can increase transparency, help humans to understand how things work, and enable proper oversight of decisions made with the aid of AI. Yet explanations by themselves do not ensure that the system is trustworthy, since after-the-fact explanations can be incomplete, unstable, or even potentially misleading accounts of how the model behaves. The results thus show that trustworthy AI needs a multidimensional evaluation framework that goes beyond predictive performance. This kind of framework should take into account accuracy, the quality of the explanations, fairness, robustness, accountability, and effective human oversight as interconnected aspects of the system's trustworthiness. The article concludes that in order to use AI responsibly in high-stakes settings it is necessary to give equal attention to technical performance, interpretability, ethical safeguards, and human governance so that the decisions supported by AI are not only accurate but also understandable, reliable, equitable, and properly accountable.

detail.abstract: Two decades after Qian Xuesen's famous question—"Why do our schools consistently fail to produce outstanding talent?"—China's structural shortage of top-tier R&D talent remains unresolved at the level of the system rather than of the individual. In July 2026, Hong Wang and Yu Deng, both members of the 2007 undergraduate cohort of Peking University, were awarded the Fields Medal, a historic first for Chinese nationals; yet the decisive phase of both laureates' intellectual formation unfolded within overseas research ecosystems, which turns Qian's question from an inquiry about quality into an inquiry about systems. Grounded in complex-systems science and Haken's synergetics, this paper reconstructs talent cultivation as an open complex system far from equilibrium and introduces a dynamical dichotomy between fast variables (examination skills) and slow variables (research capability, which constitute the order parameters of the system). Through a comparative case study of Zhiyu Liu—an International Mathematical Olympiad perfect-score gold medalist who subsequently left mathematics—and Hong Wang, the 2026 Fields Medalist who resolved the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture, together with talent-gap data from China's semiconductor and artificial-intelligence industries (a shortfall on the order of 300,000 in semiconductors and more than five million in artificial intelligence), we argue that exam-oriented education projects a high-dimensional cognitive system onto a low-dimensional linear exercise space, prematurely exhausting cognitive plasticity and dissipating the talent order parameter before the phase transition can occur. The emergence of R&D talent instead depends on the sustained accumulation of slow variables, the long-run openness of the cognitive system, and atypical interdisciplinary coupling. Four empirical research traditions—self-determination theory, flow theory, the age dynamics of scientific creativity, and the atypical-combinations literature—are marshalled as supporting evidence. We distill eight core order parameters of R&D talent, and we propose institutional pathways that reconstruct the constraint conditions of the education system so as to shift it from entropy increase lock-in to entropy-reduction emergence, thereby enabling the transition of talent cultivation from a "problem-solving execution" paradigm to a "paradigm-reconstruction" paradigm.

detail.abstract: Demand responsive transport (DRT) has spread widely across Japanese municipalities, but almost none of it is published as GTFS-Flex. This report describes the construction of GTFS-Flex feeds for two municipal DRT services on the same platform, Choisoko Fuso in Fuso Town and Choisoko Yatomi in Yatomi City, Aichi Prefecture, using only material the municipalities publish for their residents. The two municipalities publish their boarding points differently, and the feeds follow two routes. In Fuso Town, where the points appear only on a printed map, coordinates were recovered by georeferencing the map, checked against geocoded stop names, and completed by hand for four points. In Yatomi City, which publishes the points with coordinates, the stop files were produced by conversion alone. Both feeds share one structure, pass the Canonical GTFS Schedule Validator 8.0.1 with no errors, and are recognized as Fixed-Stops Demand Responsive Transit. Geocoding the stop names of both municipalities returned about two in five of them as a single point at the municipal office. A usable feed can thus be reconstructed from a map, but the effort and the reliability of the result depend on whether the municipality publishes coordinates.

detail.abstract:
Focused hospital units enjoy better performance than less focused units. However, few studies examine how
full-service hospitals absorb the variability in conditions that they treat. We address this gap by studying a
large hospital that cares for patients with a wide range of conditions. Prior to July 2018, the Dedicated Obser-
vation Unit (DOU) was a focused unit that treated only simple observation-status patients. Consequently,
complex observation-status patients were scattered throughout the hospital. This placement was suboptimal
because observation-status patients do not need inpatient-level care and their care is reimbursed at lower
outpatient rates. Post July 2018, the DOU switched to being a variability-absorbing unit that could treat
both simple and complex observation-status patients. To handle the increased patient volume and clinical
complexity, the DOU implemented a bundle of changes that increased inflow and capacity, developed coor-
dination with internal and external clinical collaborators, and created standardized pathways. Collectively,
we refer to this bundle as the Variability-Absorbing Bundle (VAB). Unsurprisingly, naive analysis compar-
ing pre-post length of stay (LOS) revealed that adding complex observation-status patients to the DOU
increased average LOS by 18.5%, implying worse DOU performance. This variability-absorbing performance
improvement might therefore be undervalued by hospital management because the benefits of increased focus
accrued to medical/surgical units, while the costs were borne by the DOU.To accurately assess the impact
of VAB, we conduct rigorous analysis using an instrumental variable approach to address endogeneity of
patient placement. We find that VAB results in a 7% shorter LOS for observation-status patients treated in
the DOU than those treated in medical/surgical units. Our study contributes to the healthcare operations
management literature by examining successful strategies for creating variability-absorbing clinical units.

detail.abstract: Land, in an agrarian and rapidly urbanising economy such as India, is not merely an economic asset but the primary source of livelihood, identity and social security for a vast section of the population. The power of the State to compulsorily acquire private land for a "public purpose"the doctrine of eminent domain-has therefore always sat in uneasy tension with the individual's right to property. This paper examines whether the present legal regime governing land acquisition in India, principally the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (RFCTLARR Act), succeeds in its avowed object of delivering "fair" compensation to persons displaced by acquisition. The study traces the historical journey of land acquisition law from the colonial Land Acquisition Act of 1894, through the constitutional transformation of the right to property from a fundamental wide-ranging statutory exemptions under the Fourth Schedule, chronic delays in disbursement, and uneven implementation across States dilute the protective intent of the legislation. The paper concludes with recommendations for strengthening valuation mechanisms, closing exemption loopholes, and ensuring time-bound, litigation-free payment of compensation.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how the composition and evolution of public debt relate to inflation dynamics in Sierra Leone, using annual data for 1980-2023 and a disaggregation of domestic and external debt from 2003 onward. Combining OLS and ARDL estimates with robustness checks and tests of predictive direction, it finds no robust long-run association between aggregate debt and inflation once monetary and external conditions are controlled for. Domestic debt, which is short-term, costly, and largely held by local banks, is positively associated with inflation over 2003-2023, particularly during the recent episode of inflation and financing stress, but robustness tests caution against reading this association as a stable long-run effect. Monetary conditions, reserve adequacy, and exchange rate pressures are more informative for inflation, and the predictive direction runs from inflation to subsequent domestic borrowing rather than the reverse. External debt, mostly concessional, shows no positive association with inflation and matters mainly through reserve and exchange rate pressures. The paper links these results to the Ebola, COVID-19, and 2023 episodes and draws implications for debt management, the monetary anchor, and central bank independence.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the institutional redesign proposed by the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong on 21 September 2026 for corporate spin-offs. The proposal would permit qualifying Main Board parents to self-assess compliance with Practice Note 15, shorten the post-listing moratorium from three years to one, remove the assured-entitlement requirement, and-through the accompanying reform of notifiable transactions-raise the shareholder-approval threshold for most major transactions from 25 to 50 percent. The paper develops an institutional-substitution framework in which ex ante permission, shareholder voice, and allocation entitlements are partly replaced by board certification, enhanced disclosure, continuing-listing safeguards, and ex post enforcement. Its central tension is that these mechanisms are complementary but not interchangeable: a faster process may improve organizational flexibility while simultaneously reducing independent review and direct minority participation. The historical record supports a proportionate review. The Exchange approved 123 spin-offs during 2021-2025; more than 60 percent involved an overseas listing, more than 80 percent of those overseas cases went to Mainland exchanges, and more than 60 percent of historical cases would have qualified for self-assessment. The paper therefore focuses on the boundary conditions of reform rather than assuming either deregulation or protectionism. It is a design and institutional-analysis paper rather than a completed causal estimate. It establishes a pre-analysis framework for historical counterfactual classification of Hong Kong spin-offs, threshold stress tests, an announcementdate exposure design, and a post-implementation research protocol. The accompanying registry distinguishes the official aggregate universe from a source-linked case subset and does not report a case-level qualification share before the denominator and threshold inputs are reconciled. The analysis contributes to the corporateseparation literature by examining a regulatory regime that frequently governs subsidiary IPOs and crossborder carve-outs rather than the pro rata distributions emphasized in conventional U.S. spin-off research. Because the consultation remains prospective, the paper does not claim causal effects of the proposed rules; it identifies testable predictions, measurement requirements, and the institutional conditions under which disclosure and board accountability could credibly substitute for prior approval and minority-shareholder participation.

detail.abstract: Credit union mergers and acquisitions can expand services, strengthen operating capacity, and support long-term resilience when their benefits are tested against member needs and institutional risk. This article distinguishes credit union mergers from purchase and assumption transactions and evaluates the potential gains in reach, technology, lending capacity, and financial resilience. It argues that loan-level portfolio due diligence, concentration analysis, governance, cultural integration, and reliable systems conversion are necessary to translate a transaction thesis into results. Drawing on regulatory guidance and practical transaction experience, the discussion presents a framework for linking preclosing findings to accountable postclosing action. The proposed test of success includes service continuity, prudent lending, financial strength, employee capability, and measurable member outcomes over time.

detail.abstract:
Background: Timely colonoscopy after a positive colorectal cancer (CRC) screening result is essential for maximizing the benefits of screening. However, uniform waiting-time targets may not account for heterogeneity in both vulnerability to delayed colonoscopy and underlying risk of advanced colorectal neoplasia (ACN) across individuals. We evaluated relative and absolute risks of ACN associated with time to colonoscopy to assess their potential implications for risk-adapted colonoscopy prioritization.

Methods: We conducted a population-based retrospective cohort study using data from a province-wide CRC screening program in China from 2020 through 2024. Participants with a positive fecal immunochemical test (FIT) or questionnaire-based risk assessment who underwent colonoscopy within 2 years were included. Multivariable logistic regression was used to estimate associations between time to colonoscopy and ACN detection, with interaction terms to assess effect modification. Absolute risks were estimated using marginal standardization. 

Findings: Among 437,489 participants, 63,849 (14.6%) had ACN, comprising 49,892 (11.4%) advanced adenomas, 9,140 (2.1%) advanced serrated lesions, and 4,817 (1.1%) CRCs. Longer time to colonoscopy was associated with progressively higher detection of advanced adenoma, advanced serrated lesion, and ACN (all P for trend <0.01), but not CRC (P for trend = 0.315). Compared with colonoscopy within 1 month, waiting 2–4 months was associated with 11%–15% higher odds of ACN detection. Relative associations were stronger among younger participants, women, never-drinkers, those without multimorbidity, and FIT-positive participants. In contrast, absolute ACN risks were higher among older participants, men, those with a family history of CRC, and FIT-positive participants.

Interpretation: The relative and absolute risks of ACN associated with longer colonoscopy waiting time varied substantially across subgroups. Integrating these complementary dimensions of risk may complement uniform waiting-time targets and help inform risk-adapted colonoscopy prioritization when endoscopic capacity is constrained.Funding: Noncommunicable Chronic Diseases-National Science and Technology Major Project, National Natural Science Foundation of China, Natural Science Foundation of Zhejiang Province, Science and Technology Program for Disease Prevention and Control of Zhejiang Province, Medical and Health Science and Technology Plan of Zhejiang Province, and Postdoctoral Science Foundation of Zhejiang Province.

detail.abstract: Since the path-breaking work of Imbens and Newey (2009), the quantile-based control function has become fundamental to identify nonseparable triangular models. However, its extension to nonscalar heterogeneity is still challenging, because it relies on the nested left-to-right ordering of the real line. To handle this case, I leverage the theory of center-outward monotone rearrangement of R d. I show that even if both the first-and second-stage have multidimensional disturbance, a center-outward distribution function can satisfy all the required conditions for identification, namely invertibility and quantile normalization. Instead of using a product of half-open rectangles which is not nested in general, this approach define the unobserved heterogeneity as a random vector U = τ ϕ, where τ ∈ [0, 1] is a radial norm and ϕ taking values on the hypersphere S d-1. This ensures uniqueness via nested contours of multivariate center-outward quantiles. On the other hand, as the scalar ranking τ ∈ [0, 1] is preserved irrespective of the dimension of U , we can define a structural multivariate quantile treatment effect.

detail.abstract: Public transport stops shape the daily travel experience, yet their quality is often overlooked in hot-arid cities where heat exposure affects comfort and safety. This study examines how bus stop quality influences perceived thermal comfort, safety, accessibility, commute satisfaction, and mobility-related quality of life in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. A mixed-methods design combined audits of 120 bus stops, microclimate measurements at 30 stops, and intercept surveys with 600 riders. Regression results show that the Bus Stop Quality Index (BSQI) significantly predicts perceived thermal comfort, safety, and accessibility (p < 0.001). These perceptions positively influence commute satisfaction, which in turn predicts mobility-related quality of life (MR-QoL). Bootstrapped mediation confirms indirect pathways linking stop quality to satisfaction through perceived experience variables. Effects are stronger for frequent riders and users with mobility constraints. The findings highlight the importance of climate-responsive stop design and targeted upgrades to support equitable public transport use in hot-arid cities.

detail.abstract: This article examines the balance that Directive (EU) 2026/470 (“Omnibus I Directive”) strikes between sustainability, simplification and harmonization. It analyzes the Directive’s amendments to the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CS3D) against the simplification agenda developed in the Letta and Draghi Reports and in the Commission’s Competitiveness Compass. The article distinguishes genuine simplification of regulatory requirements from the contraction of their scope. Under the CSRD, several amendments reduce unnecessary complexity, but the substantial narrowing of mandatory reporting weakens the availability, comparability and assured quality of the company-level information on which the wider sustainable finance framework depends. The CS3D presents a more mixed picture: the revised due diligence process is more practicable, while higher thresholds, the repeal of the transition-plan obligation, and the removal of uniform civil liability conditions entail a more substantial retrenchment. The Directive also adopts a selective approach to harmonization, strengthening it for the core due diligence obligations while returning other matters to national law. The article traces these choices to a structural constraint: because maximum harmonization requires a degree of precision that itself generates compliance costs, simplification and harmonization have in significant part been reconciled by narrowing the class of undertakings subject to the regime rather than by calibrating the obligations imposed within it. The resulting trilemma between sustainability, simplification and harmonization would be more satisfactorily addressed through a more differentiated application of proportionality.

title: Constructing Behavioural Dynamic Discounting (BDD) and Systematic Risk Adjusted Inaccuracy (SRAI) as Ex-Ante and Ex-Post Complementary Extensions of The Hedonic Pricing Model

detail.title: Constructing Behavioural Dynamic Discounting (BDD) and Systematic Risk Adjusted Inaccuracy (SRAI) as Ex-Ante and Ex-Post Complementary Extensions of The Hedonic Pricing Model

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: Self funded

detail.abstract:
Purpose – The first purpose of this paper is to present a theoretically-derived and empirically justified behavioural dynamic discounting (BDD) technique for estimating transaction-price proxy, as an ex-ante prerequisite for implementing Hedonic Pricing Model in opaque markets. The second purpose is to present a systematic-risk-adjusted inaccuracy (SRAI) as a calibrated indicator of valuation inaccuracy in the Hedonic Pricing Model. Design/methodology/approach – The behavioural dynamic discounting (BDD) incorporates the coefficient of variation as a measure of price dispersion, a seller urgency index, and a listing-price correction rate. These components represent the collective behavioural characteristics of a sub-market and allow the discount rate to vary across spatially defined urban segments. The resulting transaction-price proxy is then used as the dependent variable in the HPM. The validity of the BDD technique is assessed by comparing its performance with alternative fixed and generic area-specific discount-rate specifications. Once the Hedonic Pricing Model is finalised, a normality test is conducted on the residuals followed by a Monte Carlo Simulation using truncated random residuals. The generated residuals are then combined with the predicted response to produce the simulated response. The relative difference between the transaction-price proxy (TPP), treated as the actual response, and the simulated response is defined as valuation inaccuracy and expressed as a percentage. The systematic component (β) is estimated by regressing the actual response against the simulated response. β is then converted into a systematic-risk adjustment factor (SRAF) to accommodate both β < 1 and β > 1. Multiplying the SRAF by relative valuation inaccuracy produces the systematic-risk adjusted inaccuracy (SRAI). 
Findings – The output of the behavioural dynamic discounting technique is broadly consistent with international empirical evidence on the spread between listing price and selling price, with the estimated discount exhibiting a median of approximately 16% and a standard deviation of approximately 7% in the study area. When applied in the hedonic regression, the BDD technique increases 𝑅2 from 84% to 86% compared with the fixed-rate discount specification and reveals statistically significant relationships for predictors that remain undetected under the fixed-rate approach. The resulting SRAI provides a systematic-risk-adjusted measure of valuation inaccuracy that can be expressed as a collateral haircut. 
Originality/value – The first contribution of this research is the empirically validated behavioural dynamic discounting model, which integrates price-correction behaviour, price dispersion, seller urgency, and sub-market characteristics, to estimate the transaction-price proxy. The second contribution is the development of a systematic-risk adjustment factor (SRAF) and systematic-risk-adjusted inaccuracy (SRAI) for calibrating valuation inaccuracy. Furthermore, by incorporating two underexplored dimensions (the behavioural basis of  property valuation and the explicit treatment of sub-markets within the hedonic pricing framework) the research extends the application of HPM in opaque, information-asymmetric markets. 
Practical implications – The discounting technique presented in this paper is directly relevant to residential-property valuation in opaque, emerging markets by providing a dynamic approach to deriving a transaction-price proxy. The resulting risk-adjusted valuation inaccuracy provides an empirical basis for collateral-related risk mitigation, including the determination of risk-derived haircuts. 
Research limitations – This paper does not present the methodology and results of Hedonic Pricing Model in detail in order to maintain the focus on the construction and validation of the proposed ex-ante and ex-post extensions to the HPM.
