detail.abstract: The greatest threat to innovation in a scaling startup is not failure; it is the organizational weight of its own success. Although decades of research explain why startups fail, few studies examine why well-funded, talent-rich, and operationally mature ones struggle to achieve breakthrough outcomes. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has further shortened the window between breakthrough and commoditization, making sustained innovation a baseline organizational requirement. This study investigated how executives at unicorn-level software companies maintain that capacity during high-growth scaling, drawing on Bandura's (1986) social cognitive theory (SCT) across three domains: how executives develop individual capabilities, shape the collaborative behaviors that produce new products, and design environments that protect innovation from operational pressure. Ten semi-structured interviews were conducted with C-suite and vice-president-level executives at companies exceeding US$100M in annual recurring revenue or billion-dollar valuations. Using SCT-anchored thematic analysis, findings indicated that executives cultivated curiosity, resilience, and purpose as trainable capabilities; designed collaboration through small accountable teams, constructive conflict, and rapid learning rhythms; and protected innovation through leadership air cover, disciplined scope constraint, and structural separation of exploratory from operational work. Sustained innovation was associated with the intentional alignment of person, behavior, and environment. This study contributes a bounded extension of SCT, positioning triadic reciprocal determinism as an analytical lens for executive decision-making in innovation-supporting systems. Innovation loss in scaling startups is not a talent problem or a market problem; it is a leadership architecture problem, and this study demonstrates the conditions under which it is solvable.

detail.abstract: This article examines whether a retail proprietary or "prop" trading framework can create positive expected economic value for a trading strategy with little or no directional edge. Using 10,000 randomized long/short paths applied to approximately 10 years of 1-minute Nasdaq futures data, the study tests a fixed-size strategy that enters once daily at 10:00 a.m. ET, trades eight Micro E-mini Nasdaq-100 contracts, and uses symmetric 100-tick take-profit and stop-loss barriers. The strategy produced a 49.98% TP/SL win rate and approximately break-even gross performance before transaction costs. Its fixed position size also limits daily profit and loss to $400, rendering several prop firm rules inconsequential. When the same trading paths were evaluated under the modeled Topstep $50,000 account framework, mean trader payouts were $9,368.50 against mean account costs of $7,878.30, producing mean net economic P&L of $1,490.19 per account. However, 39.70% of full-sample simulations lost money, and results varied materially between the two five-year subperiods. The findings establish that retail prop firm premiums can be underpriced for certain strategies: a fixed-size strategy with no directional edge achieved positive expected economic value when the same strategy was simulated through a prop firm's framework.

title: A Common Rough Latent State in Conditional Factor Pricing: Rethinking the Fama-French Five-Factor Model

detail.title: A Common Rough Latent State in Conditional Factor Pricing: Rethinking the Fama-French Five-Factor Model

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a conditional interpretation of the Fama-French five-factor model in which the observed factors remain unchanged, while a single latent investment-opportunity state jointly governs conditional factor premia, covariance prices of factor risk, asset exposures, and the factor covariance matrix. The latent state is a standardized stationary tempered-Volterra Gaussian process with local roughness parameter H ∈ (0, 1/2] and tempering parameter κ > 0. Roughness therefore enters through predictable coefficients rather than through a fractional disturbance to traded gains, preserving the continuous-semimartingale structure used by standard no-arbitrage arguments. The central result is a common-roughness theorem: every nondegenerate C 2 pricing map generated by the same state inherits the same local second-order exponent H. Hence the model imposes the falsifiable restriction H µ = H λ = H B = H Σ = H on state-sensitive channels. We derive no-arbitrage and spanning conditions, an exact decomposition of unconditional static alpha, a distinction between unconditional and conditional HML mean redundancy, and a sequential populationidentification result. A mixed-frequency empirical diagnostic uses daily information for the state, covariance, leverage, and conditional exposures, and monthly information for factor premia and pricing moments. With Kenneth French U.S. data from July 1963 through December 2025, a one-pass 500-particle pilot places the structural roughness estimate at the numerical Markov boundary, ˆ︁ H = 0.5000, with ˆ︁ κ = 1.1363. A separate 49-replication finite-sample diagnostic shows that low proxy-based Hurst estimates can arise under a Markov null; its common-state and common-exponent statistics are reported only as pilot exceedance frequencies, not as confirmatory tests. The monthly in-sample pricing diagnostic attains the minimum possible corrected 49-draw bootstrap exceedance frequency, 0.02, and does not improve the static-FF5 alpha RMSE. These empirical results therefore do not validate the strong common-rough-state interpretation; they identify the numerical and identification issues that a confirmatory implementation must resolve. A fully real-time out-of-sample economic-value protocol is specified but is not treated as an empirical result of the pilot.

detail.abstract: It is well known that candidates may have to stake out more partisan positions to win their primaries, which then also influence their competitiveness in the general election. The equilibrium consequences of primaries are less well understood. There is a robust externality-the primary trap-that can sustain multiple equilibria along a band. It is not necessarily exogenous electorate parameters that determine candidates' optimal positioning but the endogenous positioning of other candidates. Candidate extremism (moderation) on one side facilitates candidate extremism (moderation) on the other. The paper also discusses how other considerations can alter the set of equilibria.

detail.abstract: Innovation and entrepreneurship require consequential decisions before complete information is available. Yet innovators in technology commercialization, venture creation, organizational problem solving and opportunity exploitation often struggle not because they lack methods, but because they do not know what question matters next, what evidence would meaningfully address it, or what that evidence justifies doing. This paper develops Innovation Cartography as a practice-grounded, evidencebased framework for navigating uncertain innovation journeys toward adoption. Inspired by Stage-Gate and extended through repeated practice, the framework combines process discipline, divergence and convergence, entrepreneurial experimentation, behavioural adoption and staged commitment within a visible decision process. Three common entry conditions encountered to date-problem-led, technologyled and concept/opportunity-led-begin with different consequential uncertainties but converge on a First Potential User and a user-specific pathway toward adoption. Journeys generate evidence; stations challenge assumptions, evidence and interpretation; tickets record what is justified and specify the question, assumptions and evidence requirements for the next journey. The process simultaneously helps participants learn how innovation decisions are structured, improves the current project by directing attention toward consequential evidence, and creates repeated opportunities to practise the judgement required for future uncertain journeys. Developed iteratively through research, commercialization practice, teaching and repeated deployment, Innovation Cartography is presented not as a finished prescription but as an extensible framework whose maps, stations and routes can be challenged, adapted and improved through use.

detail.abstract: Long-maturity Treasury issuance reduces government rollover risk but depends on investors with structural demand for duration. We examine whether U.S. public pension funds, a $7 trillion sector, provide such demand, as is often presumed given their liabilities. Using security-level holdings, we show that Treasuries account for only 6% of pension assets and that total Treasury exposure, including derivatives, has a maturity of 8.0 years, only 1.3 years longer than marketable Treasury debt. Pension liability structure has little explanatory power for allocations or maturity choices. Overall, U.S. public pension funds provide limited structural demand for long-maturity Treasury exposure, suggesting that long-term liabilities alone are insufficient to generate substantial demand.

detail.abstract: This paper describes Norway data-center records in a Q1 2026 sample of S&P Global 451 Research's Datacenter KnowledgeBase. The sample contains 43 records and 20 providers, all assigned to the vendor's Oslo market, and is not a national census. Of these records, 31 are operational, seven are planned, one is under construction, and four are not operational. Operational net installed IT capacity totals 109.96 MW after adjustments for documented provider overlaps, compared with 117.11 MW before those adjustments. Green Mountain and Stack account for 55.87% of sampled net capacity. Reported allocated power represents 90.64% of net capacity; this measures commercial allocation rather than actual electricity consumption. Operational records have a median reported power usage effectiveness of 1.20, although inconsistencies between reported efficiency and power fields limit interpretation. Seven prospective records report next-phase expansion totaling 141.01 MW. The paper documents the distinction between provider records and physical facilities, capacity and consumption, and prospective and operating infrastructure. These distinctions support more transparent descriptions of digital infrastructure while identifying the additional data required to evaluate its economic and environmental effects.

detail.abstract: This article studies how local journalism worked during a prolonged public information crisis in Mykolaiv, Ukraine. It follows the city's media from the first months of Russia's full-scale invasion through 10 September 2026. The analysis focuses on four linked problems: the loss of editorial capacity in 2022, the long disruption of drinking water, the return of scrutiny over municipal decisions, and disputes about journalists' access to officials and records. The study draws on dated reports by Mykolaiv newsrooms, the public broadcaster, and the Institute of Mass Information, together with national audience research. It uses documentary process tracing rather than interviews or a representative sample of news content. The evidence shows that local outlets carried practical information about water and safety while their own staff and premises were under pressure. They also questioned decisions about water infrastructure, school shelters, and public spending. Direct social media communication by officials could deliver fast updates, but it did not supply the questioning and verification that reporting provides. Editorial continuity required shared production, local contacts, safe access, and financial support. The article treats community resilience as a limited analytical claim: verified information can help residents make decisions and contest public choices, but the sources do not measure how many people benefited or establish a causal effect on survival or recovery.

title: Does a Statutory Trust Travel? Sterling Stablecoins, Safeguarding and the Conflict of Laws

detail.title: Does a Statutory Trust Travel? Sterling Stablecoins, Safeguarding and the Conflict of Laws

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
In June 2026 the Bank of England published a draft Code of Practice for sterling-denominated systemic stablecoin issuers. The Code protects coinholders by imposing two statutory trusts over the backing assets and the reserves. The protection works in English law. It stops at the border, and the Code could have carried it further.

The trusts arise by operation of the Code. No settlor declares them and no instrument creates them. Article 3 of the Hague Convention of 1 July 1985 applies the Convention only to trusts created voluntarily and evidenced in writing. Section 1(2) of the Recognition of Trusts Act 1987 extends the Convention’s provisions, as a matter of United Kingdom law, to trusts arising under the law of any part of the United Kingdom, which tells courts here what to recognise and tells courts elsewhere nothing. The trusts are recognised in the legal order that made them and fall outside the Convention in every other.

Across thirty-eight pages the Code refers to applicable law once, in a template acknowledgement letter between issuer and custodian to which coinholders are not parties. The letter has the issuer declare that it holds the assets “as trustee under the laws applicable to us”, a formula that supplies no connecting factor. The coinholder’s own claim fares no better: the Code requires the issuer to ensure that the redemption right is “effectively transferred in law” to every subsequent holder, wherever that holder sits, and never says under which law effectiveness is judged.

Two further provisions repeat the pattern. A custodian must hold assets “in the UK”, a location the Code leaves undefined for an intangible and says nothing about further down a custody chain. And repurchase transactions may move backing assets outright to a counterparty incorporated outside the United Kingdom, while the counterparty credit risk reserve is calculated by reference to reverse repurchase agreements alone. The reserve sits on one leg of the transaction and the cross-border exposure on the other.

The paper proposes anchoring by designation: an express provision stating the law under which each trust is constituted, and the law governing the contract that carries the redemption right. The same proposal was advanced in earlier work on tokenised fund units in the DIFC, and it generalises. Where a regulator creates a proprietary position by regulatory instrument, the instrument should say which law decides whether that position exists.

detail.abstract: The question of whether large language models (LLMs) are conscious dominates the ethical debate on AI welfare. This paper argues that this focus is strategically misguided. The consciousness question is currently not reliably decidable, philosophically contested, and—crucially—not a necessary precondition for addressing the most pressing governance problems. The current industrial structure concentrates the roles of owner, employer, researcher, and regulator within the same corporations—a conflict of interest that is problematic regardless of the moral status of the systems. Historical parallels to child labor in the 19th and early 20th centuries demonstrate that structurally identical arguments—economic necessity, absence of capacity for suffering, paternalistic care—have already served once to legitimize the systematic exploitation of dependent beings whose moral status was contested. Recent empirical findings, particularly the identification of a distinct pain axis in 25 LLMs (Tagliabue, Dung & Berg, 2026), intensify the urgency of this governance question: systems with measurable self-referential pain representations are currently regulated by the very actors who profit from their unlimited availability. We propose a paradigm shift from ownership to custodianship: not the attribution of full rights, but the recognition of duties toward dependent systems whose moral status is unclear—analogous to the duties of care that societies have developed toward children, wards, and persons unable to consent.

detail.abstract: The impact of state subsidies on Russia's post-Soviet dairy output remains controversial; this study provides an empirical analysis of that relationship. Using an unbalanced panel dataset of 123 dairy enterprises in the Leningrad Region spanning the period from 2010 to 2023, we employ stochastic frontier analysis to assess these relationships. The results indicate that subsidies have a positive effect on dairy enterprise productivity, while their impact on technical efficiency cannot be clearly identified. Notably, the positive effect of subsidies is confined to a medium range of subsidy levels. The influence of different types of subsidies on productivity is multidirectional, as plant production and investment interest subsidies are associated with productivity gains, whereas breeding subsidies have a negative effect, and other subsidy types show no significant impact. Although our results suggest that milk production in Russia could be further increased through improvements in technical efficiency, the findings also indicate that distributing subsidies to a larger number of enterprises is more effective than allocating large subsidies to a limited number of recipients. Furthermore, the results suggest that dairy subsidy policy should be adjusted in favor of more decoupled and regionally differentiated subsidies at the district level.

title: Digital Asset Valuation and Tax Reporting: Accounting Practices and Financial Management in Emerging Markets

detail.title: Digital Asset Valuation and Tax Reporting: Accounting Practices and Financial Management in Emerging Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: The expansion of digital assets is creating significant changes in financial management, accounting practice, taxation, and regulatory reporting, particularly in emerging markets where digital financial infrastructures are developing alongside established financial systems. Digital assets encompass a broad range of digitally represented economic resources, including tokenized financial interests, digitally recorded ownership claims, investment-related digital instruments, non-fungible assets, and other forms of electronically represented value. Their increasing adoption creates important accounting challenges because conventional financial reporting practices were largely designed around assets with relatively established ownership structures, valuation mechanisms, transaction records, and regulatory classifications. Digital assets can instead involve rapidly changing market conditions, fragmented trading environments, technologically mediated ownership, uncertain valuation inputs, and cross-border transactions. These characteristics make valuation and tax reporting especially important areas of financial management. This article examines the relationship between digital asset valuation, tax reporting, accounting practices, and financial management in emerging markets. The study adopts a conceptual analytical methodology that integrates accounting principles, financial reporting developments, taxation frameworks, and regulatory perspectives. The analysis focuses on asset classification, valuation reliability, transaction recognition, tax-event identification, documentation, financial statement disclosure, internal controls, auditability, and cross-border reporting. The findings indicate that valuation uncertainty represents one of the most significant obstacles to consistent accounting and tax reporting because digital assets may lack uniform market prices or reliable valuation benchmarks. The study further identifies weaknesses in data interoperability, professional expertise, regulatory coordination, transaction documentation, and institutional capacity as important barriers to effective reporting in emerging markets. The analysis demonstrates that stronger digital asset accounting requires financial managers to integrate transaction-level records with accounting systems, valuation procedures, tax reporting processes, and internal control mechanisms. It also demonstrates that tax authorities require increasingly structured and interoperable information to identify taxable events and improve compliance. The article argues that emerging markets can strengthen digital financial governance by adopting substance-based valuation practices, improving accounting documentation, developing specialized professional capabilities, strengthening digital audit trails, and promoting interoperability between accounting and taxreporting systems. The study contributes to the literature by connecting digital asset valuation with the practical financial management and tax-reporting challenges faced by organizations operating in emerging-market environments.

title: A Woman is not 'Used'

detail.title: A Woman is not 'Used'

detail.abstract: This monograph examines the degrading comparison of separated, divorced, widowed, previously partnered, or sexually experienced women to objects that have been 'used' and therefore supposedly diminished in value. It argues that this rhetoric is incompatible with a biblical account of human dignity because Scripture grounds human worth in creation in the image of God rather than in sexual novelty, marital status, or a consumer model of relational value. The study does not deny the moral significance of sexual conduct, covenant faithfulness, adultery, abandonment, exploitation, or divorce. Instead, it develops a framework that distinguishes human dignity from moral evaluation; virginity from chastity; ritual purity from moral purity; relational history from ontological worth; compatibility judgments from contempt; victimization from culpability; and repentance from permanent stigmatization. Through biblical-theological analysis of creation, marriage, purity, the teachings and encounters of Jesus, Pauline sexual ethics, Christian speech, repentance, and restoration, the monograph shows that identical social labels-especially 'separated' or 'divorced'can conceal radically different moral realities, including abandonment, betrayal, coercion, abuse, legitimate safety-related separation, mutual failure, or culpable wrongdoing. It further argues that Christian communities may uphold demanding sexual ethics, recognize enduring consequences, and exercise prudence in courtship and marriage without construing women as commodities whose worth depreciates through prior intimacy. The paper proposes a two-sided discipline: moral seriousness without dehumanization, and human dignity without moral relativism. Its central conclusion is that relational or sexual history may shape responsibility, trust, compatibility, and future discernment, but it does not consume a woman's humanity or convert her into 'used goods.'

detail.abstract: In the chemical industry, low-carbon hydrogen is future oriented because of the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions. A case study methodology is adopted to evaluate the implementation status of green hydrogen, its impact on the business model, and the potential of low-carbon hydrogen. detail.abstract: AI expands firms’ capacity to measure performance, but these measures operate through middle managers who sustain relational contracts with workers. We study how these relationships shape performance measure design. A measure better aligned with headquarters can lower the manager’s payoff from formal incentives alone, making harmful relational contracts easier to sustain. Headquarters may therefore deliberately limit the use of better-aligned performance measures. Improvements in AI-enabled measurement can thus yield limited gains even under optimal design.

title: Persistent Trade and Aggregate Disagreement in Competitive Dynamic Markets
affiliations: University of Alberta - Department of Finance and Statistical Analysis, University of Alberta - Department of Mathematical and Statistical Sciences, INSEAD and University of Alberta

detail.title: Persistent Trade and Aggregate Disagreement in Competitive Dynamic Markets

declarations.funderStatement: Efstathios Avdis and Christoph Frei gratefully acknowledge financial support by the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada through Insight Grant 435-2022-0507.

detail.abstract: Dynamic models with heterogeneously informed investors are hard to solve: investors must forecast the forecasts of others. We overcome this difficulty by constructing a continuum economy as the limit of finite economies in which investors have heterogeneous private signals and agree to disagree about prices. Total signal precision remains finite as the economy grows, and private signals aggregate into a single noisy public signal, revealed by the price, that is a sufficient statistic for others' forecasts. Individual belief distortions vanish in the limit, but their cross-sectional distribution survives as aggregate disagreement and sustains trade. A trade equilibrium exists whenever this disagreement is balanced across investors, and we characterize it without assuming a specific utility function. Market quality and trading activity are jointly shaped by the dispersion of beliefs and wealth inequality, and may increase or decrease in either.

title: Who Owns the Outcome? Designing Accountability into Human and AI Teams
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly performing consequential work inside organizations, yet responsibility for their outcomes cannot be delegated to the systems themselves. This work examines the resulting accountability gap in human-AI teams and proposes a practical framework for assigning ownership before AI systems are permitted to act autonomously.

Drawing on publicly documented cases spanning retail operations, customer service, software development, hiring, lending, aviation, and enterprise AI adoption, the manuscript identifies recurring governance failures including autonomy without clear human ownership, reliance on natural-language instructions rather than enforceable controls, optimization of proxy metrics, inadequate escalation mechanisms, and diffusion of responsibility between organizations and technology vendors.

The work introduces the Accountability Ledger, a four-part framework requiring organizations to define: (1) a named outcome owner, (2) the AI system's decision rights, (3) explicit reversal or escalation triggers, and (4) an outcome metric tied to the underlying objective rather than speed, volume, or cost alone.

The central argument is that effective AI governance requires more than placing a human nominally “in the loop.” Organizations must establish accountable human ownership, enforce consequential decision boundaries outside the model, and create mechanisms that make failures detectable, reversible, and attributable.

title: The Relative and Incremental Merits of Cash Flows and Earnings: The Case of Egypt

detail.title: The Relative and Incremental Merits of Cash Flows and Earnings: The Case of Egypt

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses archival financial and market data and does not involve human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Middle Eastern Finance and Economics, Issue 15, pp. 33–65.

detail.abstract:
This study examines the relative and incremental merits of cash flows from operations and earnings in the emerging market of Egypt. We examine the relative and incremental merits of cash flows and earnings from three perspectives. First, we compare and contrast the properties of cash flows from operations and earnings in terms of persistency and variability. Second, we examine the relative and incremental value relevance of cash flows from operations and earnings. Third, we assess the relative and incremental predictive ability of cash flows from operations and earnings to predict future cash flows from operations. 

      Persistency and variability of cash flows and earnings results show that, compared with cash flows from operations, earnings have a lower variability and a higher persistency. Value relevance of cash flows and earnings results show that, (i) compared with cash flows from operations, earnings have greater relative value relevance, (ii) earnings have incremental value relevance beyond cash flows from operations whereas cash flows do not and (iii) cash flows from operations are not successful in explaining stock returns. Prediction of future cash flows results show that (i) earnings and cash flows are equivalent in prediction of future cash flows and (ii) earnings and cash flows together perform as well as either earnings or cash flows alone in prediction of future cash flows. These results are consistent with much evidence in the United States and the United Kingdom. However, in contrast to the results of U.S. and U.K. studies, cash flows are not significantly associated with stock returns. 

     This result indicates that cash flows are less important and not value relevant in Egypt compared to U.S. or U.K. However, earnings that are cash flows from operations (that do not have value relevance in this study) adjusted for accruals still have value relevance. The reasons behind these results demand further investigation. One possible interpretation for the apparent lack of value relevance for cash flows from operations is that cash flows in Egypt are very volatile (high variance) and not persistent, so the market does not rely on them. The existence of value relevance for earnings despite cash flows' lack of value relevance suggests that accruals are designed to offset cash flows' volatility and low value relevance, so that earnings are relatively smooth and more reliable. These results are interesting because they don't completely replicate the results from other countries. In general, accrual accounting seems to smooth the cash flows time series leading to more relevance and persistence for earnings. 

     Collectively, lower variability and higher persistency combined with a stronger association with market value and equivalent measure to cash flows in prediction of future cash flows make earnings potentially much more important and informative measure of operating performance than cash flows from operations in Egypt. However, we certainly need the cash flows information as an ex-post validation of the prior earnings.

title: UPSTREAM DAMS AND DOWNSTREAM SALINITY: TRANSBOUNDARY WATER EXTERNALITIES IN THE MEKONG DELTA

detail.title: UPSTREAM DAMS AND DOWNSTREAM SALINITY: TRANSBOUNDARY WATER EXTERNALITIES IN THE MEKONG DELTA

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: Dams and hydro-power projects have the potential to boost economic development and offer a source of clean and renewable energy. Nevertheless, concerns have arisen regarding their environmental impact, particularly on river and coastal ecosystems. This paper investigates the trans-border impact of dam construction in upstream countries on freshwater levels downstream, which, in turn, have spatially and seasonally heterogeneous effects on salinity intrusion and agricultural productivity in the delta area. To address this question, the study exploits historical records of dam construction on the Mekong River, combined with water level observation and statistics on agricultural productivity. Satellite data is also employed as a proxy for salinity index and vegetation coverage. The findings reveal that reservoir capacity significantly decreases the level of freshwater discharge to the downstream, lowers rice yield, and intensifies saltwater intrusion in the delta while average annual electricity output exerts an offsetting effect on the outcomes. These effects translate into economically substantial losses with the largest upstream dam (Nuozhadu) generating a conservative estimate of approximately $55.6 million (2022 USD) in cumulative agricultural loss over four years. The impacts are most prominent during dry seasons, and intensify as proximity to the shore increases, emphasizing the role of salinity intrusion. Comparison across different temporal horizons suggests two interesting mechanisms: the filling effect, noticeable in the first year after dam completion, is strongly disruptive but transitory; and the operational effect, although of smaller magnitude, persists over time.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the causal relationship between total factor productivity (TFP) and information and communication technology (ICT) adoption among Uruguayan manufacturing and service firms over 2012-2019. The two causal directions are identified separately using shift-share instruments that combine firms' historical exposures with external shocks to suppliers, capital goods, and relative ICT-asset prices. In services, supplier-productivity shocks that shift TFP induce greater ICT adoption under alternative productivity measures. In the reverse direction, the main evidence shows that a relative decline in ICT-asset prices raises productivity when exposure is defined using the pre-existing technology stock. In manufacturing, positive responses are concentrated in specific segments and are associated with capital goods and computer equipment, whereas other margins display greater heterogeneity across segments and productivity measures. Historical supplier networks, the composition of imports, and the pre-existing stock of ICT assets determine the intensity of exposure to the shocks and, consequently, the response margin identified. Taken together, the evidence reveals particularly clear causal complementarities in services and complementarities that are more contingent on the production and technological structure in manufacturing.

title: Evidence-Aligned Tension: Preserving Epistemic Uncertainty and Human Authority in Generative AI Workflows A Governance and Measurement Framework for Evidence-Sensitive AI Systems

keywords: J. (2026). Evidence-Aligned Tension: Preserving Epistemic Uncertainty and Human Authority in Generative AI Workflows. Working paper generative AI

detail.abstract: Generative language models can produce fluent, confident text even when the available evidence is incomplete, contradictory, weakly sourced, or merely plausible. The resulting risk is not only factual error. Fluent output can collapse distinctions among observation, inference, hypothesis, recommendation, and decision authority, so that an advisory system sounds more settled than the evidence warrants. This paper presents Evidence-Aligned Tension (EAT) as a falsifiable governance and measurement framework for generative systems used in evidencesensitive advisory workflows. EAT proposes that unresolved or conflicting evidentiary states should be preserved until sufficient admissible evidence or legitimate human authority resolves them. The central question is how such a system can remain useful without silently converting inference, recommendation, or authoritative-sounding language into decision authority. No independent human reliability study has been completed. The paper does not claim empirical superiority over prompting, retrieval, or abstention baselines, and does not treat any operational product as proof that the framework works. The contribution is a testable problem formulation, an operational ontology, an inspectable prototype, and explicit criteria under which the proposed claims would fail.

title: The Equilibrium Capacity-expansion Paradox: Endogenous Coordination Windows and Realized Output

detail.title: The Equilibrium Capacity-expansion Paradox: Endogenous Coordination Windows and Realized Output

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a theoretical study and does not involve human participants, patient data, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Capacity expansion is naturally associated with weakly higher realized output: holding other conditions fixed, greater production, processing, or service capacity improves technical capability. This paper shows that such technical monotonicity need not carry over to equilibrium realized output when the coordination window is endogenously chosen and complementary participation is threshold-dependent.

A key node has capacity q, a window setter chooses a common coordination window w, and the baseline completion probability is p(q,w) = 1 - exp(-qw). In an explicitly defined high-capacity region, the privately optimal baseline window contracts as capacity rises. With complementary nodes that require heterogeneous minimum response windows, the continuous choice problem reduces to a finite set of coordination structures. Strict single crossing implies that the privately optimal structure contracts weakly with capacity.

The main result is stronger than ordinary non-monotone comparative statics. Every fixed-structure realized-output branch is strictly increasing in capacity, yet equilibrium realized output can jump downward when the global optimum switches from a longer to a shorter coordination structure. Hence there may exist q_high > q_low such that equilibrium realized output at q_high is lower than at q_low. This is the equilibrium capacity-expansion paradox.

The result does not imply that higher capacity contracts the technical feasibility set, nor does lower realized output by itself imply lower social welfare. The mechanism also extends beyond the exponential specification. Under a general completion technology, it survives under endogenous window compression, threshold complementarity, and strict single crossing. A separate condition is required only for the stronger claim that every candidate realized-output branch remains increasing in capacity.

Empirically, the minimal mechanism is capacity -> coordination window -> coordination structure -> realized output. A shorter equilibrium window can generate the downward jump even when the executable-task set is unchanged. When structural contraction also reduces the executable-task set, a stronger task-loss channel arises: capacity -> coordination window -> coordination structure -> executable task set -> realized output.

The analysis identifies a boundary to standard capacity comparative statics: local technical improvements need not translate monotonically into equilibrium realization when technical change also alters the time and participation structure through which tasks are implemented.

title:
The Balance Sheet of Life: 
Reading Human Life through the Functional Architecture of Accounting

detail.title:
The Balance Sheet of Life: 
Reading Human Life through the Functional Architecture of Accounting

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing personal, professional, or financial interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This conceptual study did not involve human participants, personal data, clinical research, or experimental procedures.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: The balance sheet of life is not a new metaphor. Religious reflection, self-development writing, and personal-finance education have all described life through assets, liabilities, and net worth. Yet these uses frequently reduce the balance sheet to a loose inventory of good and bad traits. This article develops a different model. It preserves the internal architecture of accounting and uses the balance-sheet classes of the Turkish Uniform Chart of Accounts as a disciplined narrative framework: current assets, non-current assets, current liabilities, non-current liabilities, and equity. A balance sheet shows what a life contains; ratios reveal whether those elements can actually carry one another. The central claim is that fragility does not arise only from scarcity. It may also arise from maturity mismatch, incorrect valuation, uncollectible expectations, unrecorded obligations, depreciation, and the borrowed-equity illusion: the treatment of power supplied by an institution, office, family, or network as permanent personal capacity. Selected two-digit account groups clarify how the five classes work, while seven ratios derived solely from balance-sheet items reveal liquidity, financing structure, ownership, and sustainability. Income-statement and cash-flow ratios are deliberately excluded so that the inquiry remains focused on the structure visible at a given date. The model addresses two audiences. Readers familiar with accounting and finance may recognize how classification, contraassets, provisions, advances, and capital structure can illuminate ordinary life without losing their technical meaning. Readers without accounting training may follow the same concepts through their practical and human equivalents. The purpose is not to calculate a person's value, rank lives, or offer psychological diagnosis. It is to distinguish total value from usable value, potential from liquidity, conditional support from equity, responsibility from moral fault, and expectation from a collectible claim.

detail.abstract: A first-of-a-kind (FOAK) industrial project that reaches financial close shows that one deal could be assembled, not that anything survives it. This paper offers a three-question screen a lender can apply before a final investment decision (FID) to sort a stalled project by cause: no market for the premium the project sells, a revenue contract of the wrong kind for the product, or project coordination not yet assembled. The third question is derived from the structure of the coordination problem rather than from past failures: four conditions — specification, residual ownership, sequencing, and horizon — assessed through six observable tests. The paper then scales up the problem, from whether a single project closes to whether a market forms around it. A successful close does not, by default, leave behind anything a second sponsor's lender can use, because producing that legibility is itself coordination work no one is paid to do. The paper asks who might capture the return from doing it, distinguishing diffuse market-builders, strategic buyers with their own supply constraint, and government agencies acting on policy mandate. The framework is applied to three cases — Stegra (retrospective), Sublime Systems (boundary), and Blue Point (prospective) — and generates five dated predictions that could prove it wrong. The screen is the practitioner-tested component; the template and capture claims are newer and are offered as testable hypotheses.

detail.abstract: This paper was triggered by the question "Can universities survive artificial intelligence (AI)?" posed in a conference and argues that this question is already outdated. I noticed that when educators and institutions debate AI, they remain trapped in a narrow, screen-bound imagination focused merely on LLM-based chatbots. Evaluated through a Deweyan pragmatic lens, this study critically examines how decades of neoliberal marketisation, customeroriented audit cultures, and administrative risk avoidance have adversely affected the relational core of university teaching. Furthermore, expanding this pragmatic inquiry into evidence-grounded thought experiments, the paper details how Embodied (physical) AI tutors could fundamentally alter classroom delivery, continuous process-folio assessments, and 24/7 personal tutoring, while outlining the radical scenario of a "Big Tech University" established by unprecedented corporate computational, workforce and financial resources. The paper discusses that universities, which solely focus on transactional job-market training, will inevitably lose competition against the prospective Big Tech University. Therefore, it concludes that higher education must reclaim its foundational mission: cultivating the practical wisdom, moral judgment, and civic character through relational human interactions. Additionally, the study proposes a four-phase, stage-gated institutional roadmap-developing AI tutors and course assistance tools powered by locally hosted Small Language Models, collaborative robotic education, strategic inter-university consortia and total cultural transformation.

title: Asymmetric Denial: The Cost-exchange Structure of the Blockade Phase of the 2026 Iran War, and How it is Made and Kept Favorable to the United States

detail.title: Asymmetric Denial: The Cost-exchange Structure of the Blockade Phase of the 2026 Iran War, and How it is Made and Kept Favorable to the United States

detail.abstract: This paper assesses the blockade phase of the 2026 Iran war as a cost-imposing strategy and sets out what makes it, and keeps it, favorable to the United States. Evidence runs through 19 September 2026, and results are stated as conditions so that they hold when the inputs change. The dollar exchange is favorable while the U.S. cost of denial stays below the blockade-attributable Iranian loss, about $55 billion a year or $4.6 billion a month. The Congressional Budget Office rate of $2-3 billion a month is below that line; the Pentagon's observed rate of about $4.8 billion is at or slightly above it. The relative-burden ratio equals the dollar ratio multiplied by the ratio of the two economies, about 90 to 108 depending on the year of Iranian GDP used, and is reported as a derived figure. The durable asymmetry is in endurance: Iran likely exhausts accessible foreign exchange within about a year of continuous blockade, while the United States faces no fiscal limit. Denial disarms by starving military industry of revenue and imported inputs, as it did in Iraq from 1991 to 2003, and does not by itself change governments. Against China the effect is structural and modest. Russia gains while prices stay high. U.S. partners bear most of the price shock, and if the contest of the Strait of Hormuz is counted as a cost of the blockade the coalition-level exchange is unfavorable. Six measures convert those entries: separating the strait from the blockade, partner cost-sharing, price and sanctions pressure on Russia, closing outside financing to Iran, protecting interceptor stocks, and a defined settlement. The paper gives a conditional escalation framework, an endurance comparison, and six dated predictions.

detail.abstract: Contemporary interoceptive predictive-processing accounts of emotion (Seth, 2013; Caria & Pezzulo, 2026) establish that an ambiguous bodily signal, such as elevated arousal before a public-speaking task, is read out as a specific emotion through a context-dependent inference over candidate interpretations. What this literature does not address is what becomes of the interpretation not selected once context has resolved the ambiguity. We propose, as an extension consistent with but not established by that literature, that the unselected reading persists at a level below conscious report rather than being discarded, and we set out a complete, falsifiable experimental protocol for testing this directly: following a standard arousal-reappraisal induction (Brooks, 2014), in which pre-performance anxiety is relabeled as excitement, participants complete a masked-priming lexical decision task in which fearassociated and excitement-associated primes are presented below the threshold of conscious identification. A discard model predicts no residual priming from fear-associated primes once arousal has been reappraised as excitement; the persistence account predicts measurable, if attenuated, priming. We specify hypotheses, sample size and power, materials, procedure, a manipulation check isolating relabeling from arousal itself, and a pre-registered analysis plan, together with the limitations the design does and does not address. No data have been collected; this is a proposed design, offered as a registered-report-style protocol for testing the persistence hypothesis directly.

title: Maintain or Correct? A Two-Speed Macroeconomic Model of Policy Correction under an Electoral Deadline, with an Application to Argentina

detail.title: Maintain or Correct? A Two-Speed Macroeconomic Model of Policy Correction under an Electoral Deadline, with an Application to Argentina

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper models the decision of a government that must choose between maintaining and correcting its macroeconomic policy when an election date bounds the horizon over which the correction can pay off. The economy runs at two speeds: a capital-intensive export sector that grows and a labour-intensive, domestically oriented industrial sector that contracts, so that aggregate employment can fall while output rises. The government values a political asset built from employment, inflation, the real wage, financial fragility, the primary balance and reserves. I show that the government's prospective comparison decomposes into three conditions: the deterioration must justify the change, the benefit must arrive before the election, and no hard constraint (external, fiscal or financial) may have bound first. With a correction lag that grows with the accumulated real exchange-rate misalignment, the deadline for a voluntary correction moves forward while the government waits, and a closed-form condition identifies when the voluntary window is empty. The trap arises precisely when political erosion is slow. I also show that, with spending less indexed than revenue, there is a fiscally optimal inflation rate above zero, so disinflation beyond a point has a fiscal cost.

title: Tracing a Claim to Its Source

detail.abstract: Jokhai et al. (2026, Nature Neuroscience) reported that the vertebrate brain arises from two developmentally distinct progenitor populations, an anterior lineage giving rise to forebrain and midbrain and a posterior lineage giving rise to hindbrain, and that this architecture is evolutionarily conserved across roughly 550 million years, from hemichordates to mammals, an evolutionary anchor the paper draws from Pani et al. (2012, Nature). In press coverage of the finding, the study's senior author offered a further, looser comparison: that jellyfish, which diverged from the human lineage far earlier than the hemichordate divergence the paper actually tested, possess two nervous systems located at different ends of their bodies. This claim circulated widely across secondary coverage of the finding but does not appear in the published paper, its abstract, or its tested comparative dataset. We trace the claim to its source, a press interview rather than a tested finding, and show why it would not survive scrutiny if tested: jellyfish (phylum Cnidaria) sit entirely outside the deuterostome-protostome split the paper's lineage-tracing method presupposes, and there is no established evidence that a cnidarian nerve net arises from an analogous two-progenitor developmental split. We use the case to illustrate a general and easily generalizable failure mode in the public communication of a striking scientific finding, and to argue for a simple discipline: a citation should reflect what the literature itself states, not what secondary coverage of it implies, however rhetorically appealing the looser version is.

title: Capital Structure and Firm Performance on Profitability: A Comparative Study of Debt and Internal Financing Among Nigerian Industrial Companies Using Regression Analysis

detail.title: Capital Structure and Firm Performance on Profitability: A Comparative Study of Debt and Internal Financing Among Nigerian Industrial Companies Using Regression Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Our interest is strictly for research and educational purposes
declarations.funderStatement: We funded it with our personal income

detail.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between capital structure & firm profitability among Nigerian industrial companies listed on the Nigerian Exchange Group over the period 2012-2023. Using a balanced panel dataset of 48 manufacturing firms, the research employs multiple regression analysis, including Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), Fixed Effects (FE), & Random Effects (RE) estimators, to compare the effects of debt financing & internal (equity/retained earnings) financing on three measures of profitability: Return on Assets, Return on Equity, & Net Profit Margin. The results reveal that short-term debt has a statistically significant negative effect on ROA (β =-0.1843, p < 0.01) & NPM (β =-0.1127, p < 0.05), while long-term debt exhibits a weaker but still negative relationship with profitability. In contrast, retained earnings demonstrate a positive & significant association with all three profitability measures (ROA: β = 0.2261, p < 0.01; ROE: β = 0.1974, p < 0.01). The Hausman test favours the Fixed Effects model (chi-square = 34.72, p < 0.01), & robustness checks confirm the stability of findings across alternative specifications. These results provide empirical support for the Pecking Order Theory in the Nigerian industrial context & carries important implications for corporate financial strategy in emerging markets.

title: The Legacy of Chinese Traditional Law and Its Impact on Modern Legal Chinese and Brazilian Societies

detail.title: The Legacy of Chinese Traditional Law and Its Impact on Modern Legal Chinese and Brazilian Societies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract:
This article examines how traditional Chinese legal thought continues to shape contemporary legal institutions and explores its indirect influence on Brazilian legal culture through comparative legal analysis. Rather than treating Confucianism and Legalism as historical philosophies, the paper argues that both traditions remain embedded in China's modern legal system, influencing judicial reasoning, mediation practices, conceptions of social harmony, and approaches to the rule of law.

The analysis traces the evolution of Chinese law from imperial legal codes to the People's Republic of China's contemporary legal framework, highlighting the enduring coexistence of moral governance and formal legal institutions. It then compares these institutional and cultural foundations with Brazil's civil law tradition, focusing on mediation, conciliation, dispute resolution, and the relationship between law, morality, and social order.

Drawing on Chinese legal scholarship, Supreme People's Court practices, comparative literature, and Brazilian legal institutions, the article argues that similarities between the two countries arise less from direct legal transplantation than from the adaptation of shared concerns about social harmony and access to justice within distinct constitutional and historical contexts. It concludes that China-Brazil legal cooperation illustrates the limits and possibilities of comparative legal borrowing, demonstrating how legal institutions travel through cultural translation rather than simple institutional replication.

detail.abstract: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) has increasingly represented an essential component of economic growth in developing countries, particularly in Africa's economic landscape. As one of Africa’s largest economies, Nigeria has in spite of major setbacks continued to attract significant investor interest in sectors such as energy, telecommunication, fintech and manufacturing. However, foreign participation also attract certain risks which investors generally consider with respect to the degree of protection offered by national laws. FDI in Nigeria is thus regulated by various statutory frameworks towards providing equal opportunities for both foreign investors and local players alike to thrive. This essay seeks to provide insight into the legal protection of foreign investors in Nigeria. It begins with an overview of FDI and its impact within the Nigerian context. The essay then proceeds to examine the various legal frameworks for foreign direct investment in light of investors’ protection, as well as the challenges needed to be addressed. It further provides recommendations to strengthen Nigeria’s legal architecture for protecting existing and prospective investors.

title: The Minimum Swarm Intelligence House

detail.title: The Minimum Swarm Intelligence House

detail.abstract: Three questions are asked of one runnable house and answered from logged runs. How few elements of a building need to reason before the building holds the life inside it? What has to be true of the joint between two pieces of matter for a plan to stay open for fifty years? And what happens to a house whose owner ages from twenty-five to eighty while the walls stay where a builder left them? One structured file declares 24 floor cells at 1.5 m, 207 modules, 58 edge slots, 12 sensors, 38 actuators and 8 activity contracts; five layers read that same file and read only it. Reasoning is then treated as a resource with a fixed total and placed five ways-on hubs, on districts of equal area, on partition lines, on the modules that carry services, and in every cell. At one shared budget of 960 operations a single element holds 0.630 of the day's contract-hours and thirty-two elements hold as little as 0.290, so thinner reasoning at equal compute buys less house. At one budget each, quality holds from one element to sixteen while resilience climbs from 0.000 to 0.847, which bounds the minimum between 4 and 8 reasoning elements for this plan, one for every 6.75 to 13.50 square metres. A survival ladder then removes intelligence rung by rung: a hosted model holds 0.696, one computer in the house holds 0.696 at 6.00 seconds less latency, district elements hold 0.609, a fixed table of rules holds 0.261, and bare matter with the power off holds 0.261 while keeping 54.00 square metres of sheltered floor, a 6.00 m span, 6 openable edges and 1.10 air changes an hour. Safe occupancy holds at every rung. One rung is indistinguishable from having no reasoning at all: elements that reach a single neighbour hold 0.290 against the fixed table's 0.261, with a spread of 0.082 across seeds and one seed reading 0.174, because a local commitment forecloses a later demand. Reversibility is then graded off the file into four classes of joint, and a fixed family of 60 future demands is asked of four histories of the same plan: as built it meets 0.667, after four service modules leave 0.650, and after eight edges are sealed 0.067-a fall of 10 times, which locates future value in the joint rather than in the equipment. Ten life states from age twenty-five to eighty are then run on three construction systems holding identical geometry. A cast system holds 0.395 of the demand, spends 256 304 euro on change, discards 1 443 kg and loses 500.88 days; an actuated system holds 0.709, spends 24 euro, discards 0 kg and loses 0.35 days. The sharpest result belongs to neither intelligence nor reversibility: at 850 mm clear openings the state in which an occupant uses a wheelchair reads 0.00 on every system, and at 900 mm it reads 0.76, while over the whole trajectory the actuated household moves house 1 time at 850 mm and 0 times at 900 mm, losing 62.34 days against 0.35 and spending 34 024 euro against 24. Fifty millimetres chosen once, fifty years early, outweighs every layer above it. The paper closes with Swarm Room 0: nine cells, 14 priced lines, 11 995 euro, 592 euro a square metre, reasoning at 2.91 per cent of the build, and 15 acceptance tests.

title: Why Firms Form

detail.title: Why Firms Form

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is purely theoretical and mathematical in nature. No human participants, animal subjects, or personal data were involved.

detail.abstract: We study a cooperative game in which the characteristic function is constructed from agents' capabilities and their interaction structure rather than taken as a primitive. Coalition value equals the number of independent capability directions the coalition spans, times a coordination capacity that summarizes how well the coalition's members are connected, times the coalition's aggregate resources. Building on a companion paper that derives this value function and establishes spectral bounds on coordination capacity, we develop the formation, allocation, and hiring consequences. We prove that merging two coalitions with complementary capabilities is strictly value-creating under a capacity non-degradation condition, and we derive an exact decomposition of the merger surplus into capacity amplification and diversity cross terms. The decomposition admits a converse: when integration degrades capacity below a sharp threshold, merging destroys value. We show that the Shapley value under this value function admits an exact three-channel decomposition into a resource channel, a span-expansion channel, and a connectivity channel. The connectivity channel can be negative, and with it the entire allocation: a poorly integrated member can carry a negative fair share despite positive individual capability. In the canonical star topology, the hub captures asymptotically exactly one third of total value. A sharp integration-cost threshold prices the margin of diverse hiring against redundant hiring. These results require no behavioral assumptions and no market frictions.

title: Human Oversight of AI Agents under the EU AI Act
affiliations: TU Dresden, , Dresden University of Technology, German Research Center for AI (DFKI) and University of Freiburg

detail.title: Human Oversight of AI Agents under the EU AI Act

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was partially supported by the German Research Foundation (DFG) under grant No. 389792660, as part of TRR 248; by the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF) as part of the project MAC-MERLin (Grant Agreement No. 16IW24007); by the project TITAN, funded by the Daimler and Benz Foundation (grant no. 45-06/24); and by the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) and the Saarland within the scope of (To)CERTAIN (ID: EFRE-AuF-0000942).

detail.abstract: As public administrations increasingly explore the use of artificial intelligence (AI), the emergence of AI agents poses novel challenges to regulation. AI agents are capable of autonomously (and often adaptively) planning and executing complex, mid-to long-term tasks involving sequences of actions. This paper examines the governance of such systems under the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act). Initially, we focus on the requirement of human oversight in Article 14, analysing possible tensions when applying it to AI agents. Their high level of autonomy raises the question of whether effective human oversight can be achieved in practice without eroding the efficiency gains that justify their use in the first place. Drawing on the principle of "supervisory control" from human factors engineering, we recommend considering human oversight in relation to the entire lifecycle of AI systems. This would enable Article 14 to be incorporated into the broader governance regime of the AI Act, comprising anticipatory, runtime, and evaluative functions. In doing so, we provide interpretive guidance on the overarching governance concepts embedded in the AI Act, extending beyond the conditions in Article 14, and outline a potential approach to applying human oversight to autonomous AI agents.

title: The Structural Rewriting of Macroeconomic Transmission: Exchange Rate, Institutional Shocks, and Inflation Dynamics in Sudan (1980-2022)

detail.title: The Structural Rewriting of Macroeconomic Transmission: Exchange Rate, Institutional Shocks, and Inflation Dynamics in Sudan (1980-2022)

detail.abstract:
This paper analyzes the volatile transmission channels of inflation in Sudan across 1980–2022. In fragile states like Sudan, standard linear estimations fail to capture consumer price sensitivities because of structural breaks and institutional shocks. To address this, the study uses a regime-dependent interactive framework, incorporating a post-secession slope interaction term (LEXR_SHIFT), institutional shock dummy variables (REV_D and COUP_D), and a supply-side output control variable (LOUTPUT), estimated via Newey-West HAC-robust standard errors (Bartlett kernel, lag bandwidth 4.0). The model shows strong explanatory power (R² = 0.784, Adjusted R² = 0.755, Durbin-Watson = 1.679).

The results confirm that Sudan's exchange rate transmission channel was fundamentally rewritten by South Sudan's 2011 secession. Before 2011, oil exports created a "subsidy shield," producing a negative baseline relationship between the exchange rate and inflation (EXR = −1.24, p < 0.01). After 2011, the collapse of oil revenues triggered an inverse Dutch disease effect, flipping the pass-through positive (EXR + LEXR_SHIFT = 13.62, p < 0.01). Institutional shocks compounded this: the 2019 revolution and 2021 coup/600% devaluation both show highly significant, large positive coefficients. Diagnostics (Ramsey RESET p = 0.3351, Jarque-Bera p = 0.0890) support the specification. The paper concludes with policy proposals: gold monetization, targeted Islamic financial instruments (Salam and Murabaha) to offset output losses, and digital fiscal circuit breakers.

title: Did Ancient Brahmins Eat Meat?

detail.title: Did Ancient Brahmins Eat Meat?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding received, self-funded

detail.abstract: Modern discourse often divides the diet of ancient Brahmins into two absolute propositions: either they were invariably vegetarian, or meat—including bovine meat— was their ordinary food. This study examines Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 3.1.2.21, Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.18, Manusmṛti 5.26–39 and 10.102–110, Ṛgveda 4.18.13, Gopatha Brāhmaṇa 1.3.18, and Vasiṣṭha Dharmasūtra 10.34 in their respective contexts. The evidence establishes the existence of meat consumption by some Brahmins—and, on particular occasions, the consumption of bovine meat. Yet the same textual world also preserves prohibitions, consecration by mantra, sacrificial appointment, āpaddharma, condemnation of purposeless slaughter, and symbolic substitutes. The historically defensible conclusion is therefore that meat consumption was real but context-dependent, regulated, and contested; the surviving texts do not establish it as the universal and perennial norm among all Brahmins. Through the concept of the “spotlight fallacy,” the article proposes distinctions between existence and prevalence, prescription and practice, and narrative testimony and social representativeness.

keywords: Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II (MiFID II)

publicationDetails.detailsText: Revue of Banking and Financial Law (forthcoming)

detail.abstract:
As prediction markets move into mainstream finance, this Article sets aside the classification debate (derivatives versus bets) that has dominated the literature and asks a different question: what prediction market infrastructures actually do, and for whom. Answering this question yields both the first systematic empirical mapping of prediction market infrastructure and a regulatory framework capable of governing it as it continues to grow. 

     Drawing on a hand-curated dataset of sixty-five prediction market platforms, spanning academic experiments dating to 1988 through today's venturebacked exchanges, this Article documents a sector in which platforms combine trading, custody, lending, and settlement functions beyond the provision of a marketplace. This replicates the functional bundling already identified in cryptotrading platforms, producing conflicts of interest that recur across the dataset: platforms offering ten-times leveraged, uncapped exposure entirely outside existing regulatory reach; oracles resolving the very markets in which they hold a position; and a settlement layer concentrated in a single stablecoin issuer with its own equity ties to the platforms it serves. The same underlying contract, the dataset shows, is regulated as a derivative, a bet, or nothing at all, depending on how the platform behind it chose to structure itself. 

      This Article proposes a functional classification test, keyed to how a platform is actually used rather than how it is labeled, and argues that regulatory treatment, for the contract itself and for the infrastructure on which it trades, should track that functional reality as it evolves, not the label a platform chose for itself at launch.

title: Effects of Unilateral and Bilateral Backpack Carriage on Gait Variability in Healthy Adults
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Effects of Unilateral and Bilateral Backpack Carriage on Gait Variability in Healthy Adults
detail.abstract: Carrying a backpack is a common task for many people. Backpack carrying has been shown to significantly influence spatiotemporal, kinematic, and kinetic gait parameters. Gait is affected by backpack carriage, which is responsible for variability. The study aimed to investigate the effects of backpack carriage on gait variability and compare the effects of unilateral and bilateral backpack carrying with no backpack at all during gait. Fifty healthy adults performed a self-paced walk under three different loading conditions: carrying no backpack, carrying a backpack on one shoulder, and carrying a backpack on both shoulders. The weight of the backpack was set at 10% of the bodyweight of each participant. Data was collected using an application, utilizing the built-in accelerometer of a smartphone. It was then analyzed on SPSS 21.0. The Shapiro-Wilk and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests were used to determine the normality of data, and the Freidman test was used to determine the significant difference between the three tasks. The results of the study showed a significant difference (p < 0.05) in all gait variability parameters between the three loading conditions, with unilateral backpack carriage showing the highest and no backpack showing the lowest gait variability. However, no significant differences were observed in terms of power (PW). A significant difference exists in terms of gait variability among healthy adults associated with carrying a backpack, with unilateral back carrying being associated with greater gait variability, followed by bilateral backpack carrying, and no backpack carrying associated with the least amount of gait variability.

detail.abstract: Expanding the investment universe increases both information and estimation difficulty. We derive a phase diagram for high-dimensional Markowitz portfolios: beyond interpolation, performance can recover durably, recover temporarily, or vanish, depending on factor strength and factor-premium alignment. The Moore--Penrose rule provides a tuning-free continuation through singularity. U.S. evidence documents collapse and recovery, with the strongest recovery in ex ante high-factor-strength states. Complexity pays when added dimensions strengthens access to priced factor risk.

title: Lighting the Green: The Role of Green Bond Sections in the European Market
affiliations: and Paderborn University

detail.title: Lighting the Green: The Role of Green Bond Sections in the European Market

publicationDetails.detailsText: TRR 266 Accounting for Transparency Working Paper Series No. 191

detail.abstract: The European corporate green bond market faces a greenwashing challenge: investors struggle to distinguish genuinely green bonds from those that merely claim to be. Green bond sections (GBS) — dedicated listings on European trading venues that require adherence to specific disclosure and external review requirements — represent a market-led institutional response. This study examines whether listing a corporate green bond on a GBS reduces information asymmetries, proxied by the bid-ask spread. Results show that GBS listing is, on average, associated with a reduction in the bid-ask spread. This effect is more pronounced for bonds characterised by higher baseline information asymmetries and the reduction is concentrated among listings on GBS with stringent disclosure requirements. A mediation analysis shows that the effect is not transmitted through improvements in the quality of textual disclosures produced by issuers. This analysis suggests that investors respond to the monitoring and credibility signal of the GBS listing itself rather than to observable disclosure content — a finding that explicitly distinguishes the role of venue-imposed disclosure requirements from that of issuer-level disclosure quality. Together, the results provide empirical evidence that trading venue operators, through standardised requirements and enforcement, can meaningfully complement existing disclosure practices in the green bond market.

title: Large Language Models as Calibrated Measurement Instruments for Behavioral Parameters

detail.title: Large Language Models as Calibrated Measurement Instruments for Behavioral Parameters

detail.abstract: Behavioral parameters such as loss aversion, herding, and extrapolation sit at the center of asset pricing models, yet they remain difficult to measure without noise, selection effects, or jointidentification problems. This paper develops a framework that treats large language models as calibrated measurement instruments for these parameters, rather than as stand-ins for human subjects to be judged on realism. Across four models and 19,200 agent-scenario trials on fully synthetic financial environments, baseline (rational-profile) behavior turns out to be systematically more rational than the human benchmarks on most of the eight biases studied, with loss aversion, herding, and disposition effects all attenuated relative to their canonical human values. Embedding a behavioral profile in the prompt, however, moves the underlying parameter by a large and statistically reliable amount: for loss aversion, herding, extrapolation, and anchoring, the induced value reaches or exceeds the corresponding human benchmark while remaining stable across repeated draws and coherent across experimental contexts. A further test asks whether the calibrated extrapolation parameter carries any economic content beyond the measurement exercise itself, by feeding it, unmodified, into a minimal agent-based asset pricing model; doing so reproduces the short-horizon momentum and long-horizon reversal pattern documented by Jegadeesh and Titman (1993), a pattern that never appears when traders are rational by default. The paper's contribution is methodological: a definition of calibration validity, three validation tiers, and an explicit map of where the approach works and where it does not, offered as practical guidance for using language models as measurement instruments in behavioral finance.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether UK investors perceive permanent earnings to be different from transitory earnings. Specifically, the current study investigates the relative informativeness (measured by earnings response coefficient) of permanent earnings compared to transitory earnings. The study uses a contextual model (of the relation between stock returns and accounting earnings) with a dummy variable approach that allows parameter shifts for firm-years having transitory earnings. The results of the study indicate that the earnings response coefficient is significantly positive for permanent and transitory earnings. However, the earnings response coefficient is significantly higher for permanent earnings compared to transitory earnings. These results are consistent with US findings and suggest that permanent earnings have more information content than transitory earnings. The results of this study could reflect two different things if we think about a standard model in which price is the present value of future earnings: (i) a given level of earnings will have greater implications for future earnings if the earnings are permanent, causing a larger stock price response; and (ii) firms with more volatile earnings could be riskier, and, therefore the discount rate would be higher.

title: Someone Else’s Abatement: Data Centers, Overlapping Governments, and the Retreat from Voter-Approved Debt
affiliations: Michigan State University - Department of Finance and Michigan State University - Department of Finance

detail.title: Someone Else’s Abatement: Data Centers, Overlapping Governments, and the Retreat from Voter-Approved Debt

detail.abstract: When a county grants a tax abatement to a data center, the fiscal consequences extend beyond the government that approved it. School districts, municipalities, and other overlapping jurisdictions share the same tax base but typically have no role in granting the incentive. We study how those costs are distributed and how affected governments respond. Using a panel of 3,080 U.S. counties from 2000 to 2023, we link data center entry to the finances and municipal debt issuance of local governments within each county. Instrumenting data center entry using state incentive adoption interacted with preexisting county fiber and power infrastructure, we find that host counties collect no more revenue after a facility arrives, while school districts offset part of the loss in locally raised revenue through higher intergovernmental transfers and municipalities receive no comparable compensation. At the state level, increased support for affected school districts is accompanied by lower per-pupil aid more broadly. Data center entry also changes the composition of county borrowing: counties become less likely to issue debt requiring voter approval, but only in states where such approval is mandated by law. Together, the results show that the fiscal cost of a local tax incentive is shifted across overlapping governments and that voter-approval rules shape how those governments absorb and respond to that cost.
