detail.abstract: I solve a sovereign debt model with exceptional spending shocks. Positive debt is sustained solely by the threat of losing access to borrowing. The key assumption is that rapid asset sales used to fund exceptionally large government expenditures entail liquidity costs, giving a comparative advantage to more liquid sovereign bond issuance. The paper also provides a novel mechanism by which less patient governments can borrow more debt. This liquidity friction positively interacts with other standard debt-sustaining mechanisms.

detail.abstract: This Comment explains how the duty to consult, seek, and secure consent functions as a procedural safeguard mechanism of Indigenous rights. detail.abstract: Forecast comparisons can misattribute the value of a newly released quarterly target to monthly information when a challenger and benchmark use different information dates. We distinguish the held-AR replacement comparison (H), the same-date operational comparison (O), and a fixed-operator monthly-input counterfactual (M). In simulations with an informative target update but no monthly signal, the test based on H rejects in 45.1% of replications, versus 0.9% and 1.1% for O and M. We evaluate five mixed-frequency procedures and eight benchmarks at twelve monthly issue dates for 42 quarters of Korean aggregate gross fixed capital formation. Across 48 evaluation cells, only the O comparison for seasonally adjusted annualised quarteron-quarter growth at h = 0 survives Holm adjustment (raw p = 0.0003; Holm-48 p = 0.0144). The equipment-only restricted MIDAS bridge has the lowest RMSE (5.623), outperforming every higher-dimensional MIDAS specification. The calendar-based pseudo-real-time design uses latest-vintage histories, observed evaluation-period target-release dates, a rule-based earlier calendar, and assumed predictor lags rather than complete historical vintages. The evidence supports synchronised benchmarks and economically grounded bridge comparators, not general MIDAS dominance or a uniform marginal value of monthly updates.

detail.abstract: PredictIt is a CFTC-regulated US prediction market focused on political outcomes. It was very successful in attracting participants in the 2016-22 period, running liquid markets on topics predecessors had tried unsuccesfully. During this period, investors were limited to $850 positions in each contract, which limited arbitrage trading. PredictIt exhibited much larger pricing biases than previously studied prediction markets. Bid prices often persistently added to more than 110, implying an immediate arbitrage profit even after fees. Prices exhibited an overpricing of longshots that was larger than in other prediction markets. The experience of PredictIt suggests that limiting stakes may undermine the ability of prediction markets to accurately price event probabilities.

detail.abstract: Purpose: This study develops and validates a composite South African Municipal Governance Index (SAMGI) that integrates institutionally auditable indicators across financial management, audit quality, administrative capacity, service delivery, political-institutional design, and transparency. Design/Methodology/Approach: The index is constructed for a purposive sample comprising all eight metropolitan municipalities and a stratified random sample of district and local municipalities in South Africa (n = 32). Six theoretically grounded dimensions, operationalised through twenty-four indicators drawn from credible public datasets (Auditor-General of South Africa, National Treasury, Statistics South Africa, SALGA, and COGTA), are aggregated using Principal Component Analysis as the primary method, balanced by equal-weighting and Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) expert-weighted composites as sensitivity benchmarks. Findings: The hybrid specification yields a valid, reliable and discriminating governance index (Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin = 0.78; Cronbach's α = 0.83) with a regional ordering of six dimensions that broadly converges with the Auditor-General's audit outcomes and National Treasury's financial health assessments for 2024/25. Fiscal and audit dimensions dominate the first principal component, while service delivery and transparency contribute distinct secondary components that capture non-fiscal variation in governance quality. Practical Implications: The SAMGI offers a defensible, replicable, and policy-relevant tool for benchmarking municipal governance quality. It enables national and provincial treasuries, sector regulators, and oversight bodies to identify structural weaknesses, target Section 139-type interventions more precisely, and track governance reform trajectories over time. Originality/Value: The study contributes to the public governance measurement literature by combining the systemic, theory-driven indicator framework of the Worldwide Governance Indicators and the Mo Ibrahim Index of African Governance with the institutional granularity of South African municipal reporting. It is the first composite index to integrate 2024/25 audit, Measuring Municipal Governance Quality-Pamba (2026) fiscal, household-survey, and administrative variables in a single rigorously validated metric for South African municipalities.

detail.abstract: This paper analyses EU and Member State fiscal responses to two fuel price crises: the 2022-23 Russia-Ukraine shock and the 2026 Iran-Hormuz shock, across Eurosuper 95, diesel, and heating oil. Using weekly z-score analysis of Brent, wholesale, and retail price series, we document a consistent one-week crude-to-retail transmission lag and persistent "rockets and feathers" asymmetry in both episodes. A panel fixed-effects demand model estimated across 26 Member States (1999-2024) finds price-inelastic demand; VAT and excise components are uniformly insignificant, indicating that tax interventions operate through the retail price channel alone with no instrument-specific salience effect. Major intervening Member States collectively forgone approximately €19.3 billion, stimulating 1,543 thousand additional tonnes of consumption at a cost of roughly €12,500 per tonne. Croatia's shift from price caps to excise adjustment between the two crises, provides a natural experiment in crisis instrument design.

title: A Flood of Reports

detail.abstract:
A flood of reports and analysis is showing up everywhere. On LinkedIn. In company communications. In board packs, market scans, strategy notes and weekly updates that used to take a week and now take an hour.

So here is the question I keep asking. Will all of this raise the real asset of a company — a knowledgeable workforce? Or will it leave us with thousands of plans and analyses that nobody reads, and managers who cannot decide anything because there is always one more report coming?

My prediction is that both are already happening, and which one wins inside a particular company depends on one thing: the current knowledge level and expertise of its management. Not the tools. The people receiving the output.

detail.abstract: Aggressive corporate tax planning may benefit stakeholders economically while conflicting with norms of fairness and corporate responsibility. Tax transparency and public scrutiny make firms' tax practices salient to stakeholders, potentially bringing moral concerns into conflict with the economic benefits of affiliation. We examine how individuals resolve this moral-economic trade-off as prospective investors, consumers, and employees. In an incentivized online experiment with 6,773 participants across eight OECD countries, we measure the additional compensation-the moral premium-required to affiliate with a firm presented as tax aggressive rather than tax responsible. Sixty-three percent demand a positive premium; across all participants, the average is 2.65 percentage points. Employees are most likely to require compensation and investors least likely, whereas consumers demand the largest premiums among those requiring compensation. These stakeholder-specific patterns are broadly consistent across countries, although average premiums vary substantially. At the country level, moral premiums are positively associated with stronger institutional representation of employee stakeholder interests and negatively associated with institutional quality and a more right-leaning average political orientation. Our findings demonstrate that moral concerns about corporate tax avoidance can affect stakeholder choices even when acting on those concerns entails foregoing private economic benefits, providing a behavioral basis through which tax transparency can generate reputational pressure.

detail.abstract: We experimentally study how uncertainty about future profit taxation affects firms' investment plans and other business decisions. Using a randomized information experiment with German firms, we vary perceived tax uncertainty around a common expert-based forecast of expected change in profit taxation. The treatment increases posterior uncertainty without inducing corresponding differences in changes in posterior expected tax path. Higher perceived tax uncertainty reduces planned investment, particularly in intangible investment and R&D, with stronger effects at longer planning horizons. Firms also adjust other planned decisions. Overall, the results show that the uncertainty of future profit taxation matters for firm behavior independently of the expected tax-rate changes.

title: Inheritance Customs and the European Marriage Pattern
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Universite Libre de Bruxelles, and

detail.title: Inheritance Customs and the European Marriage Pattern
detail.abstract: Centuries before the demographic transition, the European Marriage Pattern (EMP) limited fertility in Western Europe through high celibacy, late marriage, and nuclear households. Whether the EMP reflected female empowerment or instead financial hardship remains debated. This paper shows that local inheritance institutions determined where economic opportunity strengthened the EMP and where the EMP reflected poverty. We construct a new atlas of 2,486 rural and urban inheritance customs in France and Belgium and combine it with genealogical data on 75,000 women born between 1500 and 1750. We show that the EMP manifested alongside earning opportunities where inheritance included women and younger siblings, but that the EMP reflected economic distress where inheritance was inegalitarian; that effects differed between urban and rural areas; and that they persisted over centuries. We develop and estimate a structural model in which inheritance rules affect marriage decisions through female empowerment and financial constraints. The estimates imply that roughly 65 percent of celibacy reflected choice rather than constraint, suggesting that the EMP was heterogeneous but primarily a positive force for female empowerment.

title: Who Benefits from Copyright? The Evidence So Far and a Research Agenda
affiliations: University of Lausanne - Faculty of Business and Economics (HEC Lausanne)

detail.title: Who Benefits from Copyright? The Evidence So Far and a Research Agenda
detail.abstract: Copyright can encourage creative production by giving owners control over the use of a work, but the same control can make access and follow-on creation more costly. Assessing this tradeoff requires knowing how copyright revenue is distributed along the creative value chain and which economic decisions change as a result. We synthesize empirical evidence on creative labor, contracts and payments, investment by intermediaries, and the licensing and use of existing works. Historical and experimental evidence shows that expected rewards and additional resources can increase creative activity, although the response depends on the payment arrangement and the task. Contracts divide revenue and specify who supplies finance and services and who bears demand risk. Evidence that the share retained by intermediaries causes additional creative production remains limited. For existing works, fragmented ownership can obstruct licensing and the consolidation of complementary permissions can increase use, while creator control is associated with greater availability. Generative artificial intelligence makes the unresolved distributional question especially visible: the owners paid for access to existing material are not necessarily the creators whose future sales or commissions face competition. We develop a research agenda around three questions: who ultimately receives copyright revenue, whether additional income changes production, and how ownership affects access and reuse. Evidence on these relationships is needed to distinguish private returns from copyright's effects on social welfare.

title: Shipping to America
affiliations: Tsinghua University, , ,  and University of Oxford

detail.title: Shipping to America
detail.abstract: We study the macroeconomic and trade-policy implications of disruptions to U.S.-bound shipping routes. Standard models treat them as iceberg-cost shocks, conflating the shock with the response to it. Using satellite vessel-tracking data, we construct route-level measures of potential and effective capacity for all U.S.-bound container ships from 2016 to 2025. Uti-lization losses in recent disruptions ran 20 to 40 percentage points, and began months before port congestion became visible. We embed these measures in a general equilibrium model in which firms reallocate a common fleet without internalizing the congestion they create and price above marginal cost, while importers’ sourcing responds to route profitability. The reallocation triggered by a disruption then has first-order welfare effects, and the route’s Do-mar weight is not a sufficient statistic for its welfare cost. The 2021 West Coast crisis and the 2023–2024 Red Sea attacks cost 0.69% and 0.35% of output. Naval protection of Red Sea shipping generated benefits of 0.04–0.08% of output at a fiscal cost of 0.02%. Tariffs decongest the routes they tax, offsetting or even reversing their conventional welfare cost.

title: Implications of Inflation Forecast Targeting for Fiscal Policy
affiliations: University of Heidelberg and Heidelberg University

detail.title: Implications of Inflation Forecast Targeting for Fiscal Policy
detail.abstract: Many central banks, such as the ECB, explicitly tie monetary policy decisions to medium-term inflation forecasts. Standard New Keynesian models, however, typically abstract from this feature. This paper studies equilibrium determinacy in a New Keynesian model in which monetary policy targets inflation at a forecast horizon larger than one. When policy reacts to sufficiently distant inflation expectations, it may fail to pin down a unique equilibrium. In fact, stronger reactions to expected inflation can make indeterminacy more likely. Whether monetary policy can achieve determinacy at a given forecast horizon depends not only on satisfying the Taylor principle, which provides a lower bound on the inflation coefficient, but also on an upper bound. This upper bound becomes more restrictive as the forecast horizon increases, until determinacy becomes impossible, and depends critically on the slope of the New Keynesian Phillips curve. A sufficiently flat Phillips curve preserves a non-empty determinacy region even at longer forecast horizons. Introducing fiscal policy can restore determinacy across all forecast-horizon targets by ensuring a unique stationary equilibrium. However, this holds only if fiscal policy does not actively stabilize government debt, which implies that inflation forecast targeting at medium horizons puts monetary policy in a passive position and invites fiscal dominance.

detail.abstract: Biodiversity loss is among the most severe environmental externalities facing commodity markets, yet its pricing in futures and spot markets remains poorly understood. Agricultural commodities, timber, and livestock are simultaneously the primary drivers of global habitat destruction and the assets most directly exposed to the ecosystem services they degrade. This double materiality operates more immediately in commodity markets than in the equity and bond markets on which the biodiversity-finance literature has concentrated its attention. This paper provides a critical review and research agenda organized around three pillars. First, we map ecological indicators, footprint-based metrics, and text-based attention proxies. Second, we trace the transmission channels through which ecosystem degradation reaches commodity prices: physical supply disruption, regulatory transition risk, and the financial investor channel, with particular attention to the scale-versus-intensity distinction in regulatory design. Third, we review the theoretical frameworks for commodity biodiversity pricing, explain why equity and bond results cannot be transplanted into commodity markets, and present the first systematic commodity-market evidence, consistent with intensity-based biodiversity risk being priced in spot but not futures returns. Because the commodity-specific pricing literature is nascent, the empirical section combines a review of existing conditional evidence with an original empirical analysis of a commodity return panel data set. We conclude with a structured research agenda centered on causal identification, the spot-futures wedge, climate-biodiversity integration, and data infrastructure.

title: Assessing Hypothetical Scenarios for Estimating Labor Supply Responses: Evidence from a Pension Reform

detail.title: Assessing Hypothetical Scenarios for Estimating Labor Supply Responses: Evidence from a Pension Reform
detail.abstract: We assess whether survey responses to hypothetical policy scenarios can recover actual labor supply responses from policy variation. We study the German Mütterrente, a pension benefit crediting parents for child-rearing, benchmarking against Artmann et al. (forthcoming). Surveying mothers and fathers about a hypothetical reform modeled on that expansion, we find that mothers expect to reduce their labor supply, with an implied marginal propensity to earn of −0.65—close to the quasi-experimental estimate of −0.54. The response is sensible across subgroups, falls mainly on the extensive margin, and spills over to fathers. In the aggregate, spousal predictions match partners’ own reports.

detail.abstract: A market maker on an options book loses to counterparties who know something and earns from those who do not, but on an anonymous venue the two can only be told apart by proxy. Derive settles on chain, so its public tape names both wallets. On 603 940 fills in BTC, ETH and HYPE options between January 2024 and September 2026, the maker's mean markout thirty minutes after the fill is +13.05 USDC per contract: a half spread of +15.70 less adverse selection of-2.65. Fees, rebates and delta hedging leave a net edge of +8.93. The loss is extremely concentrated, with ten taker wallets carrying 90.5 per cent of it, and those ten are almost the entirety of the two professional counterparty classes. Trade size and sweeps, the standard proxies for toxic flow, explain none of it once instrument-by-day fixed effects are included. Four hypotheses were registered before any markout was computed; three are rejected.

title: Terra Incognita: The Economics of a Shrinking World
affiliations: and

detail.title: Terra Incognita: The Economics of a Shrinking World
detail.abstract: As of 2026, humanity is likely below replacement fertility. That has never happened before, not in wars or pandemics. But the real surprise is that the fall has been concentrated in low- and middle-income countries and among poorer and less educated women. We fit a single-factor model to 236 countries since 1950: the common component peaked in 1978, and what drives fertility down today are country-specific trends, 219 of them negative and not one leveling off. None of the commonly cited mechanisms can account for this pattern, so we offer a conjecture: modernity itself, which makes a third child expensive and childlessness cheap. Children come in integers, so it takes very little to move a cohort’s fertility rate from 1.8 to 1.3. And nothing in an economy pushes fertility back to 2.1. We close with the main economic consequences, in particular slow growth.

detail.title: The Impact of Senior Living Facilities on Medicare Spending

detail.abstract: With the growing elderly population in the U.S., senior living facilities-residences that provide auxiliary services for seniors-have drastically expanded to serve the increasing needs of this population. These services are often much less intensive than those provided by skilled nursing facilities, yet they still have the potential to impact residents' health outcomes and healthcare usage. Despite this potential, the literature lacks a clear understanding of the impact of senior living facilities on healthcare utilization among seniors. In this paper, we study the effects of senior living facilities on Medicare utilization by employing an instrumental variables approach on the entirety of Medicare fee-for-service claims data from 2011 to 2019. The analysis reveals that a higher density of senior living facilities in a Health Service Area (HSA) reduces admissions to, and payments for, skilled nursing facilities and home health services. Our estimates suggest that a one-standard-deviation increase (0.246) in senior living facilities per 1,000 Medicare beneficiaries leads to annual reductions in Medicare expenditures of $27.623 million for skilled nursing care and $17.958 million for home health services within an HSA. These results have important implications for policymakers seeking cost-effective strategies to manage Medicare spending amid rising enrollment pressures.

title: The Stories We Tell: Societal Narratives and Support for the Far Right
affiliations: NHH Norwegian School of Economics, WZB Berlin Social Science Center,  and Technische Universität Berlin (TU Berlin)

detail.title: The Stories We Tell: Societal Narratives and Support for the Far Right
detail.abstract: In two studies using AI-assisted qualitative interviews, we ask a representative sample of the German electorate (N = 1, 013) to reflect on the most important societal events of the last 15 years. We document that far-right supporters construct systematically different narratives about the recent past. First, they recall different events — with a strong focus on migration-related issues. Second, even when they do consider the same events, they are more likely to blame the establishment and describe events more negatively and with greater emotional intensity. We further document that these narratives are associated with policy preferences, and that far right supporters are more inclined than supporters of other parties to prioritize cultural over economic issues. Together, our findings reveal that partisan divides extend to how citizens remember and interpret shared national experiences.

title: Estimating Ethnic and Status Inequality in Pakistan without a Group Identifier

detail.title: Estimating Ethnic and Status Inequality in Pakistan without a Group Identifier

detail.abstract: No Pakistani household survey records ethnicity, caste, or religion while the census that records them collects no welfare measure. This article argues that group inequality in Pakistan runs along two structurally different axes, measures both, and situates them within the personal distribution of income. The horizontal axis separates territorially concentrated ethnolinguistic groups which are formally equal before the law. The vertical axis separates ranked status groups namely the zat and biradari hierarchy among Muslims and the religious minorities whose subordination is partly codified. Joining 2023 census composition to district poverty and literacy estimates across 126 districts and recovering group means by populationweighted ecological inference, the article finds between-group inequality of 0.323 in the poverty headcount and 0.143 in literacy. A mean logarithmic deviation decomposition places between 14 and 24 per cent of total consumption inequality between ethnolinguistic groups. This share is insensitive to the assumed national Gini. Disaggregated by sex, between-group inequality in female literacy is 0.241 against 0.080 for males. So, ethnic inequality in Pakistan is principally an inequality in the schooling of girls. The same method fails on the vertical axis and returns the wrong sign for Punjab's Christian population which lives in the country's richest districts while occupying its most stigmatised occupations. That reversal is evidence for the nesting claim and it contains a corollary for the decomposition. The withingroup residual is not individual inequality since the entire ranked status axis sits inside it unmeasured. Set against World Inequality Database estimates that give Pakistan's top decile 41.7 per cent of pre-tax national income, the result is an inequality structure in which one group axis is measurable while second is structurally invisible.

title: A Path is not a Forecast: Information Structures in Macroeconomic Scenario Analysis An Application to Oil-market Disruptions from the Iran Conflict

detail.title: A Path is not a Forecast: Information Structures in Macroeconomic Scenario Analysis An Application to Oil-market Disruptions from the Iran Conflict

declarations.declarationOfInterest: As a part of my research at KAPSARC. It does not reflect in any way KAPSARC opinion and all the mistakes and arguments are purely my own.

detail.abstract: Macroeconomic scenarios are typically defined by paths for conditioning variables. We argue that a path is not a sufficient statistic: the same realised path can generate different decisions depending on whether agents know it in advance or experience it as a sequence of unanticipated innovations, and on how they price uncertainty around its continuation. A simple analytical model shows that, when impact resources are predetermined, information primarily changes their allocation. We quantify these mechanisms in a nonlinear DSGE model of an oil-exporting economy during the 2026 Iran conflict. The conflict combined a large oil-market disruption with conflicting and repeatedly revised signals about its duration and resolution, so the same current outcome could support very different beliefs about its continuation. Holding the realised oil-price and oil-production paths fixed, we cross two information structures: i) full-path information and ii) sequential surprise with linear and nonlinear decision rules, and add higher-order risk-pricing and stochastic-volatility counterfactuals. This design isolates the value of full information and separates it from nonlinear curvature, approximation error, constant-volatility risk, and time-varying uncertainty. We find that information element is negligible in the impact output but large in consumption, investment, sectoral allocation, and the external account. Full information can substantially discipline investment, while nonlinearities make the information effect strongly state-dependent. Higher perceived volatility induces investment retrenchment and external saving even when the realised oil path is unchanged. A macroeconomic scenario should therefore specify a realised path, an information structure, and a conditional risk law.

detail.abstract: News shocks should influence decision making, but only when they contain novel information. We test this hypothesis using high-frequency trading-card sales data. We exploit the natural experiment created by hall-of-fame (HOF) announcements by estimating interrupted time series models. Overall, HOF announcements trigger a 29% jump in card prices. However, this is driven by announcements regarding marginal candidates whose inductions were not fully expected. We distinguish between "anticipated" and "surprise" inductees using advanced statistics. There is only modest price movement in players whose inductions were expected, while surprise inductees experience a statistically significant, 35% boost.

title: A Model of Macroeconomic Policies with Endogenously Insurable Exchange Rates
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Model of Macroeconomic Policies with Endogenously Insurable Exchange Rates
detail.abstract: We propose a tractable small-open-economy model in which uncovered interest parity premia on foreign exchange (FX) markets arise from the endogenous lack of insurability of exchange rate risks. Asymmetric information about monetary policy can make the tails of the exchange rate distribution uninsurable in FX hedging markets, which in turn generates premia in FX spot markets because of the risk aversion of lenders holding the external debt. There is a role for government intervention because of an information sensitivity externality: agents do not internalize that their actions can reduce the insurability of exchange rates. The model predicts that premia may be amplified by weaknesses in monetary, fiscal, and financial policy frameworks, and can be reduced through reforms which reduce the sensitivity of exchange rates to private information. The constrained efficient policy depends on the composition of external lenders and may include delegation of monetary policy to an “aloof central banker”, constraints on fiscal policy, more active use of macroprudential tools, and institutions which limit asymmetric information.

detail.abstract: Aggregate inflation conceals how a large price shock is distributed across sectors and how that distribution evolves. This paper asks whether large inflationary episodes reveal a cross-sector response geometry that recurs across events while the timing and sign of propagation remain event-specific. It then compares the realised sectoral disturbance with both the price direction reached by monetary tightening and the sectoral location of the accompanying production adjustment. Applied to harmonised euro-area and US data, the approach reveals a recurrent hierarchy of relative price mobility but no universal propagation path. In a 39-sector euro-area validation, the hierarchy explains 72.8% of held-out response variation, with median cosine similarity 0.874 and median rank correlation 0.811. Identified ECB tightening aligns most clearly with the household-energy source; its downstream price-direction coverage is limited and uncertain, while the contraction in production is broader and differently allocated. The resulting separation between response geometry and event-dependent propagation provides a compact diagnostic of where monetary policy reaches an inflationary episode and where its real adjustment is borne.

detail.abstract: This article challenges the assumption that legal harmonization within the European Union ensures effective anti-corruption governance. Despite EU-compliant frameworks, institutional integrity remains highly uneven across subnational territories. We introduce the Regional Integrity Framework (RIF), a diagnostic approach that integrates citizen perceptions, procurement indicators, and enforcement activation measures to capture regional integrity performance. The analysis suggests that formal convergence can conceal functional divergence, as peripheral regions often exhibit weaker administrative capacity, limited oversight, and uneven institutional activation. A mixed-methods application that combines panel analysis with an illustrative comparison of Sofia and Vidin, Bulgaria, demonstrates how the RIF can diagnose territorial integrity gaps within a shared legal framework. Conceptually, the study reframes anti-corruption as a territorially embedded problem of institutional activation; methodologically, it offers a transferable framework for identifying enforcement asymmetries and governance disparities in multi-level systems.

detail.abstract: This paper develops feasible inference for the continuous leverage effect, volatility of volatility, and normalized continuous leverage effect from high-frequency data in the presence of jumps, market microstructure noise, and random observation times. Building on the Truncated S-TSRV, we construct estimators that remain valid when the observation times are general stopping times, without imposing restrictive parametric or regularity conditions on the sampling mechanism or specifying a particular form of price-time dependence. We establish central limit theorems and consistent asymptotic variance estimators through a new framework for handling nested overlapping windows, which is applicable to a broad class of volatility estimators. Monte Carlo simulations examine the finite-sample performance of the proposed methods, and an empirical application to high-frequency ETF data illustrates their practical relevance.

detail.abstract: The rapid, near-universal availability of generative artificial intelligence has quietly dismantled a load-bearing assumption of modern education: that the ability to produce a correct answer, unaided, is a reliable proxy for competence. When a free chatbot can solve, explain, and format the majority of tasks assigned in a conventional grade-ladder curriculum, the traditional coupling of assessment to information recall and reproduction becomes unstable. This paper argues that the appropriate response is neither to ban AI from education nor to treat it as an unqualified substitute for instruction, but to redesign the underlying architecture of how learners progress and how that progression is verified. We introduce Open Adaptive Competency Education (OACE), a design-science artifact that reorganizes learning around a competency graph rather than a fixed age-grade-subject ladder, and that embeds a reliance-aware progression mechanism: a formal logic by which a learner’s documented pattern of tool dependence — measured using constructs adapted from the emerging AIreliance and cognitive-offloading literature — becomes an explicit input into whether, when, and how a learner advances to the next competency node. This integration is, to our knowledge, novel: existing work independently addresses competency-graph curriculum structures, AI-reliance measurement, and assist-versus-test transfer effects, but no prior architecture connects reliance measurement directly to progression logic within a single implementable system. Following the Design Science Research (DSR) methodology of Hevner et al. (2004) and the process model of Peffers et al. (2007), this paper (1) identifies the problem and its objectives, (2) presents the OACE architecture and its core mechanism, (3) demonstrates the architecture through an illustrative learner walkthrough, (4) evaluates its plausibility against existing empirical findings, and (5) proposes a concrete pathway — a factorial study design — for future empirical validation. We conclude by discussing the architecture’s risks, equity implications, and the honest boundaries of what a conceptual, non-empirically-validated design contribution can claim.

title: Book Review: Critical Wage Theory: Why Wage Justice is Racial Justice
affiliations: Cornell University ILR School

detail.title: Book Review: Critical Wage Theory: Why Wage Justice is Racial Justice

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: Ruben Garcia's Critical Wage Theory makes one consensual argument and three less-consensual ones. The consensual claim—that movements for better wages and movements for racial justice are politically and normatively aligned—is well-trodden ground, and Garcia covers it capably, case by case, chapter by chapter. I take up his three sub-theses in turn. I endorse his preference for wage law over antidiscrimination law as the better vehicle for racial justice: antidiscrimination law has failed, and wage law has not. His agnosticism toward the economics of wages, I reject; ignoring the politics of that economics—as when the NAACP endorsed Uber's minimum-wage evasion in the name of jobs for people of color—does the project no favors. His focus on wages and employment as the site of struggle, at a moment when platforms, LLMs, and uncounted care work already operate outside that frame, leaves me ambivalent. Garcia's book is a useful map of a consensus few in the field now question. Whether that consensus can hold as waged employment itself frays is a harder question, and not one the book's conclusion answers.

title: Internet Connectivity as Development Multiplier
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Internet Connectivity as Development Multiplier

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Loose Affiliation with United Nations. ECOSOC application pending.
declarations.funderStatement: Institute of Internet Economics

detail.abstract: This paper examines how expanding internet capability is converted into broader economic and human development. Its central argument is that connectivity matters not as access in itself, but because it enlarges the range of actions available to households, firms, governments, and institutions. By reducing the costs of information, coordination, and exchange, digital networks can broaden participation, reorganize production, and improve the reach and quality of public and private services. Those gains can, in turn, make further investment in skills, infrastructure, and digital capacity more valuable, producing a cumulative structural effect rather than a fixed broadband-to-GDP multiplier. Evidence from markets, firms, public services, connected infrastructure, and advanced computing suggests that outcomes depend less on the presence of the technology than on the capacity of institutions to absorb and use it. The relevant measure of success is therefore broader human prosperity: higher productivity and income, stronger services, wider inclusion, and sustained improvements in living standards.

title: Agreement and Unawareness under Misinterpreted Evidence
affiliations: Monash University - Department of Economics and Monash University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Agreement and Unawareness under Misinterpreted Evidence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicting interest to declare
declarations.funderStatement: No funder to report

detail.abstract: Agreement and no-speculation can survive systematic misinterpretation of evidence. On a finite state space, actual signals and their interpreted meanings form two matched partitions. Non-deludedness requires their encodings to agree pointwise; mass balance requires agreement in distribution. Mass balance restores partitional common belief and an Aumann-style agreement theorem despite individual failures of truth and introspection. The ordinary informationpartition theorem is a special case. Once the interpretation rules admit a full-support balancing measure, agreement and the stated no-speculation conclusion are robust to changes in the shared conditioning measure. More generally, a sharp bound controls disagreement by the balance defect relative to the probability of the common-belief region. We also study symmetric higher-order ignorance: under partition range, global KU requires at least five states for nontriviality, while an inclusion-antichain range rules out Boolean closure of awareness. A contracting game links these interpretation errors to strict speculative trade and identifies a second-order belief obstruction to commonly believed execution. All constructions use ordinary events and probability measures on one state space.

title: Diversity as Value, Resilience, and Adaptability in Coalitions

detail.title: Diversity as Value, Resilience, and Adaptability in Coalitions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is purely theoretical and mathematical in nature. No human participants, animal subjects, or personal data were involved.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: We study cooperative games in which the characteristic function is not assumed but constructed from the structural properties of the agents who compose the coalition. Each agent carries a capability that decomposes into a scale component and a directional component; the coalition's collective state is summarized by a matrix that aggregates these directional components. The value of a coalition equals the number of independent capability directions it spans, times an aggregate resource measure. Because the characteristic function now has internal structure, three problems that classical cooperative game theory leaves open can be addressed. First, we show that agents with complementary capability directions are worth strictly more together than apart, and we derive an exact decomposition of the Shapley value into a scale-weighted base return and a bonus for expanding the coalition's capability span. The span bonus is a scarcity rent that dissipates as the coalition grows past its capability dimension. Second, we show that the coalition's vulnerability to environmental shocks is governed by its weakest capability direction: the threshold for catastrophic failure is positive if and only if the coalition spans the full capability space, and near homogeneity this threshold is controlled linearly by a continuous diversity measure. Third, we establish that the coalition's expected adaptive improvement under random shocks is proportional to the variance across members' capability directions. A separation theorem shows that all structural quantities are invariant to the choice of aggregate resource function, establishing a two-layer architecture in which structural diagnosis is domaininvariant while economic valuation is domain-specific. We apply the framework to extractive institutions, where a structural fragility result establishes that extractiondriven homogenization destroys all three channels simultaneously.

title: Micro-foundations of Extractive Institutions

detail.title: Micro-foundations of Extractive Institutions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is purely theoretical and mathematical in nature. No human participants, animal subjects, or personal data were involved.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: We study the micro-foundations of extractive institutions (allocations in which an identified elite captures more than its fair share of the coalition's value). Classical cooperative game theory takes the characteristic function as an unexplained primitive, and its stability machinery requires convexity, which fails in the present setting. Using Coalition Intelligence Theory, which endows the characteristic function with an explicit, decomposable causal structure, we derive the three-class partition that extractive institutions impose on the society (elite, enforcers, masses) as a theorem rather than an empirical regularity. From the single allocation primitive that the elite's capture exceeds its Shapley value, together with three empirically grounded postulates on enforcement technology, collective action, and within-mass allocation, we establish four groups of results. First, the value game is provably non-monotone and non-convex, ruling out core-based stability methods. Second, sustaining extraction at scale forces a three-class partition with a strict per-capita pay hierarchy. Third, each period of tolerated coordinated opposition taxes the regime's survival probability geometrically, and deep extraction (paying the masses below standalone value) forces atomization of every mass subcoalition, while shallow extraction admits an indefinite stalemate, locating a structural bifurcation at a measurable pay rate. Fourth, the inclusive allocation itself can be blocked in this non-convex game, sharpening the open stability problem. No solution concept, ideology, culture, or ruler psychology enters the derivation; every instability claim is existential and certified by comparing a coalition's standalone value to its actual pay.

title: How Do Income Shortfalls Relative to Recent Living Standards Explain Households’ Depressive Symptoms?
affiliations: Pondicherry University - Department of Statistics, Szent Istvan University and Southampton Business School, University of Southampton

detail.title: How Do Income Shortfalls Relative to Recent Living Standards Explain Households’ Depressive Symptoms?
detail.abstract: We examine whether income losses relative to a household's recent living standard explain mental health more strongly than comparable income gains. Using longitudinal data from the Korea Welfare Panel Study, we construct a household-specific income benchmark from realised disposable income over the previous three waves and decompose deviations from this benchmark into downside shortfalls and upside gains. Our results show a pronounced asymmetry for depressive symptoms: income below the recent benchmark is associated with higher epidemiologic depression scores, whereas income above the benchmark is associated with an improvement that is approximately one-quarter as large in absolute value. This asymmetry is concentrated among households with low predetermined liquid assets, for whom the downside association is roughly twice as large as among households with greater liquidity. By contrast, the evidence is weaker for self-esteem and directionally similar but imprecise for new-onset suicidal ideation. The benchmark-relative association remains after accounting for annual income changes, current income, individual specific trends, and a series of placebo and robustness tests, including benchmark shuffle exercises. Although the estimates should not be interpreted as identifying a structural reference-point mechanism, they suggest that recent living standards contain information beyond current income in understanding the mental health consequences of income loss. The findings imply that analyses of economic hardship should consider not only current income but also whether households have fallen below their own recent standard of living and their capacity to smooth adverse income shocks.

title: Internet Economic Spheres and the New Geography of the Global Internet
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Internet Economic Spheres and the New Geography of the Global Internet

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Loose affiliation with United Nations. ECOSOC Application pending
declarations.funderStatement: Institute of Internet Economics

detail.abstract: The Internet is technically global; the economies that have developed through it are not. As connectivity has spread, countries have developed recurring differences in Internet reach, economic use, institutional support, and dependency. This paper describes those regional associations as Internet Economic Spheres, or the Internet Economies of the world. The framework identifies eight geographic Internet Economic Spheres: USA + Canada; Latin America; Europe; Asia excluding China; China; MENA and the Levant; Sub-Saharan Africa; and Australia + New Zealand. A ninth analytical classification, Developing, sits alongside the geographic spheres without constituting a sphere itself. It captures a recurring developmental condition across regions where connectivity has advanced faster than the institutional, commercial, financial, or productive systems required to use it fully. The spheres are evaluated as multidimensional economic profiles rather than reduced to a single maturity score. ICT reach establishes the technical base; household, business, financial, institutional, and productive use reveal how connectivity is absorbed and to what ends. Persistent internal structural differences form sub-economies within the parent spheres. The result is an additional layer of terrestrial economic geography: one interoperable network sustaining regionally differentiated economic systems.

title: How Much Authority Should a Predictive Signal Have in Portfolio Choice?
affiliations: , FernUniversität in Hagen - Faculty of Business Administration and Economics and University of Münster - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: How Much Authority Should a Predictive Signal Have in Portfolio Choice?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicting interests.
declarations.funderStatement: Schüssler acknowledges financial support from the Danish Finance Institute.

detail.abstract: Equal weighting is hard to beat. Yet this need not mean predictive information has little portfolio value. Comparing 1/N with an optimized portfolio bundles two decisions: which assets to hold and how much to allocate to each. We study the intermediate case in which predictive information selects a fixed-size equal-weight subset and, holding membership fixed, receives progressively greater authority over relative position sizes. In a stylized model, the predictive gain from selection is first order in the scale of predictive information, whereas attainable weighting gains are at most second order. In a Controlled-Information Experiment on realized U.S. stock returns, selection becomes valuable at weaker predictive alignment than weighting and remains more important when forecast magnitudes are attenuated accordingly. Feasible return forecasts reproduce the asymmetry pseudo-out-of-sample. Equal weighting can thus let predictive information determine membership while restricting its authority over position sizing; shrinkage regulates how much authority it receives.

title: Water, Water, Everywhere, Nor Any Drop to Drink? Rainfall Shock and Caste Violence in India
affiliations: University of Calcutta - Department of Economics and University of Calcutta - Department of Economics

detail.title: Water, Water, Everywhere, Nor Any Drop to Drink? Rainfall Shock and Caste Violence in India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.funderStatement: No funding for this paper.

detail.abstract: We investigate whether rainfall shocks influence ethnic violence against India's socially disadvantaged Scheduled Castes (SCs). Our findings indicate that both positive and negative rainfall shocks significantly increase crimes against SCs, with negative shocks having a greater effect. Beyond testing our baseline hypotheses, we propose two caste-specific conflict channels, access to drinking water and agrarian land relations, and examine their relevance. Our analysis suggests that crimes against SCs during rainfall shocks are more likely when water sources are located far from SC households but near upper-caste households. These effects are primarily driven by untouchabilityrelated and other hate crimes, with stronger effects observed during dry shocks. Interestingly, drought-prone areas experience fewer such incidents than non-drought-prone districts. We argue that districts regularly affected by drought tend to develop mechanisms of intercaste cooperation, which mitigate violence against SCs. Additionally, we find that rainfall shocks result in fewer anti-SC crimes in districts with a higher number of assembly constituencies reserved for SCs.

title: Systemic Resilience to Multi-Hazard Risk in Interconnected Economies: Transboundary and Intersectoral Spillovers in a Macroeconomic Agentbased Model
affiliations: International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA), International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA), , International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA), International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA), University of Hamburg and Karlsruhe Institute of Technology

detail.title: Systemic Resilience to Multi-Hazard Risk in Interconnected Economies: Transboundary and Intersectoral Spillovers in a Macroeconomic Agentbased Model

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There are no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was carried out as part of the MYRIAD-EU project, funded by the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme under grant agreement No. 101003276.

detail.abstract: Natural disasters can cause economic losses that extend beyond the directly damaged assets and locations through production, demand, credit, and trade linkages. Yet disaster-economic assessments often remain focused on single events, single countries, or direct-damage estimates, providing less evidence on how multi-hazard shocks propagate through interconnected economies and sectors. This paper applies a multi-country, multi-sector macroeconomic agent-based model, covering twenty-six EU Member States and sixty-two NACE industries, to analyse a stakeholderinformed sequential flood-drought-earthquake stress-test scenario in the Danube basin. The scenario is compared with a no-disaster baseline using matched-seed Monte Carlo simulations. The results show that cumulative output losses concentrate in directly affected economies, while economies without direct hazard exposure show positive deviations relative to baseline in several output, labour-market, and fiscal indicators; these deviations are interpreted as modelled reallocation of economic activity rather than welfare gains. Sectoral disruptions are concentrated in a limited set of country-sector pairs, particularly in agriculture, forestry, fishing, trade, tourism, and utilities, while bilateral trade flows show rerouting and reconstruction-related adjustments rather than a uniform collapse. The findings indicate that disaster-risk assessment in interconnected economies should complement direct-damage measures with diagnostics of transboundary propagation, sectoral persistence, and fiscal and labour-market spillovers.

title:
Reproductive Identity
Language, Reason, and Artificial Intelligence after Hegel and Marx 
Augustine's Psychological Trinity, Analytic Philosophy, and Ecological Realism

detail.title:
Reproductive Identity
Language, Reason, and Artificial Intelligence after Hegel and Marx 
Augustine's Psychological Trinity, Analytic Philosophy, and Ecological Realism

declarations.ethicsApproval: I have used AI to search for sources, structure the text, and finalize it.

detail.abstract: This article reconstructs a history of language, reason, and practical activity from Augustine through Kant, Hegel, Marx, the European linguistic turn, and analytic philosophy in order to formulate the concept of reproductive identity. Reproductive identity is not sameness, a fixed inner essence, or the final conceptual possession of the world. It is the historically open, materially conditioned work through which embodied individuals and communities sustain, repair, and develop the relations that enable their continuation. Augustine's psychological trinity supplies an early grammar of memory, understanding, and will or love; Kant clarifies the conditions of judgment and practical reason; Hegel understands concept and reality as mutually realised in activity; and Marx translates this movement into the communal metabolism through which human beings reproduce life in and through nature. The linguistic turn and analytic philosophy provide indispensable accounts of disclosure, difference, reference, truth, use, and normativity. The section on analytic philosophy distinguishes formal validity from situated inquiry and reconstructs practical reason as both normatively articulated and causally efficacious. Neither tradition, however, can settle the material and institutional conditions of the forms of life in which language works. The final sections develop ecological democracy and politically subordinate artificial intelligence as institutional consequences of the argument. Artificial intelligence is treated not as a sovereign subject but as a reversible public infrastructure whose legitimacy depends on ecological admissibility, traceability, contestability, repair, and the common reproduction of internal and external nature.

title: Brain Drain in Nigeria’s Health Sector: Patterns and Drivers of Early Career Health Care Workers Migration
affiliations: , Federal Medical Centre Ebute-Metta, Federal Medical Centre Ebute-Metta, Federal Medical Centre Ebute-Metta, Federal Medical Centre Ebute-Metta, Federal Medical Centre Ebute-Metta, Federal Medical Centre Ebute-Metta and Federal Medical Centre Ebute-Metta

detail.title: Brain Drain in Nigeria’s Health Sector: Patterns and Drivers of Early Career Health Care Workers Migration

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no conflict of interest to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was gotten from the Federal Medical center Ebute Metta
declarations.funderStatement: It was not funded

detail.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Nigeria is facing a substantial outflow of healthcare workers, particularly among early-career professionals, which is intensifying an already fragile health workforce crisis. This trend is occurring amid severe staffing shortages and doctor- and nurse-to-population ratios that remain below World Health Organization recommendations. The continued loss of skilled personnel threatens healthcare delivery and system performance. Understanding the patterns and underlying drivers of this migration is therefore critical for informing effective retention strategies and strengthening the long-term resilience of Nigeria’s health system. METHODOLOGY A facility-based, cross-sectional mixed-methods study was conducted among early-career healthcare workers at the Federal Medical Centre, Ebute Metta, Lagos, Nigeria. Data were collected using a structured, validated online questionnaire assessing migration intentions and their determinants, with qualitative insights obtained from open-ended responses. Data were analyzed using multivariable logistic regression and thematic analysis, with statistical significance set at P < 0.05. 
RESULTS: Among the 52 early-career healthcare workers surveyed in January 2026, most were young (69.2% aged 25–29 years), single (96.2%), medical doctors (86.5%), and house officers (75%) working in public facilities (80.8%). Participants reported working 60–80+ hours weekly with poor remuneration. Migration intention was near-universal (98.1%), with 88.5% planning to leave within five years and 71.7% already undertaking preparatory steps such as licensing and credential verification. Key push factors included poor working conditions, low pay, weak health system management, insecurity, and excessive workload, with 63.5% reporting job dissatisfaction. Preferred destinations were the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom. Notably, 88.5% indicated they would consider staying if salaries, staffing, infrastructure, and work–life balance improved. 
DISCUSSION: This study demonstrates that many early-career Nigerian healthcare workers are actively planning to migrate due to unfavorable working conditions, inadequate remuneration, excessive workload, and weak system management. These drivers mirror global trends in health workforce migration, where structural challenges strongly influence mobility decisions. Participants emphasized that improved compensation, better infrastructure, and supportive policies could reduce migration intentions. Overall, migration decisions were largely systemic rather than personal. While the study is limited by its small sample size and reliance on self-reported data, it provides timely frontline insights. Addressing these structural challenges is critical for workforce retention and long-term healthcare sustainability in Nigeria.

title: Protection Without Control? Gendered Formalisation Pathways for Female Informal Waste Pickers in Hanoi Amid Vietnam's Circular Transition
affiliations: , National Economic University, National Economic University, National Economics University of Vietnam (NEU) and National Economics University of Vietnam (NEU)

detail.title: Protection Without Control? Gendered Formalisation Pathways for Female Informal Waste Pickers in Hanoi Amid Vietnam's Circular Transition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship and/or publication of this article.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study used qualitative interviews with adult female informal waste pickers and involved no medical, clinical or other intervention. Under the institutional procedures applicable to this study, formal ethics committee approval was not required. This study emphasised voluntary participation, respectful engagement, written consent, anonymisation and confidential handling of interview data. Audio recordings were permanently deleted after transcription and transcript verification.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Policies for cleaner production and the circular economy increasingly formalise collection, traceability and recycling, but poorly designed formalisation can exclude workers who already recover valuable materials from waste. This study examines how gendered care responsibilities, occupational autonomy, technical and digital capability, informal market relations and institutional trust shape acceptable formalisation pathways for female informal waste pickers in Hanoi. This study draws on 30 semistructured interviews conducted in person over three months in 2026. The analysis identified seven connected themes and a pattern of conditional acceptance. Participants valued recognition, safer conditions, social protection, transparent prices, infrastructure and access to formal recycling systems. They resisted fixed schedules, burdensome administrative and digital reporting, loss of route autonomy and arrangements that severed trusted buyer relationships. Only five participants preferred employment as their primary pathway. The remaining 25 preferred hybrid arrangements, recognised independent work, protection without employment or flexible collective arrangements. This study identifies five pathways centred on workers and conceptualises formalisation as a configuration of protection, autonomy, capability, market access and control rather than a binary status change. For extended producer responsibility and municipal recycling systems, inclusive formalisation should strengthen traceability and worker protection while preserving the flexibility and relationships that sustain material recovery livelihoods.

title: Navigating the Patent Cliff: How Innovation Pipelines and Research and Development Intensity Drive Corporate Bond Yields and Capital Structure in Big Pharma

detail.abstract: The global pharmaceutical industry faces continuous structural challenges, most notably the "patent cliff", which threatens future cash flows and corporate solvency. While extensive research focuses on equity valuations and mergers and acquisitions (M&A) in life sciences, the implications for fixed-income markets remain less synthesized. This systematic review investigates how patent expiration timelines, research and development (R&D) intensity, and pipeline productivity influence corporate bond credit spreads and debt maturity structures in "Big Pharma". Furthermore, it examines how credit rating agencies price these intangible innovation risks. By synthesizing peer-reviewed literature and financial market research, this paper provides a comprehensive framework for understanding how corporate treasuries navigate intangible assets within debt capital markets (DCM).

title: Bipolar Blocs in the Eastern Mediterranean: Mecca Pact vs. Achilles Shield
affiliations: Lebanese University

detail.title: Bipolar Blocs in the Eastern Mediterranean: Mecca Pact vs. Achilles Shield

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this study.
declarations.funderStatement: NONE

detail.abstract: This article examines the emergence of two rival security architectures in the Eastern Mediterranean: the Greek-Israeli Achilles Shield air defense pact and the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement among Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan. Analyzing the timing, institutional design, and stated rationales of both agreements, the article argues that their near-simultaneous conclusion in August 2026 reflects a deliberate countervailing logic rather than coincidence. It traces how each pact combines military, economic, and energy dimensions, and assesses how Pakistan's nuclear status alters the regional deterrence calculus. The article further identifies a crisis-stability problem arising from the absence of cross-bloc communication channels and concludes that, despite the risks of a hardening bipolar order, avenues for expansion and diplomatic engagement remain open on both sides.

title: Macroeconomics of War and Recovery
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, International Monetary Fund (IMF) and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Macroeconomics of War and Recovery
detail.abstract: This paper studies the macroeconomic dynamics of conflicts and post-conflict recovery using a newly assembled global dataset covering 194 countries, including 170 conflict onsets and 158 conflict terminations, over the period 1946–2024. Using a local-projection difference-in-differences framework complemented by geocoded firm-level evidence, we trace the evolution of macroeconomic aggregates around conflict onset and termination. We make four contributions. First, output losses from conflicts typically exceed those associated with banking, currency, and sovereign debt crises, as well as severe natural disasters. Second, external-sector dynamics constitute a central mechanism through which wars amplify macroeconomic challenges, despite policymakers’ efforts to contain the war shock. Third, post-conflict recoveries are slow and uneven and depend critically on the durability of peace: conflict resumption stalls recovery prospects, while sustained peace produces only gradual recoveries relative to wartime losses. These recoveries are typically labor-led, while capital accumulation and productivity remain subdued. Fourth, firm-level evidence confirms this labor-led recovery and points to persistent financial constraints that hinder capital rebuilding during the postconflict period.

title:
Quantitative Assessment of Risk Factors Influencing Bunker Fuel Procurement and Price Volatility in the Nigerian Maritime Sector.

This is a Working Paper Currently Under Peer Review at Maritime Policy & Management

detail.title:
Quantitative Assessment of Risk Factors Influencing Bunker Fuel Procurement and Price Volatility in the Nigerian Maritime Sector.

This is a Working Paper Currently Under Peer Review at Maritime Policy & Management

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests.​
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Marine bunker fuel procurement accounts for 50% to 70% of commercial vessel operating expenditures, yet empirical quantitative modeling of bunkering price formation and volatility dynamics in West African littoral corridors remains absent from mainstream maritime economics literature. Operating along the critical Gulf of Guinea shipping corridor, the Nigerian bunkering market exhibits persistent structural frictions characterized by foreign exchange illiquidity, severe port congestion, offshore lightering overheads and maritime security surcharges. This study models long-run spatial price integration, dynamic asymmetric price transmission, error-correction mechanics and conditional price volatility for delivered Very Low Sulfur Fuel Oil (VLSFO 0.5% S) offshore Lagos relative to international energy benchmarks.

 

Using a high-frequency weekly dataset spanning January 2020 through June 2026 (T = 338), the empirical methodology integrates unit root tests with endogenous structural breaks (Zivot-Andrews), an Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) bounds testing procedure, a Nonlinear ARDL (NARDL) specification to test for asymmetric pass-through in the mean (“rockets and feathers”) and an asymmetric Exponential GARCH (EGARCH(1,1)) framework with a Student’s t error distribution. Bounds testing confirms a statistically significant long-run cointegrating relationship (F = 6.184, p < 0.01). Linear long-run pass-through elasticity from Rotterdam 0.5% VLSFO to delivered Lagos bunker prices is incomplete at 0.742, rejecting frictionless Law of One Price (LOOP) assumptions. Deviations adjust slowly (eta = -0.342), requiring approximately 2.9 weeks (20 days) to correct back to equilibrium.

 

The NARDL model reveals marked structural asymmetry in the mean: positive international price shocks transmit substantially faster and more completely (L+ = 0.892) than negative shocks (L- = 0.584), with Wald tests confirming long-run asymmetry (F = 11.42, p < 0.001). EGARCH estimation reveals strong volatility persistence (beta = 0.9124) and a statistically significant inverse leverage effect (gamma = 0.1384), demonstrating that positive price and supply shocks induce wider conditional volatility swings than downward corrections. An empirical decomposition of the delivered basis spread isolates an average $94.80/MT “Nigeria Premium” over Rotterdam parity, with vessel waiting times/demurrage accounting for 40.7% ($38.60/MT) and maritime security surcharges/escorts contributing 27.8% ($26.40/MT). Strategic implications for commercial fleet managers (dynamic charterparty indexing, bunkering geographic optimization) and policy recommendations for maritime regulators (dedicated bunkering berths, JWC Listed Area reassessment, domestic refining integration) are discussed.

title: Does Training on Future Data Pay? Look-Ahead Bias in Forecasting with Pretrained Models
affiliations: Xiamen University, WISE and School of Economics, Xiamen University, University of Science and Technology of China (USTC), Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences and

detail.title: Does Training on Future Data Pay? Look-Ahead Bias in Forecasting with Pretrained Models

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: We examine whether post-origin training information inflates the measured accuracy and economic value of financial forecasts. We evaluate five sets of financial time-series foundation models, each comprising independently trained annual vintages under U.S., global, and factor-augmented training environments, across 14 equity markets and four forecast horizons. Rolling comparisons vary the annual vintage for a fixed forecast; fixed-vintage comparisons hold the vintage fixed as target windows move across its training cutoff. Each alternative forecast is paired with an origin-aligned point-in-time (PIT) benchmark using identical numerical histories and inference protocols. In the U.S.-trained reference environment, post-origin vintages materially revise informative PIT forecasts but generally reduce accuracy in both designs. Pooled rolling comparisons yield higher mean squared forecast errors in 18 of 20 U.S. model-set-horizon combinations. The origin-crossing update also performs worse on average than an equally long pre-origin update. Under a common constrained allocation rule using one-month forecasts, median exposed-minus-PIT differences in annualized certainty-equivalent returns are -1.77 percentage points in the United States and -2.14 points internationally. Global and factor-augmented training produce more mixed predictive effects. An exact squared-error decomposition shows that revisions improve accuracy when their error-correcting benefit exceeds their mean squared magnitude; under U.S. training, alignment with PIT errors generally falls short of this requirement. Temporal exposure therefore establishes an information-set violation, not sufficient evidence of inflated predictive accuracy or investor value.

title: Demand for Dollars
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Demand for Dollars
detail.abstract: We study the determinants of US dollar demand across market participants and traded instruments using survey-based exchange rate and macroeconomic expectations. To empirically establish the relevance of survey-based expectations for currency flows, we leverage granular foreign exchange trading data and present three main findings. First, end-user investors increase their dollar purchases when they expect the US dollar to appreciate. Investment funds and non-dealer banks adjust their synthetic dollar borrowing in the FX swap market in response to forecasted changes in synthetic dollar funding costs. Second, cross-sectionally, investors rebalance along the factor structure of currency risk into dollars following an expected dollar appreciation. Third, the predictive power of survey forecasts weakens when forecaster disagreement or uncertainty rises. Overall, our findings show that long-horizon expectations predict dollar demand across spot, forward, and swap currency markets.

title: Three Origins and Three Amplification Mechanisms of Business Cycles: A Unified Theory and Empirical Tests Based on the K-Rule (Revision 23)
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Three Origins and Three Amplification Mechanisms of Business Cycles: A Unified Theory and Empirical Tests Based on the K-Rule (Revision 23)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
This paper constructs a unified business cycle framework anchored in the K rule. The foundational innovation is an independent derivation of the K rule from the proposition that growth in nominal purchasing power must match growth in real output. This replaces the unobservable and model dependent natural rate benchmark with observable nominal aggregate demand and an approximation to potential real GDP growth, thereby sidestepping the core theoretical difficulties facing DSGE and Austrian approaches.

Building on this benchmark, the paper makes three principal contributions. First, it revises the Austrian transmission mechanism through the structure of production. It abandons the traditional zero sum transfer assumption and argues that monetary deviations generate broad based overinvestment, with upstream and long duration projects responding more strongly because their valuations are more sensitive to discount rates. Duration is treated as a local financial sensitivity measure, not a global ordering of capital intensity. This approach sidesteps Cambridge capital critiques without claiming to resolve them.

Second, it strengthens monetarist transmission mechanisms. Credit is a conditional amplifier relative to the K rule benchmark. Credit amplifies monetary deviations once money has departed from the rule. Credit possesses independent causal properties only when it expands while money remains at the benchmark. The rule is extended from narrow money to broad credit.

Third, the framework bridges monetary and real cycles. It combines monetary quantity deviations with Schumpeterian innovation diffusion, yielding six idealized interaction states. These states explain why identical monetary accommodation can produce sharply different outcomes depending on the innovation phase. Cyclical causes are classified into three categories: monetary deviations, Schumpeterian innovation, and external political or natural shocks. Transmission channels are classified into three categories: financial and credit, real expenditure, and expectations and coordination.

Empirically, the paper tests whether monetary deviations and the credit amplifier rank recession onsets in the United States and seven European monetary regime segments across five non overlapping forecast horizons. In the locked U.S. primary specification, the AUC increment from adding credit excludes zero at the one to four quarter horizon. Europe does not replicate the short horizon U.S. result. Fixed credit ratios show mixed signs across horizons. The results indicate that the information in credit and its functional form depend on horizon, measurement, and institutional setting. They do not establish a universal causal amplification mechanism.

Water Scarcity and Corporate Financial Resilience: Evidence from Water-Intensive Firms 

(A Conceptual and Methodological Framework)

Water Scarcity and Corporate Financial Resilience: Evidence from Water-Intensive Firms 

(A Conceptual and Methodological Framework)

detail.abstract: Water scarcity has shifted from a diffuse environmental externality to a first-order financial concern for firms whose production systems, supply chains, and social licenses to operate depend on the availability and quality of fresh water. This chapter develops a conceptual and methodological framework for examining the relationships among water risk, corporate water stewardship, financial resilience, and sustainable firm performance in water-intensive industries. Anchored in the Resource-Based View and Stakeholder Theory, and extending the natural-resource-based view of the firm, the framework positions corporate water stewardship as a strategic capability that operates simultaneously as a direct antecedent of financial resilience and as a moderator that buffers the transmission of water risk into financial distress. Financial resilience-captured through profitability, liquidity, leverage, and cash-flow adequacy-is modeled as the mechanism through which water risk indirectly affects sustainable firm performance, which is conceptualized in triple-bottom-line terms. Six hypotheses specify the direct, moderating, mediating, and moderated-mediation pathways of the framework. A longitudinal paneldata research design is proposed, combining fixed-effects regression with regression-based conditional process analysis and bootstrapped inference to test the framework among publicly listed waterintensive firms using basin-level water-risk indicators, water stewardship disclosure data, and accounting-based financial measures. The chapter contributes an integrated account of how corporate water stewardship can convert escalating water risk into financial resilience and sustainable performance, with implications for corporate strategy, disclosure practice, and water-security investment by development finance institutions.

title: Household Composition and The Transmission of Aggregate Shocks

detail.title: Household Composition and The Transmission of Aggregate Shocks
