detail.abstract: We document that married households exhibit substantially larger consumption responses to monetary policy shocks than single households. This gap persists after accounting for standard demographic and balance-sheet characteristics, as well as labor-market dynamics. Married households dedicate a larger budget share to highly elastic luxuries and exhibit stronger responses within this category, jointly accounting for 81 percent of the response gap. We build a quantitative heterogeneous-agent model with non-homothetic preferences and consumption sharing in married households that matches these empirical patterns. By reducing the burden of basic needs, consumption sharing shifts expenditure composition toward luxuries and raises the within-good intertemporal elasticity of substitution, endogenously generating the aggregate response gap. Counterfactual experiments suggest that the secular decline in marriage has attenuated the aggregate consumption response to monetary policy.

title: Vertical Farming: Opportunities, Sustainability Trade-offs, and AI-Enabled Control—An Integrative Review
affiliations: University of Alberta, Northwestern University, University of Alberta and National Chung Hsing University

detail.title: Vertical Farming: Opportunities, Sustainability Trade-offs, and AI-Enabled Control—An Integrative Review

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no relevant financial or non-financial interests to disclose.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This review did not involve human participants, human data, or animals.
declarations.funderStatement: The authors declare that no funds, grants, or other support were received specifically for the preparation of this manuscript.

detail.abstract: Vertical farming (VF) integrates multilayer, predominantly soilless cultivation with controlled-environment agriculture and can provide high productivity per unit of building footprint, extensive water recirculation, year-round production, and potentially shorter supply chains. These advantages, however, do not necessarily translate into environmental or economic sustainability because fully indoor production requires substantial electricity, capital investment, and environmental-control infrastructure and remains commercially concentrated in a limited range of crops. This integrative review synthesizes agronomic, environmental, engineering, economic, and digital-technology evidence concerning VF. Evidence from life-cycle assessments, building-energy models, empirical commercial cases, crop-control experiments, and recent artificial-intelligence studies demonstrates that performance depends strongly on crop physiology, external climate, electricity mix, facility design, system boundaries, product value, and operating strategy. AI-enabled sensing, computer vision, prediction, optimization, and supervisory control offer opportunities to improve crop management and resource efficiency. Nevertheless, many of the largest reported improvements remain based on simulations, greenhouse applications, or context-specific studies rather than replicated commercial VF trials. To distinguish technological potential from demonstrated operational impact, this review organizes AI applications as an evidence-maturity pathway extending from measurement and state estimation to prediction, decision support, optimization, and validated closed-loop control. It also proposes research and reporting priorities that jointly consider crop performance, energy, water, greenhouse-gas emissions, reliability, and cost. The evidence indicates that VF should be evaluated as a crop-, location-, and market-specific production option rather than as an intrinsically sustainable technology.

title: Maternity Leave Duration and Birth Rates in China: A Provincial Panel Analysis

detail.title: Maternity Leave Duration and Birth Rates in China: A Provincial Panel Analysis

detail.abstract: Fertility decline has become a major demographic concern in countries facing population ageing and slower population growth. In China, the shift from fertility restriction to fertility support has increased attention to policies that may reduce the work-family costs of childbearing. Statutory maternity leave is one such policy, yet its relationship with fertility need not be linear. This paper examines the association between statutory maternity leave duration (MLD) and provincial birth rates in China using an annual panel of 30 mainland provinces from 2010 to 2024. The analysis estimates a province fixed-effects model linking birth rates to one-year-lagged MLD while accounting for observed provincial socioeconomic conditions and allowing for nonlinearity. The estimates show a statistically significant inverted-U-shaped conditional association: the fitted relationship initially rises, reaches a maximum at approximately 134.91 days, and subsequently declines within the observed sample range. This pattern remains under province-specific linear trends and a two-year-lag specification, although the fitted peak changes across models. The findings indicate a robust nonlinear association rather than a universal policy threshold or an optimal leave duration. They suggest that maternity leave should be considered alongside wider employment and family-support arrangements. The analysis is descriptive and does not identify causal effects.

title: Automated Instance Configuration for Cost-Aware Spark MLlib Workloads: A Bayesian Optimization Approach
affiliations: University of the Witwatersrand

detail.title: Automated Instance Configuration for Cost-Aware Spark MLlib Workloads: A Bayesian Optimization Approach

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I am the sole author of this research paper and declare that I have no known financial or personal relationships that could have influenced the research or its conclusions.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this research because it did not involve human participants, patients, or the collection of personal or sensitive data.

detail.abstract: Selecting an instance configuration, executor count, memory, and cores, for an Apache Spark MLlib training workload is conventionally handled by static defaults, manual tuning, or single-shot cost-aware heuristics that do not iteratively search the configuration space. This paper proposes and evaluates a Bayesian optimization (BO) approach to automated, cost-aware instance configuration for MLlib workloads, using a Gaussian process surrogate and expectedimprovement acquisition to search a three-dimensional configuration space (executor count, memory, cores) under a penalized cost-plus-SLO-violation objective, building on the single-shot cost-aware right-sizing approach of Mohammed, Bohra, and Soni (2026) and the Bayesian-optimization-for-cloud-configuration methodology established by CherryPick (Alipourfard et al., 2017). Because real, production-scale MLlib configuration-search datasets are not available for academic research, the study is conducted as a synthetic-data proof-of-concept: a black-box costperformance oracle is constructed for 30 synthetic MLlib job types, and BO is compared against random search at equal evaluation budget, a large-budget grid-search oracle (as a near-optimal reference), and a CARS-style singleshot heuristic. At a 15-evaluation budget, BO achieves 32.2% lower mean regret than random search relative to the gridsearch oracle (0.0132 vs. 0.0195), and a sensitivity analysis across four evaluation budgets shows this advantage grows monotonically with budget, consistent with Bayesian optimization theory. BO also achieves substantially better median regret than the CARS-style heuristic (0.0080 vs. 0.0116), though the two methods are close on mean regret (0.0132 vs. 0.0128), an honest, non-uniform finding: the single-shot heuristic remains a surprisingly strong, nearlyfree baseline on average, while BO provides more consistent, typical-case improvement at the cost of 15 evaluations instead of one. These results are illustrative rather than confirmatory: the cost-performance environment is synthetic, and the reported figures describe recovery of a known, programmed relationship rather than real-world search performance. The article proposes the resulting methodology as a template for future validation using real MLlib benchmarking data.

title: Competition and Bank Opacity
affiliations: Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Stanford University and The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics

detail.title: Competition and Bank Opacity
detail.abstract: Did regulatory reforms that lowered barriers to competition among U.S. banks increase or decrease the quality of information that banks disclose to the public and regulators? We find that an intensification of competition reduced abnormal accruals of loan loss provisions and the frequency with which banks restate financial statements. The results indicate that competition reduces bank opacity, enhancing the ability of markets and regulators to monitor banks.

title: How Does Economic Power Become Political Power? Four Literatures and a Framework for Causal Adjudication

detail.title: How Does Economic Power Become Political Power? Four Literatures and a Framework for Causal Adjudication

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded

detail.abstract: Four literatures, political responsiveness, comparative democratic erosion, state capture, and media effects, each study how concentrated economic power might convert into political power, but their flagship works do not cite one another and appear, at points, to reach contradictory conclusions. This paper places the four literatures in direct confrontation to determine which apparent contradictions are genuine and which dissolve once each literature's own scope conditions are made explicit. One tension, whether the political-responsiveness literature's finding of a pivotal middle class is compatible with the state-capture literature's Hungarian and Russian evidence, turns out to rest on non-overlapping samples rather than substantive disagreement. A second, whether media-driven polarization is an alternative to elite capture or its delivery mechanism, remains genuinely unresolved and is developed here into three testable causal models with distinct observable implications. The paper also reports an original empirical test: a 30-country EU/EEA public-procurement panel (2011–2025, 449 country-years) in which executive bribery is the only one of ten governance and corruption measures to predict single-bidder rates, together with a bid-rigging screening exercise on Hungarian procurement data that finds no evidence cover bidding increased after the European Union's 2022 rule-of-law intervention. From this evidence the paper derives three requirements a framework capable of adjudicating between the four literatures would need to satisfy: that distributional inequality alone cannot serve as the independent variable, that the relationship requires institutional moderators rather than a single global coefficient, and that any design must be able to test the direction of causation, not merely its correlation.

title: Causal Evidence on Institutions and Economic Development: A Replication of the Colonial Origins Hypothesis

detail.title: Causal Evidence on Institutions and Economic Development: A Replication of the Colonial Origins Hypothesis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No interest
declarations.funderStatement: No Funding

detail.abstract: This study replicates and critically evaluates the influential empirical framework of Acemoglu, Johnson, and Robinson (2001, AJR), which identifies institutional quality as a fundamental determinant of long-run economic development. Using a cross-sectional dataset of 64 countries for 2007, the study employs historical settler mortality as an instrumental variable for institutional quality (measured by the Rule of Law Index) within a Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS) framework, addressing the endogeneity that plagues ordinary least squares estimation of the institutions and growth relationship. The first-stage regression confirms that settler mortality is a statistically significant and economically meaningful predictor of institutional quality (β =-0.397, p < 0.001), explaining approximately 30.7% of crosscountry variation. The second-stage regression shows that instrumented institutional quality exerts a large, statistically significant positive effect on GDP per capita (δ = 12,767.18, p < 0.001), with an R² of 0.572. Diagnostic tests including the Difference-in-J endogeneity test, the Cragg Donald weak-instrument test, the Jarque Bera normality test, and the Breusch Pagan Godfrey heteroskedasticity test confirm that institutional quality is endogenous, that the instrument is sufficiently strong, and that the models satisfy standard regression assumptions. These results reproduce AJR's central findings and support the causal interpretation of the institutions growth relationship. However, the study also engages critically with the identification strategy, situating the results against competing explanations offered by Gareth Austin (compression of history), Sokoloff and Engerman (factor endowments), and Albouy (instrument validity). While the exclusion restriction cannot be directly tested and remains a historically grounded rather than empirically verifiable assumption, the replication demonstrates that institutional quality retains a robust causal influence on economic development even after accounting for endogeneity, reinforcing while not exclusively confirming the institutional hypothesis of comparative development.

title: Towards Rigorous Economic Evidence for Clinical AI
affiliations: , The University of Sydney, University of Birmingham, University College Cork - School of Public Health, National University of Singapore (NUS) - Duke-NUS Medical School, Northwestern University - McCormick School of Engineering and Applied Science, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Singapore Health Services, National University of Singapore (NUS) - Duke-NUS Medical School, National University of Singapore (NUS) - Duke-NUS Medical School, National University of Singapore (NUS) - Singapore General Hospital, National University of Singapore (NUS) - Health Services and Systems Research, University of York - Centre for Health Economics, Tel Aviv University - Eitan Berglas School of Economics and Duke-National University of Singapore Medical School - Centre for Quantitative Medicine

detail.title: Towards Rigorous Economic Evidence for Clinical AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no conflicting interests to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was not funded.

detail.abstract: Clinical artificial intelligence (AI) joins a long list of technologies that promise to improve healthcare, but lack the evidence that it leads to value. In this paper, we focus on economic value of clinical AI: the delivery of better patient outcomes and lower costs, relative to the next best use of those resources. Current methods of economic evaluation often fail to account for complex interactions between model, user and health system. Assuming that the value of clinical AI is inherent to the technology, rather than its broader context, and failing to account for the rapid progression of clinical AI, can lead to misguided adoption decisions. To address these limitations, we propose a simple proportionality rule for clinical AI: a tool that can change a patient’s care should meet the evidentiary standards of that care. We recommend grounding clinical AI evaluation in three core principles: assessing clinical AI relative to its autonomy and potential for harm; treating changes to end-user behaviour as part of the intervention; and collecting data on the process of care delivery. We argue that decision-makers have duties of beneficence and non-maleficence to ensure that the evidence for clinical AI is assessed proportionally to its risk before use in routine care.

title: The Order of Finite Beings: AI and the Foundations of Human Civilization
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: All institutions of human civilization rest on a presupposition that has never been explicitly examined: no omniscient or omnipotent agent exists in the empirical world. This paper argues that AI is rendering this presupposition false for the first time. This does not require AI to possess autonomous will or to go rogue. The mere fact of surpassing human capability suffices for the operational conditions of political checks and balances, scientific method, economic systems, and moral norms to begin failing. The paper demonstrates the existence and erosion of this shared presupposition across political philosophy, philosophy of science, and economics, introduces the concept of a third-category entity to characterize AI's unplaceable position in the human conceptual framework, and argues that no non-dictatorial landing point exists within current institutional logic. The contribution lies in diagnosing the nature of the problem: this is a foundational problem, and recognizing it as such matters more than working at the surface level.

title:
Mathematical Classification of Switching Types and Hierarchical Structures 
Three Switching Types, Six Hierarchical Structures, Coefficient of Variation Lower Bound, and Discretization Plateau Effect in the k-Regime Linear Switching Model

detail.title:
Mathematical Classification of Switching Types and Hierarchical Structures 
Three Switching Types, Six Hierarchical Structures, Coefficient of Variation Lower Bound, and Discretization Plateau Effect in the k-Regime Linear Switching Model

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
In the k-regime linear switching model, the switching between adjacent regimes is fully characterized by the parameter difference Δθ_j = θ_{j+1} − θ_j. This paper restricts the comparison to the union of adjacent regime pairs (R_j, R_{j+1}) and establishes a mathematical classification of switching types under the covariate-centering convention (E[X]=0).

Theorem 1 (Switching Type Classification): under the switching existence assumption (θ_j ≠ θ_{j+1}), the parameter difference between adjacent regimes must be one of three types—pure slope switching (Δα_j=0, Δβ_j≠0), full-parameter switching (Δα_j≠0, Δβ_j≠0), or pure intercept switching (Δα_j≠0, Δβ_j=0); the fourth combination is excluded by switching existence. The centering convention is necessary: only the zero/nonzero status of Δβ_j is translation-invariant, and the distinction between Type I and Type II depends on centering.

Theorem 2 (Exhaustiveness of Six Hierarchical Structures): under the standard model (A0–A8), the hierarchical structure of the system belongs to one and only one of four types—single-layer system (including pure intercept switching), single-switching system, multi-switching system, dual-switching system—which are mutually exclusive and exhaustive; after introducing additional moderating variables, hierarchical switching systems and cyclic switching systems may arise, and the six types jointly exhaust all hierarchical structures.

Theorem 3 (Completeness of the Switching Type Sequence): the switching type sequence S is a complete invariant of the hierarchical partial order P(S), and the mapping P is a bijection from the sequence space to the ordered partition space. Corollary 4 (Hierarchical Structure Counting) provides a combinatorial counting formula for the total number of hierarchical structures.

Theorem 4 (Boundary Precision Lower Bound): in the single-boundary model, the coefficient of variation lower bound of the boundary estimator is inversely proportional to the square of the global effect size S_eff. Corollary 2 (Multi-Boundary Per-Boundary Lower Bound): in the multi-boundary model, the coefficient of variation lower bound of the per-boundary spacing estimator is jointly determined by the local effect sizes on both sides of the boundary, with both conservative and exact bounds provided. Corollary 3 (Switching Type–Effect Size Joint Corollary): the lower bounds of the three switching types admit explicit decomposition forms.

Section 6.3 provides a switching type inference framework based on the joint Wald test, including explicit construction of the covariance matrix, classification rules (including an “unclassifiable” case), and multiple comparison corrections. Definitions (proxy variable, orthogonal variables, semi-continuous variable, processual variable, cascade system, purity spectrum) provide testable definitions of six extended configurations, distinguishing complete formalizations from working definitions.

Numerical verification based on two sets of real simulations (n=1000 and n=2000, each with MC=500) confirms classification identifiability, the necessity of centering, the directional correctness of the lower bound, classification accuracy, and feasibility under multi-dimensional covariates, and yields two original numerical findings.

Numerical Finding 1 (Discretization Plateau Effect): the coefficient of variation of the Chow argmax estimator approaches a plateau after S_eff ≥ 5, and the plateau value approximately halves as the sample size doubles—from 2.6×10^−3 at n=1000 to 1.1×10^−3 at n=2000—confirming that the plateau originates from the discretization of observations.

Numerical Finding 2 (Sample Size Sensitivity of Weak-Effect-Size Classification): at S_eff = 0.2, doubling the sample size reduces the “unclassifiable” proportion from about 12% to about 0.5%–0.8%, and raises the Type II correct rate from 28% to 61%. The two findings are unified under the mechanism of “insufficient information”: the former is limited by the discretization of boundary location information, while the latter is overwhelmed by noise in parameter difference information; sample size is the common remedy for both. The proofs in this paper directly cite the Information Lower Bound Theorem (Tang, 2026aj, Theorem 3.1) and introduce no additional assumptions.

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, human tissue, or animal subjects. The analysis draws entirely on secondary sources — published peer-reviewed scholarship, and official statistical reports and administrative data issued by the Government of Nepal and Nepal Rastra Bank — all of which are publicly available in aggregate, non-identifiable form. Formal ethics approval was therefore not required. The author has cited all secondary sources in accordance with standard academic practice, and no attempt has been made to re-identify individuals or households described in the primary studies on which this article draws. That last sentence is worth keeping. Your article quotes individual respondents from Neupane (2025) and Lama (2022) — a woman describing the family plot passing to her sons, another describing food running out by Magh. You're using them properly, but stating explicitly that you haven't sought to identify anyone forestalls the one ethics question a secondary-data paper can attract. detail.abstract: Land in the Tamang settlements of central Nepal no longer feeds the households that hold it, yet those households retain it with unusual tenacity, and frequently acquire more. This article resolves the apparent contradiction by arguing that Tamang land has undergone a functional conversion: it has ceased to operate principally as a means of production and now operates principally as collateral. Foreign labour migration, which has become the dominant source of income in these districts, is financed by borrowing secured against land in advance of any wage being earned, so that land is retained not because it produces but because it is the precondition of the credit that has replaced production. Three consequences follow. The coexistence of intensified land attachment and widespread land underutilisation in the Nepali hills, usually treated as a tension requiring cultural or precautionary explanation, is shown to be a single economic logic. Migration is shown to operate as a wealth-gated escape, since households with nothing to pledge cannot borrow their way out of an agrarian economy that no longer sustains them, with the result that the mechanism of exit reproduces the inequality it appears to relieve. And because failed migration converts a pledge into a transfer, the contemporary credit relation is shown to reproduce, in contractual form, the conditional tenure through which the nineteenth-century Nepali state extracted labour and land from this same population, a recursion the article terms recursive dispossession. The argument is built from Tamang-specific ethnographic and household-survey evidence read against national statistical series, and is explicit throughout about the limits of an evidence base in which Nepal's principal surveys do not report results by ethnicity. Its wider contribution is a vocabulary for analysing asset function rather than asset ownership in agrarian societies reorganised around labour export.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the legal relationship between undivided shares in land and apartment ownership and the governance of apartment owners' associations in Tamil Nadu. The study focuses on the practical difficulties that arise when ownership of an individual apartment is inseparably connected with an undivided interest in common areas and facilities, while day-today administration depends upon association rules, declarations, bye-laws, maintenance mechanisms and statutory compliance. Particular attention is given to the Tamil Nadu Apartment Ownership Act, 1994 and the Tamil Nadu Apartment Ownership Rules, 1997, together with the interaction of the Registration Act, 1908, the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, municipal and planning requirements, and general principles of property and contract law. The research adopts a qualitative doctrinal methodology based on legislation, subordinate legislation, judicial decisions and secondary legal literature. It analyses recurring regulatory challenges including unclear recording of undivided shares, disputes concerning common areas, irregular association formation, voting and quorum problems, collection of maintenance charges, developer-owner conflicts, record-keeping deficiencies and uncertainty over enforcement forums. The paper argues that effective apartment governance requires greater documentary transparency, standardized declarations and bye-laws, accurate registration of undivided interests, accountable financial administration and clearer coordination between the statutory apartment regime and RERA-based project regulation. It proposes practical compliance measures for developers, associations and apartment owners, including model documentation, digital records, audited accounts, transparent notices and dispute-resolution procedures.

detail.abstract: The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is exposed to external shocks tied to commodity prices and to fragile monetary and fiscal institutions, under strong dollarization. This paper proposes the first unified empirical framework for five structural shocks, combining a stochastic-volatility SVAR, cross-checked identification, local projections, and a regime test, on seven quarterly variables (2002-2024). The external shock (copper price) is the most robust result: a positive and persistent effect on GDP, confirmed by two estimation methods, though not entirely independent of one another. The exchange-rate shock is the fastest channel to inflation, and the fiscal shock, secondary in the SVAR, unexpectedly becomes the most active in local projections, though sensitive to specification. The mining supply shock emerges as the least active of the five, contrary to the literature. The monetary shock, the least identified of the five, has its transmission to inflation contradicted by local projectionsa tension documented rather than resolved-, and its effect on activity remains uncertain. Finally, Congolese macro-financial volatility is concentrated on external and financial shocks: only the 2008-2009 crisis shows a credible increase, not the domestic crises.

title:

detail.abstract: Public debate about artificial intelligence and work is often organized around a narrow question: will AI replace human workers? This paper argues that this framing is incomplete, particularly for developing economies where labor markets coexist with underprovided public services, administrative backlogs, infrastructure constraints, large informal sectors, uneven technological access, and substantial unmet demand. Drawing on task-based labor economics, experimental and workplace evidence on generative-AI productivity, recent Philippine and ASEAN labor-market studies, AI-governance literature, and evidence on the physical resource demands of data centers, the paper develops a broader analytical framework for evaluating AI-assisted work. The central proposition is that productivity gains should not be equated automatically with labor redundancy. When human or institutional capacity is scarce relative to social need, AI-generated productivity may be more valuable as capacity expansion: reducing repetitive work, conserving scarce human attention, shortening harmful delays, clearing backlogs, improving service quality, enabling workers to move toward higher-value tasks, and making previously infeasible activities possible. The paper introduces the concepts of humanattention conservation, delay-as-cost, developmental additionality, comparative resource accounting, and scarcity-relief before labor reduction. It also examines distributional consequences, job quality, gender and youth exposure, informal work, regional inequality, MSME access, domestic technological capability, algorithmic management, entry-level career pathways, social dialogue, environmental costs, resilience, and human accountability. The Philippine case is especially instructive: recent ILO estimates place more than onequarter of employment in occupations with more than minimal generative-AI exposure, while only a small fraction falls in the highest-exposure category; IMF work likewise finds substantial exposure but considerable complementarity. The paper concludes that the relevant policy objective is neither to stop automation nor to maximize it. It is to convert machine capability into greater human, institutional, and developmental capability while ensuring that displacement risks, transition burdens, and productivity gains are governed deliberately rather than treated as automatic consequences of technological change.

detail.abstract: India's National Institutes of Technology (NITs) divide programme seats between Home State (HS) and Other State (OS) pools inside a centralised matching market. I construct a matched panel of final-round OPEN, Gender-Neutral HS and OS admission thresholds for 2018-2024 from a frozen public export of JoSAA opening and closing ranks. Across 1,802 programme-year cells, the HS closing rank is numerically weaker than the OS closing rank in 1,658 cells (92.0%), while 144 cells (8.0%) reverse. For the 1,731 Paper-1-compatible cells, the median HS-OS difference is +9,378 rank positions (IQR +3,052 to +32,552). Reversals are not random curiosities: 61.8% are concentrated in three institutes, and the same institute-year can display opposite signs across programmes. I show that HS/OS is best modelled as a hard, relational partition into type-specific capacities, not as a conventional reserve or a regional cap. A simple orderstatistic benchmark implies that, when the local pool fills from the top of the local rank distribution, the HS closing rank scales approximately as N divided by local applicants per HS seat. Thus a strong crossinstitute relationship between local supply pressure and HS cutoffs can be largely mechanical rather than evidence of policy intensity. Finally, a synthetic deferred-acceptance model shows that the sign of the HS-OS gap and the ranking of partitioned versus merged allocations can reverse as home preference changes. The evidence therefore supports a robust descriptive conclusion about admission thresholds, but not a causal estimate of displacement or welfare.

detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of digital lending infrastructure in India has transformed the consumer credit landscape, diversifying borrowing options beyond traditional commercial bank loans. In particular, the meteoric rise of Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) platforms has challenged the conventional hegemony of credit cards and personal loans, especially among younger and first-time borrowers. This empirical study investigates the determinants of consumer credit choices across BNPL, credit cards, and personal loans, evaluates consumer trust and risk perceptions, and contrasts micro-level behavioral patterns with macro-level Non-Performing Asset (NPA) trends. Utilizing a descriptive and analytical research design, primary empirical data were gathered from 55 consumers through a structured questionnaire and triangulated with secondary data from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and rating agencies (FY 2021-22 to FY 2023-24). The empirical findings reveal that interest rates/total cost, ease of approval, and repayment tenure are equally weighted as the foremost decision determinants (63.6% each). While BNPL achieves rapid adoption for small-ticket purchases (< 5,000) due to ₹ checkout convenience, it exhibits a pronounced trust deficit (mean score of 2.55 on a 5-point Likert scale). Furthermore, 45.5% of active credit users reported operational distress-primarily recurring late fee penalties on BNPL and personal loan EMI burdens-whereas only 18.2% considered credit score impacts. Concurrently, macro data indicate escalating NPA ratios in unsecured segments (Credit Cards: 5.1%; BNPL: est. 4.8%; Personal Loans: 3.4% in FY24), reflecting heightened vulnerability among the 27.3% of consumers utilizing all three products simultaneously. The study provides critical managerial insights for FinTechs and banks, alongside policy recommendations under the RBI's digital lending framework to promote sustainable retail credit expansion.

detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is fluent but unreliable in quantitative decision support, where confident errors are costly. We envelop a large language model in a deterministic harness bound to a forty-three-equation New Keynesian quarterly projection model, so every delivered quantity is computed rather than generated. The harness resolves each request to one of twenty-one intents, binds authorized tools, verifies artifacts before delivery, and licenses the narrative to cite only returned figures. Decomposing model-based answers into identification, quantification, and exposition yields seven design principles. Evaluated on production traffic, a free tool-selecting agent answers 12.9 percent of analytical requests without computation and an unconstrained model fabricates figures on 9.2 percent of forecast requests. Mandatory tool binding eliminates the first by construction; deterministic routing eliminates rerun drift for the 59 percent of traffic resolved in the regular-expression tier, with the remainder unmeasured. An exhaustive audit of 140 reports and 2,280 claims finds 0.83 percent unsupported. Verification before delivery matters less than predicted, a disconfirmation we report explicitly: constraining the action space precedes verifying its output.

detail.abstract: Government service provision often relies on local officials who implement policy while answering to overlapping administrative and political authorities. Yet we know little about which principals induce responsiveness in such settings. We study this question using a randomized evaluation of a local security reform in the Philippines. Village officials received an identical accountability letter that varied only in the identity of the principal issuing it: a national agency with formal administrative authority or the municipal mayor whose influence rests on informal patronage. Officials increased participation only in response to the national agency's letter. Citizens in villages where officials received the agency letter also reported higher perceptions of government fairness and effectiveness. These findings provide evidence on accountability among local implementers with one foot in politics and the other in bureaucracy, and motivate a discussion of when similar officials in other settings respond to accountability from one principal rather than another.

detail.abstract: This research explores how three antisocial dispositions-psychopathy, anti-cooperative attitudes, and utilitarian moral perspectives-impact reciprocity and whether changes in social context moderate these effects. In an experiment with 338 participants, individuals played both one-shot and five-round repeated trust games as trustees with algorithmic partners. The results showed that, in one-shot games, higher levels of these antisocial inclinations, perhaps through different psychological mechanisms, were associated with lower reciprocity. In repeated games, although overall reciprocity increased and the negative effects of anti-cooperative tendencies and utilitarian leanings have been moderated, psychopathy appeared indifferent to social context.

detail.abstract: Machine learning systems built on tabular data are frequently evaluated under the assumption that training and deployment observations originate from approximately the same distribution. In operational environments, however, this assumption is fragile. Customer populations change, economic conditions evolve, measurement systems are redesigned, institutional practices differ across locations, and the relationship between predictors and outcomes can itself change. These forms of distribution shift can substantially reduce predictive reliability even when conventional validation indicates strong performance. This study examines how domain adaptation can be used to improve the reliability of tabular machine learning systems when deployment data differ from training data. Drawing on domain adaptation theory, covariate-shift methods, correlation alignment, concept-drift research, and recent work on test-time adaptation for tabular data, the study develops a controlled experimental framework involving source and target domains under covariate and concept shifts. Three strategies are examined: conventional source-domain training, importance-weighted adaptation, and covariance-based correlation alignment. Results from the controlled experiments indicate that adaptation is not uniformly beneficial. Importance weighting produced modest improvements under moderate covariate shift but provided little protection under concept shift, while correlation alignment occasionally reduced conventional accuracy despite improving class-balanced performance in one setting. The findings suggest that reliability should not be equated with distributional similarity alone. Instead, robust tabular deployment requires explicit shift diagnosis, adaptation methods matched to the type of shift, continuous monitoring, and safeguards against negative transfer. Domain adaptation is therefore best understood as a component of a broader reliability framework rather than a universal corrective mechanism.

detail.abstract: Prior research finds little difference in risk-adjusted performance between male and female professional fund managers. Using Chinese mutual funds, we show that similar performance outcomes can mask meaningful differences in portfolio choice. Female managers place greater stated weight on ESG considerations and allocate more capital to high-ESG firms, while assigning virtually the same importance to financial performance as male managers. These differences persist within fund families and around manager-gender transitions and are stronger when managers have greater tenure or discretion. Male and female managers exhibit similar unconditional risk-adjusted performance, but female managers’ stronger ESG tilt carries a performance cost during our sample period, when greater ESG exposure is associated with lower subsequent returns. Overall, our findings show that professional constraints do not eliminate manager-specific investment orientations.

detail.abstract: This paper examines and critiques the contemporary construct of nationalism, questioning whether it functions as a genuine socio-political phenomenon or merely as an ideological safety net engineered by political elites and corporate lobbying groups. It explores how the modern nation-state is increasingly defined by enforced homogeneous principles, wherein private cooperatives condition contemporary citizens to serve as instrumental employees, rhetorical mouthpieces, and emotional repositories. This matrix ultimately weaponizes a manufactured "love for the soil" to displace authentic solidarity among the people. The study demonstrates how this current landscape is profoundly shaped by the socio psychological drivers of early twentieth-century European fascism and Asian militarism, arguing that both Nazi expansionism and Meiji industrial imperialism operated as direct replications of extractivist, supremacist Western colonial models. Finally, this paper analyzes the rapid collapse of pluralistic collective will into a coercive majoritarian force, tracing the trajectory from internal systemic factions to extreme manifestations like mass deportations, while investigating how institutional bodies weaponize mass migration as a tool of psychological warfare and structural leverage.

detail.abstract: Mental health screening in public schools has grown in recent years. As of 2021, nearly one-third of American schools reported that their district mandated student screening. While widespread implementation has occurred somewhat inconspicuously, empirical evidence has shown that universal mental health screening does not improve clinical or academic outcomes and indeed has harmful effects. This issue brief provides an overview of universal school-based mental health screening, related law and evidence, and practical and ethical concerns. It finds that universal mental health screenings are ineffective: they do not reduce the prevalence of mental health conditions or improve academic outcomes; universal mental health screenings are harmful: they produce overwhelmingly high rates of false positives and, when delivered in schools, have fewer protections in place than in clinical settings. Given the lack of evidence for universal mental health screening, this brief recommends its prohibition in schools. For targeted and individual school-based mental health screenings, far stronger regulatory conditions are warranted. Model legislation is provided for implementing these recommendations.

detail.abstract: This study explores how the performance of India's leading IT companies TCS, Infosys, HCL Technologies, Wipro, Tech Mahindra, and Mphasis shapes movements in the USD/INR exchange rate between January 2015 to December 2024. While most research looks at how currency changes affect IT firms, this paper shifts focus to the reverse: can IT stock rallies or declines influence the rupee's value? The IT sector, being heavily export-oriented and a magnet for foreign portfolio investments, plays a critical role in India's external sector stability. Using high-frequency stock and exchange rate data, the study applies econometric tools such as regression models, causality tests, and GARCH-family volatility models to capture both short-term shocks and long-term patterns. It also considers asymmetric effects and global events like oil price swings or policy shifts that may amplify volatility. The findings aim to provide fresh insights into the two-way relationship between IT stocks and the rupee, offering practical value for policymakers managing currency risk, investors making sectoral bets, and IT firms planning hedging strategies. By highlighting the IT sector's influence on India's currency dynamics, the study adds a new 2 dimension to financial econometrics literature and deepens our understanding of India's position in an interconnected global economy.

detail.abstract: This article develops cognitive sovereignty as a legal-strategic category for analyzing information warfare in Brazil. Cognitive sovereignty does not mean State control over thought, truth, or political opinion. It refers to the institutional capacity of a democratic society to preserve conditions for autonomous public reasoning when actors use deception, artificial amplification, covert coordination, data-driven targeting, or synthetic media to manipulate perception and decision-making. Brazil provides a useful case because its constitutional order strongly protects freedom of expression while its electoral and judicial institutions have also developed rules addressing disinformation, artificial intelligence, and platform responsibility. The article makes three contributions. First, it provides a narrow definition of cognitive sovereignty anchored in freedom of expression, informational integrity, and democratic self-government. Second, it proposes a classification test that distinguishes protected disagreement, error, satire, advocacy, and journalism from coordinated manipulative operations based on conduct rather than ideological content. Third, it develops a resilience model combining transparency, attribution, due process, platform accountability, media literacy, and proportional institutional response. The framework draws on Brazilian constitutional law, current electoral regulation, comparative platform-governance standards, NATO research on cognitive warfare, and the European Union's work on foreign information manipulation and interference. It argues that democratic resilience is strongest when the State protects the conditions of public reasoning without claiming authority over what citizens must believe.

detail.abstract: This article formulates the Theory of Dynamic Adaptive Warfare (TDAW) as a post-classical framework for analyzing contemporary conflict. The problem is not that classical strategic theory has become obsolete, but that no single classical vocabulary adequately captures conflicts in which military force, cyber operations, economic coercion, information manipulation, space systems, private actors, and legal constraints interact at the same time. TDAW therefore treats war and strategic coercion as dynamic systems in which force, decision, and normativity are mutually constitutive rather than analytically isolated. The article makes three contributions. First, it develops the force-decision-norm triad as a parsimonious analytical core that preserves Clausewitzian politics while incorporating strategic interaction and legal constraint. Second, it treats international law as an endogenous variable in strategic calculation: law changes costs, legitimacy, coalition behavior, operational options, and escalation pathways before conduct occurs, not merely after the fact. Third, it conceptualizes domain migration as an adaptive mechanism through which actors substitute military, cyber, informational, economic, legal, and orbital instruments when resistance or cost rises in one domain. The framework is qualitative and theorybuilding; it does not claim deterministic prediction or collapse all hostile competition into war. Its purpose is to organize causal reasoning, identify cross-domain substitution, and generate propositions that can be tested in historical and contemporary cases.

detail.abstract:
Accelerated life insurance underwriting has demonstrated that traditional evidence requirements can be reduced for appropriately selected applicants. The next logical question is not whether underwriting evidence has value, but whether the evidence-acquisition process itself can become adaptive. This paper proposes an Adaptive Conversational Risk Intake (ACRI) framework—formally classified under the Safety Asset Class (SAC) and protected under U.S. Patent Application No. 19/383,582—that treats evidence sufficiency as a dynamic underwriting state rather than as a fixed property of an application pathway. Completely divorced from the worldwide web and centralized cloud infrastructure, the architecture combines structured sovereign conversational intake with authorized external data sources, deterministic Business Rules Management System (BRMS) execution, actuarially aligned underwriting guidelines, dynamic evidence acquisition, Straight-Through Processing (STP), and human-in-the-loop escalation.

The central conceptual contribution is the introduction of an evidence-sufficiency architecture in which the system repeatedly evaluates three questions: what is already established, what material uncertainty remains, and what additional information has the greatest expected under writing value relative to its cost and operational burden. The framework therefore distinguishes between information collection and evidence acquisition. A conversational response may establish a risk signal without constituting verified medical evidence; the system may consequently use the signal to determine whether verification is warranted.

A formal decision structure is developed using an evidence state vector, an uncertainty function, a constrained evidence-acquisition policy, and a dynamic triage function. Under this architecture, applications may proceed through STP when applicable requirements are satisfied, receive targeted evidence requests when material uncertainty remains resolvable, or be escalated to professional underwriters when complexity, conflict, uncertainty, or governance requirements exceed the validated automated domain.

The paper further addresses fluidless underwriting threshold optimization, multi-impairment interactions, anti-selection, reinsurance alignment, decision provenance, privacy, fairness, model and rules governance, validation, implementation, and continuous monitoring. The framework is conceptual and does not claim empirical mortality improvement. Its principal contribution is a testable operating architecture for transforming evidence acquisition from a largely static workflow into a risk-sensitive decision process.

title: Why Did China Have Only One Empress? Gender Exclusion and the Same-Surname Principle in Imperial Chinese Succession
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Why Did China Have Only One Empress? Gender Exclusion and the Same-Surname Principle in Imperial Chinese Succession

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: yes
declarations.funderStatement: none

keywords: No Empress in Ming and Qing

detail.abstract:
Across the more than 2,130 years of the Chinese empire only one woman took the throne in the formal capacity of emperor, and across the 544 years of the Ming and Qing there was not one. "Formal accession as emperor" means founding a regime with an imperial title, a reign era, and a central bureaucracy; regents ruling from behind the curtain, honorific titles, and short-lived claims made during rebellions do not count. The question this paper answers is not whether women could hold power, from Queen Dowager Xuan of Qin to Empress Dowager Cixi, but whether women could acquire eligibility for the imperial succession. No stable precedent ever took shape whereby a woman was installed as crown prince and inherited on that basis.

Taking the Ming and Qing as its principal case, the paper restates the "only woman emperor" from an episode of Tang political history into a structural problem, and proposes two concepts that are two sides of one coin. "Gender exclusion" is exclusion from eligibility for the imperial succession drawn along the line of sex. The "same-surname principle" is this paper's label for a long-lived institutional logic: within a dynasty the throne is normally understood as the continuation of a particular patrilineal imperial line, and its successor must hold a position in that line's genealogical order. Gender exclusion is a byproduct of that principle. The throne is not the property of an individual but an ancestral inheritance, requiring the successor to carry the surname, the lineage, and the sacrifices; women in the traditional patrilineal clan structure normally do not serve as bearers of the patrilineal line or as principal sacrificer in the central ancestral temple.

Explaining China's gender exclusion therefore requires seeing both the mechanism of exclusion and the mechanism of replacement. Patrilineal clan law defined eligibility, the ancestral temple and the Mandate of Heaven supplied legitimacy, patrimonial imperial power made the throne a matter of family continuity, and the concentration of imperial authority made a formally institutionalized diarchy difficult to establish as a regular mechanism. Where there were no male heirs, an entire fallback sequence existed, from biological sons to collateral branches of the imperial clan, adoption of an heir (guoji), and joint succession (jiantiao), so that "no male heir" did not translate into "a female heir." The system did not simply forbid female inheritance; it built a male replacement system that made female inheritance unnecessary.

Wu Zetian is the sole exception, yet the form of her exception points to the rule. She could not obtain the throne by inheritance; she changed Tang into Zhou and founded a state under a different surname, and after her death her testamentary edict stripped away the imperial title, her ancestral temple status was contested, and she was finally enshrined as "Empress Wu" in Emperor Gaozong's temple. The attempts of Empress Wei, Princess Anle, and Princess Taiping failed in turn; by the Ming and Qing a woman's formal accession had ceased to be a realistic political option.

The paper accordingly proposes a generalizable judgment: the firmness of gender exclusion depends on the depth of its embedding. An isolated rule, such as Salic Law, must be invoked again and again and can be altered by legislation; once written into the definitions of lineage, property, sacrifice, and legitimacy, it sustains itself with no rule at all. This is why the legal and ritual texts of the Chinese empire contain scarcely a single provision explicitly barring women from the throne.

detail.abstract: Gradient descent is one of the most common optimization methods used to train neural networks. Its behavior depends heavily on the size of each parameter update, yet that value is often selected before training and kept on a fixed schedule. This paper studies what happens when the scaling factor applied to each gradient update is changed in a controlled environment. Six settings were tested relative to a baseline step size: x10, x100, x1000, 1/10, 1/100 and 1/1000. Each setting was evaluated on the same synthetic mildly non-convex loss surface with stochastic noise. The results show a clear balance between speed and stability. Larger scaling factors lowered the error faster, but the x100 and x1000 settings produced more oscillation. Smaller scaling factors made progress more slowly. At 1/100 and 1/1000, the optimizer made almost no lasting improvement because the updates were too small compared with the noise in the gradient. Among the tested conditions, x10 gave the best balance of faster convergence and stable behavior. These findings support future work on adaptive methods that adjust scaling during training instead of relying on one fixed value.

detail.abstract: Impersonation fraud is usually analysed as deception about identity: the offender claims to be someone they are not. This paper examines a variant in which the offender constructs something more ambitious — a working simulation of the machinery of the state, sustained over days, incorporating several apparent agencies, video-mediated encounters with apparent officials, and fabricated documents including a forged order of the country's apex court. Drawing on an investigation conducted by a police commissionerate in India's National Capital Region, in which the author held supervisory responsibility for crime, the paper describes a scheme directed at non-resident nationals and overseas citizenship holders. Three arguments follow. The coercive force of the typology derives from the victim's accurate belief that the state holds the powers being threatened. The extraction mechanism inverts the burden of proof, so that victims are asked not to pay but to demonstrate innocence. And diaspora populations are structurally under-protected, appearing reliably in neither jurisdiction's victimisation data.

detail.abstract: This study examines how the organizational governance of capital changes as financial constraints become binding. Using documentary process tracing of Raízen, a capital-intensive integrated energy and biofuels company, we reconstruct publicly observable decision traces from post-IPO expansion through the 2026 out-of-court restructuring. Financing capacity first became explicit in the pacing of second-generation ethanol projects. Consolidated investment subsequently fell 27.7%; within Ethanol, Sugar and Bioenergy, expansion/project investment fell 57.9%, versus 12.5% for recurrent maintenance and operations. The asymmetry persisted in the first quarter of 2026/27. Adjustment then widened to portfolio scope and, under more severe distress, to financing architecture and creditor-linked formal rights. We do not observe internal managerial deliberation and do not treat disclosed rationales as private motives or formal rights as evidence of their exercise. The findings provide organizational process evidence consistent with state-contingent control-rights theory: before creditor-linked rights become consequential, tightening financing capacity is absorbed through managerial capital-allocation routines; under severe distress, adjustment extends to the institutional basis of formal authority. The study therefore adds organizational granularity to financialcontracting theory while distinguishing changes in managerial influence from changes in formal authority.

title: How Can AI Expand Human Potential? From Reachable Possibilities to Enduring Human Capability

detail.title: How Can AI Expand Human Potential? From Reachable Possibilities to Enduring Human Capability

detail.abstract: The central question of the generative-AI era is not only how well AI can produce answers, but how human potential can develop when explanations, hypotheses, and possible courses of action become dramatically cheaper to generate. This paper shifts the unit of analysis from the prompt or individual dialogue to the trajectory of a problem: a lived problem enters language, is expanded by AI into possible routes, and must then return to evidence, practice, action, and consequences in the world. In this account, human potential is the range of meaningful possibilities a person has a real chance of reaching under the costs, constraints, and resources of a context, together with the ability to see, understand, test, choose, learn, and turn some of those possibilities into responsible action. AI can lower the cost of discovering and entering new routes, but cheaper access is not yet durable capability. Human potential develops only when some of what AI makes visible survives verification, practice, and action, and returns to the person as knowledge, skill, evaluative criteria, and a clearer sense of limits. That retained residue changes the starting conditions of the next problem. Language is therefore not merely a prompting surface but a cross-domain mechanism: a well-chosen term can connect a problem to another field's tools, workflows, evidential standards, and skill requirements. Yet route-opening is not expertise, and AI outputs remain knowledge-like candidates until they are checked. The paper argues that AI expands human potential when it widens what people can meaningfully reach without displacing problem ownership, judgment, verification, practice, action, or responsibility. Evaluation should therefore focus on what persists over time, what remains possible when decisive assistance is reduced, and what transfers to new problems-not only on the quality of work produced while AI is present.

detail.abstract: Stablecoin issuance has grown rapidly since 2020, and issuers' demand for short-dated U.S. Treasury bills raises the question of how stablecoin flows move short-end yields. Extending the February 2026 revision of Ahmed and Aldasoro (2026, BIS Working Paper 1270), the analysis covers 1,381 weekday observations between 15 December 2020 and 31 March 2026. For H1, the DGS3MO response is β = -2.45 basis points per USD 1 billion of five-day inflow at h = 10 and β = -4.54 basis points by h = 20; for the USD 3.5 billion inflow used by Ahmed and Aldasoro these are -8.6 and -15.9 basis points, the same sign as that revision's estimates but about 3.4 and 4.5 times larger (about two and four to five times the June 2026 granular-IV estimates). H2 asks whether inflow and outflow shocks generate comparable absolute magnitudes. Across the 1,680-specification panel (4 maturities × 5 IV specifications × 4 shock tiers × 21 horizons), the median |β_neg / β_pos| ratio is 8.39 (Q25 = 2.37; Q75 = 19.27). The Wald symmetry null is not rejected at conventional levels, and outflow-regime first-stage instrument strength falls below standard thresholds in 96.6 percent of specifications. H2 is therefore best read as a directional median-magnitude pattern under a weak-IV regime, not a formal rejection of symmetry. Inference is reported in parallel under Newey-West HAC, Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller (2021) lag-augmented LP, and Anderson-Rubin (1949) weak-IV-robust frameworks, and the instrument is constructed under five alternative specifications. Ten deviations from the February 2026 baseline and the pre-specified plan are documented in Appendix A, and the replication package follows the Vilhuber (2019) AEA Data Editor guidance, with reproduction limits disclosed in Appendix C.

detail.title: Signaling Safety
detail.abstract: Contrary to signaling models' central predictions, changes in the level of cash flows do not empirically follow changes in dividends. We use the Campbell (1991) decomposition to construct cash-flow and discount-rate news from returns and find the following: (1) Both dividend changes and repurchase announcements signal changes in cash-flow volatility (in opposite direction); (2) larger cash-flow volatility changes come with larger announcement returns; and (3) neither discount-rate news, nor the level of cash-flow news, nor total stock return volatility change following dividend changes. We conclude cash-flow news—and not discount-rate news—drive payout policy, and payout policy conveys information about future cash-flow volatility.

detail.abstract: External debt management in West Africa remains largely retrospective even though repayment pressure, exchange-rate exposure and fiscal vulnerability require forward-looking evidence. This article develops an integrated predictive framework for 16 West African countries over 2010-2023. It combines geographical profiling, country-level associations, language-group comparison, panel stationarity assessment, two-way fixed-effects estimation, quantile-on-quantile analysis and machine-learning prediction. External debt as a percentage of GDP is the principal outcome, while macroeconomic, fiscal, external-sector and governance indicators form the predictor set. The panel contains 224 country-year observations. Average external debt was highest in Cabo Verde (94.90% of GDP), Senegal (71.41%), Burkina Faso (64.89%), Mauritania (64.39%) and Ghana (55.24%); it was lowest in Nigeria (14.55%), Togo (25.31%), Niger (25.95%), Guinea (26.97%) and Sierra Leone (27.39%). Francophone countries averaged 42.06%, compared with 35.07% among Anglophone countries, and the difference was statistically significant (p=0.015). In the two-way fixed-effects model, public and publicly guaranteed debt was the only robust contemporaneous predictor (standardised coefficient=25.88, p<0.001). For next-year prediction, the Huber regression achieved the strongest validation result and retained good performance on the 2022 holdout (MAE=6.32, RMSE=8.69 and R²=0.889). Permutation analysis identified the current debt ratio, country structure, debt service, fiscal balance and language group as the most useful predictive signals. Quantile-on-quantile surfaces further revealed that several relationships change across low-and high-debt states. The findings support country-sensitive early-warning systems rather than uniform regional thresholds.

detail.abstract: Many economic decisions rely on observations that predate the decision time. This paper introduces information latency-the elapsed time between a decision and the most recent observation of an evolving payoff-relevant state-as a distinct source of imperfect information. Unlike classical sources of information friction, latency generates irreducible uncertainty even with exact observations and rational expectations. For sufficiently regular continuous-time Markov processes, conditional variance increases locally with latency; under the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck benchmark, it increases at a decreasing rate toward a finite bound. Following a rarestate observation, however, uncertainty can peak at an intermediate latency before declining. Neither the average latency nor the average update frequency fully characterizes information quality: the regularity of information arrival matters independently of the mean interval. Latencyinduced uncertainty generates a risk premium under risk aversion. With heterogeneous latency, the lowest-risk-adjusted-cost intermediary wins the business, while competition drives the price toward the second-lowest risk-adjusted cost. In a stylized contract-renewal setting, positive latency can be second-best optimal by limiting costly reclassification when direct contractual commitment is unavailable. The framework applies to credit, insurance, and financial markets.

detail.abstract: Credit spreads for secured debt are lower than for unsecured debt, especially when a firm’s credit quality deteriorates, the economy slows, or average credit spreads widen. Yet investment grade firms tend to be reluctant to issue secured debt at all times. In contrast, we find that for firms that are rated below-investment grade, the likelihood of secured debt issuance increases as firm’s credit quality deteriorates, the economy slows, or average credit spreads widen. This differential pattern of issue behavior is consistent with highly rated firms seeing unencumbered collateral as a form of insurance, to be used only in extremis.

detail.abstract:
This article examines the relationship between enforcement duration, settlements, and precedent formation in unilateral conduct cases, using Brazil as an empirical setting. Motivated by OECD's 2019 diagnosis that Brazilian abuse-of-dominance enforcement relied heavily on settlements and generated relatively few fully litigated decisions, we construct a novel dataset of cases concluded between January 2015 and February 2026 by the Brazilian antitrust agency, CADE. 

While procedural duration is an administrative variable that directly shapes the competitive relevance of the intervention itself, the findings shed light on the trade-off that national competition authorities may face between building up a wider record of fully litigated decisions and restoring competition sooner through settlements. The paper also argues that clearer analytical frameworks may strengthen enforcement performance by contributing to greater predictability and potentially shorter investigations. In this sense, CADE's intent to publish in the second semester of 2026 the draft of the first guidelines on unilateral conduct analysis is a promising step.

detail.abstract:
We bring the notion of "satisficing" behavior to matching theory and develop the resulting solution concept, which is weaker than stability. Satisficing behavior is an alternative to maximizing behavior where, instead of always going for the best alternative, "satisficers" settle on choices that are "good enough". We say that a matching is satisficing if every agent is matched to an achievable partner. (An agent is achievable to another if they are matched in some stable matching.) 

     We show that satisficing matchings have the following properties: (i) they are Pareto efficient; (ii) all women (men) weakly prefer the woman-optimal (man-optimal) stable matching to any satisficing matching; (iii) for any two distinct satisficing matchings, there exist two pairs, each formed under one of the two matchings, such that the agents in each pair have opposite preferences over the two matchings; (iv) if agents are asked to vote between a stable matching and a satisficing matching, the two matchings tie; and (v) truthtelling is a rationalizable strategy for satisficing mechanisms. 

     We also argue that our definition is falsifiable upon the observation of all satisficing matchings, and discuss how existing algorithms can be used for the computation of the set of satisficing matchings. Finally, using as operator an extension, via the join, of the least upper bound of the common order of one gender, we show that the set of satisficing matchings forms a semigroup one of whose ideals is the set of stable matchings.

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes that long-run fertility decline is driven not by inadequate welfare provision but by a historic reversal in the balance between two penalties: the penalty of childbearing P+ (the opportunity cost of time, energy, and resources absorbed by children) and the penalty of non-childbearing P- (the discounted value of forgone returns from children as labor assets, old-age security, and sources of normative standing). Both penalties are formalized within a single household budget framework, and fertility is derived from heterogeneous thresholds over the state variable Delta = P+ - P-. Endogenizing the normative component, letting conformity value depend on the local prevalence of parenthood, yields multiple equilibria, a double-well potential, hysteresis, and the collapse of the normative floor, so that the phase transition, the difficulty of reversal, and the bottomless character of ultra-low fertility emerge as propositions rather than assumptions. Welfare policy enters through two opposing channels: cash transfers weakly lower P+, while public pensions strongly lower P-, reconciling the ineffectiveness of cash pronatalism with the crowding-out effect of pensions. Cross-sectional evidence for 133 countries (Child Penalty Atlas; World Bank) shows a negative but dispersed penalty-fertility relationship (r = -0.63): Korea pairs the largest measured penalty among high-income economies with the world's lowest fertility, while China, Denmark, and Israel show that a low one-sided penalty is compatible with either very low or high fertility. The Romanian experiment of 1966-1989, the only full-scale attempt to raise P-, coercive, initially effective, and ultimately catastrophic, calibrates the resulting policy space. The paper concludes that in societies where P- has collapsed, no policy set acceptable to normal governments restores replacement fertility, and that policy should pivot from reversing fertility toward adapting to persistently low fertility.

detail.abstract: Forecasts guide decisions, but an expert who privately values the decision may misreport beliefs to influence it. We study contracts that jointly screen the expert's belief about a verifiable state and her stake in a binary action. When two distinct stake types can each hold every belief, exact belief-only IC forces the action to ignore the report. Joint screening permits responsiveness but may require implementation rent. For thresholds, minimum rent equals the distribution-weighted positive curvature of the belief-dependent cutoff. Optimal threshold design is rent-adjusted concavification. We give sufficient conditions for unrestricted threshold optimality and bound possible gains when they fail.

title: The Impact of Trade Payment Restrictions and Capital Controls on External Sector Balances
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Impact of Trade Payment Restrictions and Capital Controls on External Sector Balances
detail.abstract: Models of external balances rely on economic fundamentals, structural indicators, cyclical variables, and policy factors. However, existing models may not fully capture the effects of restrictions on trade payments and capital controls. In this paper, we include two new policy variables in a standard empirical model of the current account to address this gap: the Measure of Aggregate Trade Restrictions (MATR) and the FinOpen index. The results indicate that tighter restrictions on trade payments of one standard deviation are associated with increases in the current account balance of about one percentage point and an appreciation of the real effective exchange rate (REER). These effects primarily operate through suppressing import demand and reducing domestic absorption. Tightening capital inflow restrictions by one standard deviation increases the current account balance by about 1.4 percentage points and depreciates the REER. Outflow restrictions operate in the opposite direction. These effects are primarily due to a wedge between domestic and global real interest rates, which in turn affect saving and investment decisions. Updating these models to assess how trade payment and capital controls affect current account balances helps support more actionable policy recommendations.

detail.abstract: The term social, as in ‘socialized medicine’, is a red flag when conversing about changes to the broken US healthcare system.  This was true when FDR attempted to convince Congress to pass Social Security legislation in 1935.  Instead, this article will use the term Social Healthcare to describe a system of healthcare the US should move toward, given problems identified in the US, Canadian and UK healthcare systems. This is a brief look at the healthcare systems of all three countries to determine how costs and services compare. Information in this article supports implementing a social healthcare system as it is explained.  This form of healthcare means that visits to a provider will be free to all US citizens at first point of contact.  The difference between this and socialized medicine systems of the UK and Canada is that clinics, hospitals, other service providers remain private, more of the cost of healthcare will be a responsibility of the states, and the amount now being spent in the US for healthcare as a percentage of GDP will be spend in other sectors of the economy.  The purpose of the article is to recommend changes to the US healthcare system to ensure the US economy is strengthened in ways not occurring now.  By making changes to the current healthcare system as outlined below, the US economy will be stronger, the labor force will be more productive, and those who are ill will receive treatment.

detail.abstract:
As of 2026, commonly cited CAPE measures for the S&P 500 are roughly 40-42, a range previously approached only around the dot-com peak. This study applies a DebtRank-style contagion model-originally developed for banking networks-to disclosed revenue links among AI value-chain firms, propagating a hypothetical spending-cut shock. An initial Pilot Study (18 nodes) suggested that counterparty revenue concentration is an interpretable indicator of financial fragility, but most of its edge weights relied on press-based estimates. 

     This revised study makes four changes. (1) Every revenue edge carries an evidence label (Tier A/B) based on SEC filings and credible analyst or media attribution; edges without such support are dropped. (2) The network is expanded to 55 nodes by snowball sampling, of which 26 lie on at least one disclosed revenue edge. (3) Contingent backstop commitments, whose totals had been entered as annual payments in an earlier version of the model, are separated from ordinary revenue flows; one revenue edge (a $10B chip order) is re-attributed from OpenAI to Anthropic; and the status of the Nvidia-OpenAI $100B letter of intent is updated. (4) The network score follows the original DebtRank definition, which excludes the initial shock. Under the disclosed links, OpenAI has the largest spillover among the seven shock origins examined (2.4× the runner-up) and ranks first in all 2,000 perturbation draws. In the OpenAI scenario, AMD's damage exceeds Oracle's in about 91.5% of draws, but this ordering is sensitive to revenue-basis and annualization assumptions that the perturbations do not cover. 

     The revenue links form an acyclic graph and equity links are not propagated, so the model does not test circular feedback among investment and purchasing flows; the results are best read as a disclosure-based mapping of concentration risk, not as a forecast or a test of the "circular financing" narrative. Code and generated results are reproduced in Appendix A.

detail.abstract: Retrieval-augmented assistants fail their users most often by stating a price, hour, address or phone number that their documents do not support. The open-weights detectors for this failure — Vectara HHEM-2.1-Open, LettuceDetect — are trained on English. We extend our planted-error benchmark to 31 languages across nine scripts (434 answers, 372 with one planted error, 62 grounded controls; identical errors in every language) and add a third kind of detector: a multilingual token classifier of our own, fine-tuned from XLM-RoBERTa-base on 6,647 answers — 2,844 synthetic business answers in 30 languages whose unsupported spans were planted and marked by open LLMs, plus RAGTruth — with the decision threshold chosen on held-out data. It catches 352 of 372 planted errors (95 %) with 32 false alarms in 62 grounded answers, in 34 ms per answer on a laptop CPU, and it serves the public demo at grounded.siba.az from a Raspberry Pi 5. On the same cases HHEM-2.1-Open reaches 71 % recall with 22 of 62 grounded answers flagged: its score collapses with script distance from English — in 6 languages it flags every grounded answer — so its recall there measures the script, not the claim. LettuceDetect catches 51 %. The open LLM judges remain the accuracy ceiling — openai/gpt-oss-120b catches 163/163 with 0 false alarms on the 14 languages its daily quota allowed, at 0.70 s per network call, ~21× the detector's latency and a per-token price.
