detail.abstract: Using fine-grained data on 465,000 Florida home sales over twelve years and semiparametric machine learning methods, we examine how home prices respond to weather-related risk factors. After controlling for geography, home characteristics, and transaction features, we find that home prices are negatively related to property-level expected weather losses derived from catastrophe models, insurance premiums, and exposure to recent hurricanes, but with notably different magnitudes. Expected weather losses show the strongest association with prices and are consistent with markets rationally capitalizing anticipated future losses into current property valuations. Insurance premiums have a statistically significant but economically more modest negative effect on home prices, suggesting that housing market participants may view premium differences across properties as more transitory. Recent hurricane exposure has only a marginal effect on house prices, suggesting that hurricane risk is well-understood in Florida so that realized weather events convey little new information about future losses.

detail.abstract: Government power can protect individual rights or displace them. This paper specifies the conditions separating these outcomes. For a specified jurisdiction, policy window, and common normalization, it defines institutional capacity by C = P + R, where P is government power and R is individual action space. It further decomposes that space as R = R⁺ + R⁻: exercising welfare-compatible rights causes no involuntary, uncompensated deterioration in affected persons' protected conditions, whereas exercising destructive action space does. With capacity approximately stable over a policy window, this distinction yields a marginal criterion: if an additional unit of public power suppresses more than one unit of destructive action space, welfare-compatible rights expand even as total private action space contracts; below that threshold, further power displaces those rights. The resulting governance intensity can lie above the minimum required to protect basic rights; policy assessment turns on what power suppresses and what it preserves. The paper proposes empirical tests of capacity stability, marginal governance effects, and sensitivity to normalization choices. It also links welfare-compatible rights to the institutional conditions for discretionary expenditure and experimentation. Institutional vitality comprises adjustment within a given capacity and its expansion across generations, allowing public power and welfare-compatible rights to grow together.

title: The Collapse Trajectory of Extractive Institutions

detail.title: The Collapse Trajectory of Extractive Institutions

detail.abstract: We study the dynamic consequences of deep sustained extraction within a coalition of heterogeneous agents. An extractive institution that pays its masses below standalone value must neutralize every coordinated intermediate body (churches, guilds, unions, independent media) regardless of political orientation, because every such body is a standing witness to underpayment. Each destruction opens a computable blindspot direction in which the society cannot absorb shocks. We show that institutional destruction drives mass diversity to one effective dimension through a self-reinforcing dynamic: each destroyed institution lowers the regeneration capacity for diversity, which lowers the equilibrium diversity, which makes the next institution easier to destroy. Along the homogenization trajectory, value, resilience, and adaptability collapse together: the capability matrix converges to rank three and the collapse threshold vanishes; the population's adaptive capacity is confined to three class directions and then to nothing; and the value per unit of capability falls to at most three effective dimensions, so that extraction provably destroys most of what it set out to capture. We derive an explicit hazard curve giving the per-period probability of a fatal shock as a function of residual diversity, and prove that collapse arrives in finite time with probability one. A master theorem composes the entire chain into a single termination result. An extension shows that consecutive non-nested regimes destroy strictly more of the civil ecology than either regime alone.

detail.abstract: This dossier asks whether the economic function of a fixed-for-floating interest-rate swap can be reconstructed as an Islamic profit-rate hedge within a Malaysian Sharīʿah and legal framework without making the conventional cash-difference claim the juridical source of entitlement. It studies a hypothetical five-year USD 1 billion floating-rate financing of Malaysian Infrastructure Holdings Berhad and uses the conventional swap only as an economic comparator. The method combines exposure decomposition, formal al-takyīf al-fiqhī, source-of-entitlement analysis, authority mapping, asset and possession testing, promise analysis, quantitative hedge testing, and lifecycle review through default and close-out. The primary frame is Malaysian legislation, Bank Negara Malaysia policy, and Sharīʿah Advisory Council material. IIFM/ISDA and AAOIFI supply institutional and accounting material; IIFA supplies comparative and adverse institutional positions; classical fiqh and academic literature supply doctrinal, comparative or critical analysis. The principal finding is conditional: Malaysian materials support a controlled, structure-specific workstream, but neither a legitimate hedging purpose nor separately recognised contracts establishes permissibility of the whole arrangement. The decisive inquiry is whether each payment remains causally connected to a valid contract while ownership, possession, risk, price certainty, settlement, and close-out remain genuine. The dossier contributes a reproducible method for testing economic replication against juridical causation; it is not a fatwā, legal opinion, product approval, or recommendation to execute.

detail.abstract: We study the gains from trade when countries differ in both productive composition and market size. International trade theory offers two explanations for why nations trade (comparative advantage and product variety) but treats them as separate phenomena whose relative importance is an empirical question. We show that both channels arise from a single characteristic function that factors the value of any trading bloc into three structural primitives: the number of independent comparative advantages among its members, a variety premium that grows with bloc size, and the aggregate productive capacity. The factored form yields four main results. First, the gains from trade decompose exactly into a classical component and a variety component, and a rank condition (not an empirical estimate) determines which component dominates. Second, trading is strictly beneficial for every pair of countries, including identical economies, with no assumptions on market structure or preferences. Third, the fair division of the surplus rewards every country strictly and pays a premium for unique comparative advantage. Fourth, the stability of the trading order traces to a geometric condition on country profiles, with a structural converse showing that absorption of a member's advantage seeds instability. The framework yields prescriptive results for trade bloc design and prices the structural cost of sanctions.

detail.abstract:
Pakistan's banking system funds itself with rupee deposits and deploys them mainly in government securities. In July 2026 the sector held PKR 39.05 trillion of deposits against PKR 13.56 trillion of advances and PKR 40.83 trillion of investments, an advances-to-deposit ratio of 34.7 percent and an investment-to-deposit ratio of 104.6 percent. This paper asks why that structure persists, and evaluates a proposition that recurs in practitioner discussion: that banks could raise profitability and lower borrower costs by funding themselves in foreign currency at a rate such as term SOFR and lending in rupees at KIBOR plus a spread.

The paper argues that the proposition rests on a pricing error rather than an unexploited opportunity. On 4 September 2026 six-month KIBOR was 11.86 percent and on 18 September 2026 six-month CME Term SOFR was 4.19 percent, a nominal gap of about 7.7 percentage points. Covered interest parity implies that a hedged version of the trade returns that gap to the forward market and nets to approximately zero, less a cross-currency basis. Uncovered interest parity implies that the unhedged version is a currency carry position rather than a funding strategy. The record supports the second reading: the rupee averaged 89.24 per US dollar in FY2012 and 281.1 per dollar over July to March of FY2026, a cumulative depreciation of about 215 percent, or roughly 8.5 percent a year, which exceeds the current nominal differential. A third error compounds the first two. A Pakistani bank does not fund at SOFR. Pakistan's sovereign paid 7.50 percent on a 5.5-year US dollar Eurobond in September 2026, so the relevant foreign-currency funding cost embeds a country risk premium of roughly 300 basis points before any bank-specific spread.

The paper sets out the deposit-led model and its sovereign-lending spine, dismantles the naive arbitrage through interest parity, identifies the narrow set of borrowers whom foreign-currency funding genuinely suits and the existing channels that already serve them, and assesses the systemic, regulatory and Shariah constraints on any broader shift. Its contribution is explanatory rather than prescriptive: the value lies in understanding why the apparent arbitrage does not exist and what its absence reveals about the structure of a repressed, sovereign-dominated financial system.

detail.abstract:
Level-based Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall checks on benchmark portfolios need not control portfolio choice: common additive risk shifts leave rankings unchanged, whereas relative-risk distortions can alter the optimizer. We develop a validation-calibrated minimax-regret framework for Expected Shortfall portfolio optimization. Using a decision-relevant discrepancy that is invariant to common additive shifts, fixed candidate risk engines, an independent validation sample, and a pre-specified audit library, we form a polyhedral ambiguity set over convex aggregations of implemented risk functions. Finite-sample calibration under bounded returns, together with a Lipschitz covering argument from audits to the full feasible domain, yields a highprobability true Expected Shortfall regret certificate that separates model discrepancy, validation
error, audit-coverage error, and optimization error. The procedure also permits model-class rejection and admits an exact linear-programming reformulation for moderate ambiguity systems.

detail.abstract: India moved the closing price of every derivative-eligible equity to a twenty-minute call auction in August 2026 and made that auction price the settlement price for index derivatives. Using 31 post-reform sessions and one-second capture of auction state that no party archives, I ask whether the derivatives market agrees with the price it settles on. Largely it does not. The cash revaluation passes into index futures with a slope of 0.112 (s.e. 0.027), and on the most conservative of three covariance estimators it still lies 22.7 standard errors below complete incorporation, with no bootstrap resample of ten thousand reaching unity; the remainder is absorbed into the futures basis. The freeze that makes this possible is mandated and holds on every session for the NIFTY 50 and for the SENSEX on a separately operated venue, with a within-venue control in the one derivatives-eligible index that does not freeze. The revaluation is heavy-tailed, with an expected shortfall 3.8 times the mean and a tail index the full sample cannot place above two, though that reading rests on the reform's opening week. Finally, on one session, the venue published two different values of the same official index for 55 seconds while derivatives traded; that result establishes existence and nothing about frequency, and a sequential study of its recurrence is pre-registered.

detail.abstract: The increasing sophistication of cyberattacks and the dynamic nature of enterprise networks require intrusion detection systems that can recognize both known and previously unseen malicious activities. Traditional signature-based approaches are effective for established threats but may struggle to identify zero-day attacks because their characteristics have not been previously documented. This study presents a hybrid Convolutional Neural Network-Gated Recurrent Unit (CNN-GRU) model for adaptive network intrusion and zero-day attack detection. The proposed framework combines CNN-based feature extraction with GRU-based temporal sequence analysis to learn both local traffic characteristics and changes in network behavior over time. Network traffic is first collected and preprocessed through data cleaning, normalization, categorical encoding, feature transformation, and sequence construction. The CNN component extracts important representations from network traffic, while the GRU component learns temporal dependencies between successive observations with a relatively efficient recurrent architecture. An adaptive mechanism can be incorporated to update the model when significant changes in network traffic distributions are detected. To evaluate zero-day detection capability, selected attack categories can be excluded from training and introduced during testing. Model performance can be measured using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, detection rate, false-positive rate, and inference time. The proposed framework provides a foundation for combining automated feature learning and temporal behavioral analysis while addressing the changing characteristics of enterprise networks. However, reliable performance depends on representative data, appropriate adaptation mechanisms, robust evaluation, and effective management of false positives and concept drift.

detail.abstract: Nuclear shutdown is generally framed as dismantlement, decontamination, waste management, and land release. This paper reframes it as a site-level capital-reallocation problem. Its analytical unit is the nuclear site—not the reactor—because grid connections, cooling and water systems, industrial land, logistics access, workforce capabilities, and institutional knowledge may survive the end of generation. The paper develops four linked and falsifiable constructs within a Conversion Economy framework: the Site Capability Portfolio; a pathway-specific RBC weakest-link diagnostic; the Second Capital Dividend, defined as usable embedded capability net of adaptation and interface costs; and a Site-Transition Entity that separates nuclear liability from redevelopment risk while coordinating their interface. The framework compares restart, regulated decommissioning, nuclear repowering, non nuclear conversion, and hybrid reuse. Shutdown is treated as an operational state, decommissioning as a regulated liability-reduction process, and asset reuse as a successor pathway that may overlap with decommissioning where safety, spatial separation, and interface governance permit. Structured comparison of Fukushima Daiichi, Monju/Fukui, Hamaoka, and Tokai Daini shows why physical abundance is not equivalent to convertibility: a single binding constraint in land release, permission, finance, workforce, demand, or interface safety can dominate the rest of the portfolio. The paper therefore treats infrastructure preservation and staged land release as real-option decisions. Its contribution is a theory-building, diagnostic architecture that generates testable propositions and a replicable evidence protocol; it does not claim site-level causal estimates or investment-grade valuation.

detail.abstract: Value-at-Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES) are central tools for financial risk measurement, but both primarily characterize the marginal distribution of losses. Consequently, they can assign similar risk to two loss paths that contain the same individual tail observations but differ in the temporal organization of those observations. This paper develops Tail Episode Risk (TER), a path-dependent tail-risk functional that quantifies the severity of the most extreme contiguous cumulative-loss episode within a forecast horizon, and Conditional Tail Episode Risk (CTER), which decomposes future episode risk into (i) the conditional probability that an extreme-loss episode occurs and (ii) the conditional upper-tail severity of that episode. The framework is related to aggregate excess severity in extreme-value theory, clustered extremes, Conditional Expected Drawdown, and dynamic VaR/ES forecasting, but targets a distinct state variable: cumulative loss above a tail threshold within a contiguous episode. We establish basic properties of TER-monotonicity, positive homogeneity, translation invariance under a translation-equivariant threshold rule (in the sense of a severity/deviation functional rather than a monetary risk measure), and sensitivity to temporal clustering-and give constructed counterexamples in which two paths share identical marginal VaR and ES but differ in TER. Monte Carlo experiments confirm that TER increases sharply with serial dependence while marginal VaR and ES remain essentially flat, and adversarial stress tests show that TER responds to sustained episodes rather than to isolated tail observations. Empirically, we evaluate the framework on daily data for six equity, bond, foreign-exchange, and cryptocurrency markets over 2000-2026, with asset-specific out-of-sample windows (from 2005 for equities and FX, 2008 for Treasuries, and 2018 for Bitcoin). The evidence is cautionary. Under a strictly consistent Fissler-Ziegel scoring rule, GARCH-t is the strongest conventional benchmark and an EWMA specification a strong simple one. Episode-occurrence discrimination is weak and decays into the tail (mean AUC 0.56, 0.54, 0.47 at the 95%, 97.5%, 99% thresholds). A formal incremental test finds that augmenting a parsimonious volatility baseline with the full CTER conditioning set does not improve out-of-sample episode-severity forecasts-indeed it is significantly worse at the 95% and 97.5% thresholds and statistically indistinguishable at 99%. The evidence therefore supports a narrower conclusion: TER is a distinct pathdependent tail-risk functional that captures the temporal organization of extreme losses, while the forecasting value of its conditional extension (CTER) remains unresolved.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the practices of tax avoidance carried out by cross-border digital business actors and the challenges faced by tax authorities in determining the existence of a Permanent Establishment (Bentuk Usaha Tetap) for companies operating without a physical presence. As the digital economy evolves, multinational technology companies can generate substantial revenue from a market country like Indonesia without being subject to traditional income tax rules, leading to significant base erosion. This study uses a narrative literature review of national tax regulations, international tax frameworks, and academic journals published between 2015 and 2026, grouped thematically to identify common findings, contradictions, and remaining research gaps. The discussion covers common avoidance schemes, the inadequacy of the traditional physical presence threshold, and the implications for Indonesia's taxing rights. It also evaluates Indonesia's policy responses: Value Added Tax (VAT) on Trade Through Electronic Systems (PMSE), which had collected about Rp44.05 trillion by August 2026, the significant economic presence concept, and the global minimum tax under Pillar Two, in contrast with Pillar One, which has yet to become operational. The findings suggest that unilateral measures like PMSE VAT are effective in the short term, but long-term legal certainty requires the operationalization of the Electronic Transaction Tax and active commitment to global tax consensus.

detail.abstract: Applied policy research often examines interventions that differ in design and whose effects on downstream outcomes are uncertain in direction and magnitude, complicating welfare evaluation. We develop a transparent framework to synthesize evidence across heterogeneous policy instruments that operate through a shared intermediary outcome but lack a common treatment scale. We apply this approach to youth e-cigarette regulations and their impacts on youth smoking using data from a systematic review. We consider evidence from 11 natural experiments included in a recent systematic review, which span e-cigarette minimum legal sale age laws (MLSAs), e-cigarette taxes, and flavored e-cigarette restrictions. We standardize these heterogeneous policies based on their estimated effects on e-cigarette use and estimate their downstream effect on youth cigarette smoking using fixed and random effects meta-analysis. The evidence overall supports the conclusion that e-cigarette availability reduces youth cigarette smoking. More broadly, our framework provides a practical approach for synthesizing policy evidence when interventions share a common objective but are not directly comparable on a single treatment scale.

detail.abstract: This working paper examines the widespread inference that an unmarried adult has failed socially, relationally, spiritually, or personally. It argues that the inference is a category error. Marriage is a genuine biblical good and may provide profound forms of intimacy, mutual care, family life, and social support; yet neither Scripture nor a Christian doctrine of human dignity permits marital status to function as a ranking of human worth. The paper distinguishes singleness as a social or relational status from singleness as a chosen vocation, a temporary circumstance, a consequence of loss or rupture, a condition one hopes will change, or a stable life that may be received with peace and fruitfulness. It further separates singleness from loneliness, celibacy from involuntary non-partnership, sexual continence from social isolation, desire for marriage from personal deficiency, and fruitfulness from biological reproduction alone. The biblical analysis draws on creation, the unmarried life of Jesus, Matthew 19, 1 Corinthians 7, the family of discipleship, widowhood, Christian friendship, spiritual gifts, and the New Testament's account of vocation. Catholic sources are used as a theological dialogue partner, especially the Catechism, Familiaris Consortio, Amoris Laetitia, and Dignitas Infinita. Interdisciplinary research is examined cautiously: contemporary singlehood research documents substantial within-group variability, the importance of friendship and family support, the effects of social discrimination, age and gender differences, and real average well-being risks for some persistently single populations. These findings neither justify romanticizing singleness nor support treating it as evidence of failure. The paper proposes a dignity-and-vocation framework for churches, families, pastoral workers, and individuals: honor marriage without making it a universal measure of adulthood; name loneliness without confusing it with singleness; support people who desire partnership without shaming them; strengthen non-romantic forms of belonging; and evaluate fruitfulness by fidelity, love, service, character, and vocation rather than by marital status alone.

detail.abstract: Purpose-This study investigates the formation mechanisms of interorganizational trust in public sector governance networks and its impact on collaborative performance. Although trust is widely regarded as a critical variable in collaborative governance, its antecedents and performance transmission pathways in multi-actor governance networks remain insufficiently examined empirically. Design/methodology/approach-Drawing on social exchange theory and governance network theory, this study constructs a theoretical model comprising four antecedent variables-institutional design, communication frequency, goal congruence, and organizational reputation-with collaborative performance as the outcome variable, and inter-organizational trust as the mediating variable. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire administered to 412 midand senior-level managers serving as boundary spanners in cross-sector collaborative governance networks across environmental governance, public health, and regional development domains. Structural equation modeling (SEM) with maximum likelihood estimation was employed for hypothesis testing, and bootstrapping procedures were used for mediation analysis. Findings-Institutional design (β = 0.34, p < 0.001) and communication frequency (β = 0.28, p < 0.001) exert significant positive effects on inter-organizational trust. Trust fully mediates the relationship between goal congruence and collaborative performance (indirect effect = 0.19, p < 0.01). Organizational reputation demonstrates a positive but comparatively weaker effect on trust (β = 0.14, p < 0.05). Originality/value-This study extends trust research from the dyadic level to the network level, revealing the multi-level mechanisms of trust formation in governance networks. It provides actionable policy implications for public managers seeking to cultivate collaborative trust through institutional arrangements and relational management.

detail.abstract: The paper studies software agents built from a 2,000-neuron subgraph of MaleCNS, a reconstructed map of a male fruit fly's neural connections. The agents face Holt-Laury lotteries, the Allais paradox and a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma, with published human experiments providing the benchmarks. They make fewer safe lottery choices than humans-4.125 against 5.2-yet all 24 primary controllers exhibit the conventional Allais reversal. In repeated interaction, cooperation averages approximately 38% and declines with experience. The agents respond to a reciprocal opponent but fail to reproduce humans' high initial cooperation followed by terminal defection in later matches. Control treatments show that changes in neural connections, payoff representation and learning speed affect the agents' choices. Simulated flies thus offer a complementary class of experimental subjects for studying preferences and strategic behavior.

detail.abstract: We investigate the transmission channels of climate policy uncertainty (CPU) to the U.S. capital market using a Bayesian Structural VAR estimated on monthly data from 1994 to 2023. By jointly modeling CPU alongside the VIX and the Financial Stress Index (FSI), we isolate the mechanisms through which climate-related regulatory uncertainty affects equity valuations. Three findings emerge. First, CPU shocks significantly depress the S&P 500 index and price-dividend ratios while raising financial stress. Second, unlike conventional uncertainty shocks-which produce demand-type disinflationary contractions-CPU innovations generate supply-driven recessions, characterized by rising goods prices alongside falling asset prices, consistent with transition-cost pressures. Third, counterfactual exercises that selectively mute financial channels reveal that systemic financial stress is the dominant propagation mechanism: shutting down the FSI channel renders equity-market responses statistically insignificant, whereas muting the VIX leaves them intact. The findings are robust across a range of identification and specification exercises, including the construction of economic confidence bands from 240 alternative recursive specifications. These results establish CPU as a structurally distinct driver for financial markets, whose transmission to valuations is critically mediated by credit and intermediation frictions rather than by forward-looking volatility.

detail.abstract: Prediction-market shares differ from traditional financial products in that, with no information or outside utility, classical delta-neutral Central Limit Order Book (CLOB) market making cannot be financed by payoff-uninformative noise flow. Transaction-level evidence from a major prediction-market CLOB platform shows makers profiting not from spread but from carrying an underpriced side to settlement-the empirical signature of behavioral tail demand rather than classical, randomized noise. We build this tail demand directly into the model and study an LMSR and a CLOB on the same event. A pre-shock CLOB quote inside the common-signal band is picked off; competitive quotes therefore screen informed traders out of the book. CLOB makers earn screening rent by carrying the underpriced side to resolution, while informed flow routes to the LMSR. The venues coexist: the CLOB supplies the tail-demand rent margin that lets the LMSR recover part of its loss to informed flow, and AMM depth moves the CLOB premium with a sign set by maker-side contestability-widening it where standing quotes can be undercut, compressing it where a committed maker carries the book. With three or more outcomes, binary-book CLOBs pin switch prices but leave implied beliefs indeterminate, whereas the LMSR prices the outcome simplex coherently and uses collateral more efficiently.

detail.abstract: We study how opening private markets to retail investors affects investors and firms.  Calibrating a production-based asset-pricing model, we find that democratization raises retail investors' welfare, but barely.  Retail investors benefit little from democratization even if they face no extra cost or other disadvantage relative to institutional investors. The private market is simply too small for improved diversification to matter much.  Democratization affects firms more than investors---it substantially reshapes private firms' ownership, temporarily reduces their cost of capital, and induces a large expansion of private capital.  Private equity earns a positive CAPM alpha, which shrinks after democratization.

detail.abstract: A state's ability to integrate energy, data and logistics flows into adaptive national capabilities determines its national competitiveness, resilience and influence. The paper proposes a strategic stack architecture that integrates geographic position, strategic flow systems and ecosystem orchestration into higher-order national capabilities, supported by institutional trust and security. The framework moves beyond classical static geopolitics to argue that sustainable strategic competitive advantage does not emerge from isolated physical assets, but from the state's ability become a preferred, trusted and continuously adaptable node within a network of international corridors. Greece is used as an illustrative case in Southeast Europe, to show how a peripheral economy can aligned with global capital markets and technology ecosystems to convert regional infrastructure assets into long-term macroeconomic resilience

detail.abstract: Oil-price innovations are positively associated with the Treasury term premium, but the composition of the associated yield movement changes across periods. Monthly local projections compare 2010-2019 with 2022-August 2026 using an activity-orthogonal oil innovation and a common full-sample scale. The contemporaneous Adrian-Crump-Moench term-premium coefficients are 8.1 and 6.3 basis points, and the corresponding Kim-Wright coefficients are 4.1 and 4.7 basis points. Expected-short-rate-path estimates are smaller and imprecise. A common-regressor decomposition locates the earlier market-yield association predominantly in breakevens and the later association predominantly in TIPS real yields. The between-window change in the breakeven-minus-real-yield coefficient is-14.5 basis points, with a calendar-aware HAC standard error of 4.3 and a block-wild-bootstrap interval of [-24.3,-5.2]. This composition change is more clearly resolved than the change in the total termpremium coefficient. The positive premium association is preserved under nominal-oil and alternative CPI treatments, although the later ACM estimate is more inference-sensitive than its earlier counterpart. The findings distinguish a recurring premium association from a changing market-yield composition and provide a component-level account of energy-related Treasury repricing. The estimates are conditional associations with an oil-price innovation, rather than causal responses to a uniquely identified supply shock.

detail.abstract: We introduce an empirical asset pricing model that reconciles the flexibility of machine learning with the economic discipline of Q-theory. Our AI-Q-factor model draws on 39 profitability and investment proxies, imposing that high profitability and low investment imply high expected returns. Rather than concentrating on canonical characteristics, it diversifies across roughly 25 signals and doubles the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of the Q-factor model. Value and momentum improve on canonical Q-factors but are redundant against AI-Q-factors, even when measured using refined or high-dimensional characteristics. The AI-Q-factor model thus provides a new benchmark that improves measurement of the factors while maintaining the economic structure of the Q-factor model.

detail.abstract: Institutions accumulate procedures, thresholds and veto points, and every individual addition is defensible. The asymmetry is well documented and has been derived more than once-from blame avoidance, from collective action, from holdout among the owners of fragmented rights, from public choice in the regulatory state-and every one of those derivations runs through the holders of particular instruments, so each predicts pruning wherever those holders are weak, divided or bought out. We argue that the asymmetry survives that limit. An arrangement can require only what its instruments can be about, and an instrument is a device making one party's obligation to another operative, with a holder, a counterparty, a quantum and a forum. The number of instruments an arrangement has is not in that class: it distinguishes no proposal from another, so no quantum sorts it and no forum has it at issue. A requirement on the count is therefore not unmet but undefined, and the count drifts up because repairs add instruments and nothing subtracts them, with no party positioned on the total in either direction. Three things follow that can be checked. The drift has no limit at which it stops, because no magnitude produces it. Any mechanism built to hold the count relocates the contest to a boundary that is unheld for the same reason, which four audited attempts display in detail. And the instrument nobody defends is not removed either-the case on which this account and the literature predict opposite things.

title: The Asymptotic Meaning/Goal of Life A Formal Theory of Generalized Transmission and Survival-Regret

detail.title: The Asymptotic Meaning/Goal of Life A Formal Theory of Generalized Transmission and Survival-Regret

detail.abstract:
What is the goal of life? We approach this question through a general account of reproduction: a living system produces successors that retain the capacity to produce further successors. The connected successors form a family, or lineage, even when their physical form or reproductive mechanism changes. Starting from this account, we ask what continued existence requires of behavior. Under the stated environmental and information conditions, a lineage cannot continue indefinitely while repeatedly giving up a persistent amount of survival opportunity. This provides a conditional mathematical basis for treating lineage survival as an asymptotic objective, rather than assuming that life maximizes genes, offspring numbers, or population share.

We call the loss relative to the best attainable continuation \emph{Survival-Regret}. What is attainable depends not only on resources and information, but also on incentives and the cost of change. We therefore distinguish coordinated possibilities, arrangements that members will voluntarily follow, and complete processes that can establish an improved arrangement from the current state. A process can be best among those available while still falling short of coordinated survival.

A finite-resource reproduction model shows why these distinctions matter. Members who each seek the longest expected survival of their own family can reproduce too much and shorten their ancestor's family life. Shared parentage can remove that conflict under an explicit condition, but a better arrangement may still fail to become established. A dynamic model follows resources, individual ancestry, voluntary adoption, and competition. The contribution is a formal connection between recursive reproduction, lineage persistence, and the behavior and transitions that can preserve it.

detail.abstract: Does elite conflict cause franchise extension? I study this question in the context of the 1832 Great Reform Act in England, using surviving poll books and parish records on the formation of disenfranchising select vestries. Reduced-form analysis leveraging a difference-in-differences research design finds that political elites residing in parishes with democratic backsliding increased their electoral support for the reformist Whig party between the 1830 and 1831 general elections. I attribute the research findings to the outbreak of the Swing Riots, which occurred with greater intensity in select vestry parishes, providing an elite-conflict interpretation of the theory of revolutionary threat.

title: Beyond Financial Conditions: Measuring Structural Vulnerabilities in the U.S. Financial System

publicationDetails.detailsText: Finance and Economics Discussion Series, issue 065, 2026[10.17016/FEDS.2026.065]

detail.abstract: We introduce the Financial Vulnerability Index (FVI), a novel indicator of financial vulnerabilities in the U.S. Unlike financial condition indices, which measure current credit market conditions and spike during periods of financial turmoil, the FVI displays the gradual build-up of structural financial weaknesses and declines as such episodes materialize. We demonstrate that the FVI exhibits properties consistent with theoretical mechanisms of financial vulnerabilities. When the index is high, adverse shocks are substantially amplified, generating larger declines in consumption and investment. We provide new empirical evidence that monetary tightening is associated with gradual declines in the FVI, with this effect substantially delayed, taking a few years to fully materialize. Moreover, monetary policy transmission to prices depends on the state of financial vulnerabilities, with significantly stronger effects when vulnerabilities are low.

detail.abstract: Correction produces non-events (the failure that did not occur, the loss that never matured) and a legal order attaches a return by identifying a lapse that reduces someone's holdings by an amount it can price. The persistence of a capacity that prevents events is not such a lapse. So correction has no loss of its own, and where it is funded it is funded through a loss borrowed from elsewhere: a capacity may hold every attribute a legal order can confer and remain unfunded. A claim regime determines what investment yields a return some party can hold and defend; where returns to a capacity's persistence attach to no party, no allocation rule responsive to enforceable return will fund it-not because anyone decides, and not because the capacity is hard to code, but because the rule has nothing to respond to. Correction capacity is where this bites, since the return to correction is a non-event and a non-event attaches to nobody. Six regimes are examined, across three jurisdictions and four centuries. Those that fund correction are the ones in which its lapse falls on a party whose loss is real and individually held; the completest conferral in the set and the highest instrument in the set are both on the unfunded side, and where conferral was fullest and no such party existed, recognition produced nothing.

detail.abstract: In this study, I explore a bilateral trading problem involving a buyer and a seller. Initially, the buyer's valuation is unknown to all parties. After the seller proposes a contract, the buyer privately and flexibly acquires information by arranging costly signals that correlate with his valuation. The seller's problem is to design a contract that incentivizes the buyer to acquire information and engage in trade. The analysis reveals that a simple contract, which is independent of the buyer's valuation distribution except for the mean, is optimal for the seller, and that the buyer receives only binary signals indicating whether the good is worth buying.

title: The Price of the Performance: Surface Acting as the Measured Maintenance Cost of Inverted Virtue

detail.title: The Price of the Performance: Surface Acting as the Measured Maintenance Cost of Inverted Virtue

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not applicable.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: Not applicable.

detail.abstract:
A nurse at the end of a twelve-hour shift smiles at the relative who has shouted at her. A call-centre worker thanks a customer for his patience in a voice that has none. A flight attendant is warm to the passenger who has made her afraid. Each of them displays a disposition the occupation requires — courtesy, patience, care — and in each case what produces the display is not the disposition but the job.

The Thermodynamics of Inversion claimed that an occupied virtue must be actively maintained by whoever occupies it, while the genuine virtue need not be: the lie is expensive and the truth is free. The claim was stated as a governed analogy and has carried the warrant of one ever since. This article shows that it was measured, at the scale of a single person, by a literature the programme had never cited.

Organisational psychology has studied emotional labour for four decades and distinguishes two ways of meeting a display requirement. Surface acting changes the display and leaves the inner state untouched; deep acting changes the inner state so that the display becomes true. A meta-analysis of ninety-five independent studies found surface acting substantially associated with impaired well-being and deep acting only weakly so, with positive associations with performance. This article argues that the distinction is not analogous to the programme’s but identical to it: surface acting satisfies the three conditions of forgery at n = 1, and deep acting is an attempt to become the origin of the demanded form (T1). The maintenance-cost claim therefore gains an external corroboration it has never had, together with every limitation of the literature that supplies it (T2).

The identification pays in both directions. The programme explains a standing puzzle in the emotional-labour literature — why deep acting’s outcomes are mixed — as the averaging of an absorption process observed at different stages (T3). And it predicts something the literature has not tested: that surface acting fails discontinuously when its maintenance is interrupted, and deep acting degrades gracefully (T4). A corollary locates surface acting where display rules create a demanded form that is inspected and cannot be appropriated, which is where the programme’s decoy rule says a counterfeit will be built (C1).

Keywords: emotional labour; surface acting; deep acting; emotion regulation; maintenance cost; Thermodynamics of Inversion; forgery; absorption; virtue ethics; Philosophy of Virtues

detail.abstract: Multiple-horizon forecast panels are increasingly used to infer perceived monetary policy rules, but inference depends on how coefficients are pooled across forecasters, dates, and horizons. We treat this pooling structure as the object of inference. In a participant-date-horizon Taylor-rule regression model, we compare pooling patterns using Bayesian marginal likelihoods, applying the framework to the Blue Chip Financial Forecasts, Survey of Professional Forecasters, and the Summary of Economic Projections. The preferred specifications place much of the systematic variation in policy-rate forecasts in intercepts that vary across forecast horizons and survey dates. Evidence of "changing perceptions" of monetary policy via economically meaningful time-varying response coefficients is weak overall.

title: Substitutes or complements? Climate exposure and the joint choice of livelihood adaptation strategies in Ghana
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Environment and Sustainable Development and Ghana Institute of Management and Public Administration

detail.title: Substitutes or complements? Climate exposure and the joint choice of livelihood adaptation strategies in Ghana
detail.abstract: Households facing intensifying climate hazards rarely respond with a single action; they assemble portfolios of livelihood adjustments. Yet, most micro-level studies in Africa model adaptation choices one at a time and treat the capacity to adapt as uniform across the income distribution. Using nationally representative data on 2,276 Ghanaian adults from Round 10 of the Afrobarometer survey, this study estimates how perceived multi-hazard climate exposure shapes the joint adoption of five livelihood adaptation strategies using a multivariate probit model, and tests whether lived poverty, location and gender moderate the exposure–adaptation relationship. The five strategies were found to be strongly interdependent, confirming that they are adopted as complementary bundles rather than substitutes. Perceived exposure raises the probability of adopting every land- and water-based strategy (average marginal effects of 1.6–2.8 percentage points per additional hazard) and lifts adaptation intensity by about 11% per hazard. Critically, the exposure–adaptation gradient is significantly flatter for poorer households although the poor cope more at low exposure, their adaptation barely rises as hazards intensify, signalling a binding adaptive-capacity constraint. The findings reframe adaptation as a resource-conditioned portfolio decision and argue for adaptation finance and information services that target the climate-exposed poor.

title: Green stimulus, dynamic cash management and corporate investment
affiliations: East China Normal University (ECNU) - Faculty of Economics and Management, East China Normal University (ECNU) and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - Department of Statistics

detail.title: Green stimulus, dynamic cash management and corporate investment
detail.abstract: We study a continuous-time green fiscal stimulus problem for a firm at different levels of green investment. The firm can access government loans up to a maximum limit and balance the trade-off between shareholders' benefits and its environmental responsibility to optimise cash management and investment policies. This framework involves a challenging singular control problem of a two-dimensional degenerate diffusion system but enables a unified analysis of the marginal value of government spending and the impact of loan availability on both brown and green firms. We provide theoretical insights into the lower dividend payments and higher take-up of loans for greener firms relative to brown firms. The model predictions together with the numerical results have implications for how policymakers can prioritise green spending and plan green stimulus programmes.

title: The right place at the right time: information for optimal temporary conservation actions for migratory species
affiliations: University of Wyoming, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Idaho - Department of Agricultural Economics and Rural Sociology , Bowdoin College and University of Wyoming - College of Business - Department of Economics and Finance

detail.title: The right place at the right time: information for optimal temporary conservation actions for migratory species
detail.abstract: The movement of migratory species across space and time complicates conservation but also creates novel opportunities for effective management. Such opportunities include permeability-increasing conservation actions to facilitate migrations and temporary, ”pop-up” conservation actions at locations and times when the species is present. Yet, stochasticity in species migration movements makes targeting such actions to the right place at the right time difficult. We develop a general framework and solve an annual parameterized stochastic dynamic programming model with uncertainty in species’ movements to develop insights into the optimal location and timing for permeability-increasing, temporary conservation activities. Our framework illustrates how near real-time information enables managers to target conservation actions more effectively in time and space, thereby increasing expected migratory survival. Using stylized examples across terrestrial, aerial, and marine migratory species, we demonstrate how species characteristics and conservation costs jointly determine optimal conservation actions and the value of near real-time information, with high value from using real-time data for settings with species of limited fidelity. We also show that more-than-additive energy impact of barriers leads managers to put more action on barriers met by the species first.

detail.abstract: Does deskilling cause unrest? I study this question in the context of the First Industrial Revolution in England, using parish-level data on the adoption of skill-saving machines drawn from a corpus of newspaper advertisements. Reduced-form analysis leveraging an event study research design finds a positive causal effect of skill-saving mechanisation on unrest intensity between 1760 and 1814. Heterogeneity analysis of peaceful collective bargaining and petitioning by employers and workers identifies the weakening of labour market institutions as a plausible mechanism, attributable to the imbalance of lobbying power between winners and losers of disruptive technological change.

title: Agricultural Insurance and Biodiversity: Evidence from China
affiliations: Liaoning University and Liaoning University

detail.title: Agricultural Insurance and Biodiversity: Evidence from China
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the relation between agricultural insurance and biodiversity in China. Using a sample of Chinese prefecture-level cities from 2003 to 2023, Constructing a bird richness index using Chinese birding data, we find robust evidence that agricultural insurance has significantly improved the biodiversity, which is measured as the bird richness based on Chinese bird watching data. Specifically, we also show that this positive effect is more profound for cities with lower level of agricultural mechanization, lower natural risks, lower-endangered bird cities, and key environmental protections. Meanwhile, our findings remain valid after a series of robustness tests and controlling for endogeneity. Finally, we propose that the reduction in the amount of pesticides and fertilizers and the increase in public awareness of environmental protection are plausible channels through which agricultural insurance encourages prefecture-level biodiversity in China. Overall, these results shed light on the real effects of agricultural insurance and the determinants of biodiversity.

title: Other-regarding values and pro-social behaviour in environmental governance: An economic experiment on the potential of perspective-taking
affiliations: School of Business Administration and Economics, IUSF Research Centre - Osnabrueck University, Osnabrück University, School of Economics and Business Administration and Institute of Environmental Planning, Leibniz University Hannover

detail.title: Other-regarding values and pro-social behaviour in environmental governance: An economic experiment on the potential of perspective-taking
detail.abstract: Perceived and geographical distance among relevant actors can hinder prosocial behaviour and challenge environmental governance. Perspective-taking (the act of considering another’s perspective and circumstances) can help overcome these challenges, but its impact is far from straightforward and depends on the mechanisms it activates. We further conceptualise and explore these, focusing on the potential impacts of perspective-taking on values, perceptions and affect. Our exploratory analysis is based on an extended literature review and (qualitative and quantitative) data from an economic experiment involving 205 farmers in the lower section of an Andean watershed. In the experiment, farmers decided on a donation that would support farmers upstream, who are relatively less well-off but have contributed to stable water provision downstream. Some participants were induced to engage in perspective-taking either through a video or a field visit before deciding on their donation. We elicited their reasons for (not) donating and systematically analysed these. We show that perspective-taking fosters values (namely, outgroup solidarity and other-regarding preferences), perceptions (of closeness), and affect (compassion) among otherwise distant actors. Yet prosocial behaviour is only strongly associated with other-regarding preferences. Values, so far underexplored, thus emerge as a key pathway linking perspective-taking with prosocial behaviour. However, a comparison across experimental conditions suggests that this impact of perspective-taking arguably depends on the information medium, which shapes participants’ assessments of both others’ relative needs and the possibilities for helping. This value-based pathway, along with the specific impact of perspective-taking procedures, invites future research.

title: Ecosystem Services and Land Prices: A Scale-Sensitive Hedonic Assessment
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Mendel University in Brno, Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Leuphana University of Lueneburg - Dept. of Sustainability Sciences

detail.title: Ecosystem Services and Land Prices: A Scale-Sensitive Hedonic Assessment
detail.abstract: Most hedonic assessments of ecosystem services (ES) assume that ecological functions translate uniformly into land prices, overlooking how valuation signals depend on the spatial scale at which services operate or become visible to buyers. This paper addresses this gap by proposing a scale-sensitive framework that evaluates how ES transfer value from ecosystems to land markets across two ecologically justified distance thresholds (100 m and 1,201 m). Using over 81,000 rural land transactions in Chile’s Northern Patagonia, a region subject to intense urban-to-rural pressure, combined with expert-based ES assessments, this study compares results across eight robustness specifications and classifies each ES into scale-dependent valuation trajectories to find positive, negative and null functional valuation ES groups. Findings reveal a systematic market bias: visually salient and privately appropriable services consistently show positive capitalisation, while regulatory, biodiversity-supporting, and collectively governed functions tend to display negative or null trajectories—often decaying or reversing as the scale increases. By integrating ecological aspects with spatial scale into hedonic analysis, these findings suggest that markets selectively capture only a subset of nature’s benefits, while ignoring or penalising others.

title: Human Dignity, Frontier AI, and the Limits of Experimentation

detail.title: Human Dignity, Frontier AI, and the Limits of Experimentation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no conflict of interest with any organisations
declarations.funderStatement: Marcus and Marinne Wallenberg Foundation

detail.abstract:
AI has been said to potentially pose an existential risk to humanity. While the human rights community focuses on the immediate harms to human rights, this article argues that frontier AI, namely highly capable AI models that can exhibit a general mastery of tasks across different domains, can raise a larger existential risk concern to human rights. Bearing in mind the experimental nature of frontier AI and the eventual aim of designing artificial general intelligence, this paper addresses the question of whether human dignity sets a hard limit as to what can be experimented upon individuals and society.

It examines lessons from biotechnology regulation and social media experimentation which challenged related conceptions of human dignity in order to unpack and answer the question. It finds that two key boundaries are being blurred. First, while prior technologies can be considered as a means to an end, frontier AI technologies can be left to pursue its own (misaligned) ends, thus blurring the means/ends boundary. Its non-deterministic nature also means that lessons from how human dignity drew a line around biotechnology regulation and social media experimentation can only be imperfectly applied to frontier AI. Secondly, while it is within the purview of companies to experiment for purposes of product improvement and to improve user experience, the lines between research and product are blurring to an extent that general purpose AI models seem to occupy an in-between category of research products. The seeming necessity of experimentation through deployment of increasingly capable models to test its real-life effects would rule out the precautionary approach of non-deployment based on respect for human dignity. Instead, the paper finds that respect for human dignity necessarily entails that procedural hard limits be set as safeguards for proceeding with the experimental nature of such technology and examines the different modalities – such as within international or multilateral governance, that are available.

detail.abstract: This article investigates the stock market reaction to the European Commission's Omnibus Package, released on February 26, 2025, which seeks to amend the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD). To explore whether investors interpret this proposal as a regulatory relief or as a signal of heightened policy uncertainty, we conduct an event study on 3,292 publicly listed European firms. The release did not generate the positive reaction expected by the Commission. The evidence points instead to a negative, though modest, reaction. This may reflect uncertainty about the announcement and its timing, close to the first reporting date, which left compliance costs sunk. The most negative reactions concentrate among firms most exposed to uncertainty and compliance investments, and among firms in countries that had already transposed the CSRD into national law. These findings underline the need for clear, coherent and credible rules regarding European sustainability regulatory framework.

detail.abstract: We provide the first large-sample evidence that decentralized voting is widespread within mutual fund families. Contrary to the view that families vote as unified blocs, we find that more than one-third of families exhibit evidence of decentralized voting, starting as early as 2006. We measure decentralization using voting disagreement within the family, which is low unconditionally due to the high volume of routine proposals, but rises substantially for controversial proposals, environmental and social issues, and when proxy advisors recommend voting "against." Decentralized voting is more prevalent in families with more active funds and greater stewardship resources, and funds within a family vote more similarly when they share management structures and characteristics. Decentralization has consequences for governance and fund investors. First, it weakens the monitoring effectiveness of institutional investors-a result we corroborate using Vanguard's 2019 adoption of decentralized voting as a quasi-natural experiment. Second, funds that deviate from their family's voting stance charge higher fees without delivering higher returns for clients. Yet, funds that deviate attract higher inflows.

title: The Risk of Risk: Algorithms and Immigration Detention

detail.abstract: In 2020, the United Kingdom (‘UK’) abandoned an algorithm that was used to stream immigration applicants. Applications were triaged using a ‘traffic light’ colour code system (i.e. red, green, amber) according to the category of risk. Advocacy groups, such as the Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants and FoxGlove, claimed the algorithm was discriminatory by design, and violated the UK Equality Act 2010, because some nationalities were categorised as ‘suspect’ based on higher rejection rates. Consequently, applicants from those countries received a higher risk score and a higher level of scrutiny. Previous visa rejections were fed back to the algorithm to inform future decisions, reinforcing bias and discrimination and causing a feedback loop. Algorithmic risk assessments continue to be used for visa processing and immigration detention worldwide, including in Australia. Notwithstanding  their potential to impact fundamental human rights, including liberty and humane treatment, risk assessment tools tend to become more punitive over time, creating harmful feedback loops and avoiding the oversight of courts. Risk-based regulation of emerging technologies that include private providers of government services accompanied by meaningful reform of the scope of judicial review will be essential to addressing the rise of potentially harmful technology in Australian immigration and border control.

detail.abstract: Public international law, including legal instruments such as trade agreements and forced labor import bans, increasingly delegates the monitoring and reporting of compliance to private actors in other countries. This mimics national whistleblowing schemes that delegate reporting responsibilities to private actors. However, little is known about whether private actors in other countries are aware of the rules they should monitor or their reporting opportunities. We also do not know whether those actors trust the legitimacy of the foreign governments to which they are expected to report. Without knowledge and trust, private actors may refrain from participating in public international law initiatives, depriving governments of valuable insights and data across borders. The United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) Facility-Specific Rapid Response Labor Mechanism (RRM) calls on workers in Mexico's trade sector to monitor the workplace and report violations of Mexico's new labor law to the U.S. government. Using it as a case study, this Article describes the results of an empirical project in the Mexican auto sector that sought to ascertain workers' views on their labor rights, and their understanding of and trust in the RRM's enforcement platform. The results reveal an acute disparity in awareness and trust among many of these workers, particularly those who had not participated in the RRM or received assistance from U.S. stakeholders. The Article argues that monitoring and reporting schemes that cross national boundaries must be reconceptualized to offer private actors opportunities to learn the rules they are expected to monitor and give them reason to trust foreign government enforcement.

detail.abstract: Fraud detection, with its rings and shared-attribute groups, is an obvious target for topological deep learning, yet we are aware of no higher-order fraud benchmark and no neutral test of whether lifting beats strong feature-only and pairwise baselines under one imbalance-aware protocol. This paper is that benchmark and that test: seven real transaction, review, and financial graphs lifted to candidate-cell hypergraphs, plus a generator D(mu) in which the value of structure is known by construction. The answer separates datasets into three regimes. In the feature-dominated regime node features already carry the signal: a feature-only model matches or beats the best pairwise and higher-order models, naive message passing amplifies camouflage, and learnable liftings give no significant gain, whether their cells are selected, generated, or regularized. In the column-foldable regime a temporal signal is strongly predictive but folds into node-level feature columns, so a lifting gains nothing over that cheaper encoding; signal being present is not sufficient for lifting to pay. Only the structure-rich regime rewards lifting. There the structure carries minority signal that no node-level encoding reaches, and a label-free temporal-coherence lifting beats the temporal columns by +1.9 AP points on the Elliptic Bitcoin graph (paired t(7) of about 12.7), a margin that survives feature augmentation on Elliptic++. One decisive test, applied uniformly to six temporal crossovers over five networks, is what locates that positive rather than selecting it. The generator, the lifting model, and the evaluation harness will be released with a future version.

detail.title: The Rent-capture Gap: Two Centuries of Commodity Cycles and Institutional Readiness in Chilean Economic Development

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest and received no specific funding for this work. Generative AI assistance was used in drafting this manuscript; see the AI-Use Declaration included in the paper for details.

detail.abstract: This working paper argues that natural-resource abundance is neither a necessary nor a sufficient condition for sustained economic development, and that the gap between resource endowment and institutional readiness-the fiscal, industrial, and legal-regulatory capacity to capture, reinvest, and stabilize resource rents-is a more reliable predictor of which resource-dependent economies convert a commodity boom into durable prosperity. The argument is developed through a single national case examined across four distinct commodity cycles: Chile's nineteenth-century silver and wheat exports, the nitrate boom and collapse of 1879-1930, the state-led copper economy from the 1939 founding of CORFO through the 1971 nationalization, and the still-unresolved lithium boom of the 2020s. Each cycle exhibits a different configuration of fiscal, industrial, and legal readiness, and the paper argues that the resulting variation in outcomes-boom-bust volatility under nitrate, contested state capture under copper, an open question under lithium-tracks institutional readiness more closely than the value or scarcity of the underlying resource. For the period since 1960, where annual national-accounts data of adequate quality exist, the paper also reports a targeted econometric check-Chow structural-break tests and a Newey-West mean-shift regression on real Chilean GDP per capita-of whether the institutional ruptures the historical narrative identifies (1973, 1982, 1990, 2019) correspond to detectable breaks in the country's growth trajectory; the results partially, but not uniformly, support the narrative, and are reported with the corresponding methodological caveats rather than as clean causal evidence. The paper connects this historical and empirical pattern explicitly to the author's related work on institutional readiness for AIenabled macroprudential policy and capital-flow governance in emerging economies. The pre-1960 portion of the argument remains conceptual and illustrative rather than causal, in the absence of comparable annual data for those earlier cycles.

title: Traditionally Suspect: Common Occupations and the Right to Earn a Living

detail.title: Traditionally Suspect: Common Occupations and the Right to Earn a Living

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known personal or financial relationships that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract:
Yvette Butler, Traditionally Suspect: Common Occupations and the Right to Earn a Living, 84:2 Wash & Lee L. Rev __ (forthcoming 2027)

This Article is the first to fill a major gap in the literature on the scope of the right to earn a living. Courts have defined the right to earn a living as the right of an individual to earn their livelihood through any lawful, honest, and common calling, business, profession, or vocation they may choose, as long as the individual is not restricted by generally applicable and reasonable laws, such as criminal laws or occupational licensing requirements. Scholars have argued that economic liberties, such as the right to earn a living and occupational freedom, should be recognized as fundamental rights. As such, laws that overburden economic liberties, such as the right to earn a living, should be subject to meaningful judicial scrutiny. This article does not take issue with that claim.

Instead, this article argues that whether the right to earn is fundamental is not as relevant as (1) addressing the many threshold questions that the doctrine requires, especially the meaning of a “common occupation” and (2) articulating a just version of economic liberty that accounts for the relevant histories and experiences of multiple stakeholders, including marginalized groups. Thus, I argue that the right to earn a living should be interpreted in a way that accounts for multiple stakeholders, historical injustices, and present day realities. 

In doing so, I show that the threshold “common occupation” inquiry essentially operates as a history and tradition test subject to the very same critiques as the one created by the Roberts Court. Under this test, an occupation is common only if it is not “traditionally suspect.” This may be demonstrated where there are a “host of cases” protecting the claimed interest. This test rewards litigants whose work the law has already embraced. It leaves the occupations that were historically condemned without an on-ramp to recognition. That structure risks building epistemic injustices into the threshold itself because it asks whether an activity was once condemned while not also asking why, and by whom.

detail.abstract: How does household heterogeneity in labor income sources shape the distributional effects of carbon taxation in emerging economies (EMEs)? Using household-level data for Mexico and Brazil, we document the distribution of households by their main labor-income source, including the prevalence of self-employed-only and hybrid (salaried and self-employed) households, and estimate household-level transitions between household categories. We build a tractable macro model with salaried firms, self-employment, endogenous polluting-green energy production, and heterogeneous households whose transitions between categories are endogenous. Calibrating the model to Mexico, we study a carbon tax under two revenue-recycling schemes: lump-sum transfers to households and subsidies to green-technology adoption. The tax raises energy prices, lowers aggregate consumption and output, and shifts employment from salaried to self-employed firms. Employer households bear the largest consumption and welfare losses, followed by salaried-only households; hybrid households fare similarly to salaried-only households, while self-employed-only households are least affected. A green-subsidy scheme delivers a more uniform response across household categories than a lump-sum-transfer scheme, while also limiting the tax's adverse macroeconomic effects. Abstracting from endogenous household transitions significantly changes the quantitative distributional impact of the tax, especially among self-employed-only and hybrid households. Our results underscore the importance of endogenous household transitions for quantifying the distributional effects of carbon taxation in EMEs.

detail.abstract: This article introduces contentiousR — an R package that provides various tools and datasets for contentious politics and civil conflict research. It provides a flexible workflow for creating state panels and enriching them with socioeconomic, political, and conflict indicators — using either Correlates of War (COW) or Gleditsch-Ward (GW) country coding schemes. detail.abstract: This paper examines whether exchange-rate regimes—and, more specifically, the identity of the anchor currency—shape the transmission of pure monetary policy shocks from the European Central Bank and the Federal Reserve across African economies. We build a monthly panel covering 54 countries, with an estimation sample of up to 39 countries grouped into 27 monetary-policy decision units over 2001m1–2025m10. Monetary policy shocks are constructed symmetrically from high-frequency event-study databases and purged of central-bank information effects. Panel local projections trace responses of the bilateral U.S. dollar exchange rate, inflation, and policy rates across euro pegs, rand pegs, soft pegs, and managed or floating regimes. Confirmatory inference focuses on eight soft-peg-minus-euro-peg exchange-rate contrasts, with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors and Holm adjustment. Heterogeneity is localized rather than pervasive. Following a contractionary European Central Bank shock, the soft-minus-euro contrast reaches 1.015 percentage points at six months; following a Federal Reserve shock, the contrast is −0.687 percentage point on impact. Both survive Holm adjustment, whereas the remaining six confirmatory contrasts do not. Inflation differences are not robustly distinguishable; policy-rate heterogeneity is confined to exploratory managed-or-floating contrasts, with only the Fed contrast at six months surviving the Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment at 10%, and no policy-rate comparison is confirmatory. The results show that exchange-rate regimes, and especially anchor-currency identity, affect the margin through which foreign monetary shocks appear without implying full insulation or monetary autonomy under greater exchange-rate flexibility.

detail.abstract: Calls to tax top incomes more heavily leave open whether "more" means a higher average tax rate (ATR) or a larger share of total income-tax revenue (TAXSHARE), and which top group is meant. In a preregistered survey experiment in Germany (N = 3,129), each respondent evaluates either the top 10% or the top 1% of income earners, described by its percentile label alone, by its income threshold and income share alone, or by both. Each respondent states a fair ATR and a fair TAXSHARE separately. Given the top group's actual income and holding total income-tax revenue at its current level, ATR and TAXSHARE are two expressions of the same policy. Respondents then see each judgment translated into the other and must state one consistent pair. Before the translation, respondents state similar fair ATRs and fair TAXSHAREs for both top groups, although a given ATR implies a TAXSHARE about three times larger for the top 10%. On average, the fair ATR therefore lies 17.8 percentage points above the ATR implied by the fair TAXSHARE for the top 10% and 16.7 percentage points below it for the top 1%. Once constrained, respondents revise the fair ATR toward the ATR implied by the pre-translation fair TAXSHARE, widening the difference in fair ATRs between the top groups from 1.9 to 18.0 percentage points. Top 1% respondents keep more of the fair ATR they initially stated than top 10% respondents do. How the top group is described matters as well: holding the income figures fixed, the label raises the fair ATR by 4.3 percentage points for the top 10% and 6.5 percentage points for the top 1% and shifts whom respondents picture from professionals and managers toward generic references to "the rich". Stated preferences for taxing top incomes thus depend on whether an ATR or a TAXSHARE is asked for, which top group is evaluated, and how it is described.

detail.abstract: Electricity bills are rising faster than inflation, making a household's electricity contract an increasingly consequential decision. Deregulated retail markets generally offer a choice between fixed rate contracts (FixRCs) and variable rate contracts (VarRCs), yet their financial impact is obscured by non-linear pricing, price volatility and consumers' self-selection based on their latent characteristics. To improve transparency of rates, utilities post representative rates corresponding to a few consumption levels in Electricity Facts Labels (EFLs). Methodology/results: In collaboration with one of the largest U.S. utilities, we estimate the causal effect of contract choice on realized rates for more than 77,000 households recorded over a full year, linking each household's rate to its contract, tenure, monthly and hourly consumption, and zip-level demographics. We find that rates tend to increase with consumption variability. We address self-selection by instrumenting contract choice with lagged Google search intensity for the state's electricity-shopping platform in a Two-Stage Least Squares and a Double Machine Learning (DML) frameworks controlling for the full consumption profile. FixRCs reduce rates by approximately 4¢/kWh, roughly one fifth of the average rate; the largest savings accrue to high-income households whose consumption concentrates in winter months, the signature of electric heating. Managerial implications: The FixRC discount (commitment concession) is substantial on average. Utilities can adjust the commitment concession to achieve a specific mix of FixRC and VarRC consumers. Moreover, they can reveal this concession to attract FixRC consumers, especially to those using electric heating. We make two concrete process recommendations to utilities i) enhanced EFLs with quotes based on consumption level and variability, and ii) break-even service length informing consumers about the contract length beyond which FixRCs become cheaper than VarRCs. Enhanced EFLs and break-even service length increase transparency and in turn can help lower-income households raise their savings closer to those of higher-income households, making the market fairer.

title: Harvesting as a Stochastic Dividend: The After-Tax Efficient Frontier Revisited

detail.title: Harvesting as a Stochastic Dividend: The After-Tax Efficient Frontier Revisited
