detail.abstract: Every few years the technology industry tells itself a story strong enough to move hundreds of billions of dollars of capital spending. This paper reads thirty years of the industry's own annual reports to see what those stories did, and how far today's story has got against the last one at the same age. Every company in the S&P 500 between 1996 and 2026 that belongs to the technology chain is placed in one of six groups by what it sold, from the designers of chips to the utilities that power the data centres, and for each group and year the paper adds up what its members reported: capital spending, revenue, operating cash flow, operating income and the market value printed on the cover of the annual report, every figure taken as first filed. Twenty-seven stories are dated to the day and pointed at the groups they were about, beginning with the Telecommunications Act of 1996 and ending with the software sell-off of February 2026, and a rule written down before any number was computed records the year each group's prices, spending and revenue moved. The network build-out that began in 1996 sets the comparison. By its third year the builders were putting 24 cents of every sales dollar back into the network, they were spending nine tenths of the cash their operations produced and crossed that line the year after, and the market had taken back nearly a third of the share of the industry's value it gave the builders and their suppliers when the story arrived. If the AI build-out that began in 2022 is on the same path, those three signs should show now, three years in. One of the three shows. The AI spenders put 22 cents of each sales dollar into equipment and buildings, against the builders' 24 at the same age, a year before that build-out peaked. The other two do not. The spenders are paying out of their own operating cash at six tenths of what it produces, where the builders were at nine tenths and over the line the next year. And the market has left the second pair's share of the industry's value where it was when the story arrived, 72 percent then and 72 now, where the first pair's fell from 71 to 50. The suppliers differ in kind rather than in degree. The group registered as this story's suppliers is larger than the equipment makers ever were, 27 percent of the industry's revenue against their peak of 15, and it keeps 29 cents of operating profit on the dollar where the equipment makers' best year was 13. Most of that group's revenue is devices rather than compute: a narrower group of the four companies that sell the compute, added after the registration and marked wherever it appears, is 8 percent of revenue at 48 cents on the dollar. The one group building with outside money is the power companies, as it has been every year since 2012, and its spending against its own cash peaked in 2022 and has fallen since. The record, with every company, story, hand-read figure and rule, is published as data for the studies that will test what it suggests.

detail.abstract: This research contributes to the literature addressing the phenomenon of earnings management in global markets. The research setting is Egypt, and due to data limitations in this setting, this research examines earnings management based on firm operating performance. In particular, the question of whether ineffectively performing firms engage more in earnings management strategies compared to their effectively performing counterparts is investigated. Sign change ratio analysis, correlation analysis, and regression analysis were employed to determine the extent to which the strength of the relationship between earnings and cash flows differs between ineffectively and effectively performing firms. The results show that considered against effectively performing firms, ineffectively performing firms in the emerging market of Egypt are associated with a greater level of earnings management. Overall, this finding suggests that for listed Egyptian firms, company operating performance is a significant incentive of earnings management. Furthermore, this finding encourages the argument in favour of Egyptian corporate governance reform.

detail.abstract: In 2020, the Brazilian school feeding program introduced a policy change that limited the use of federal funds for processed and ultra-processed foods (P&UPF) to a maximum of 20% of the resources transferred to states and municipalities for food purchases in public schools. This study evaluates the policy change’s short-term effects using municipal-level school food procurement data from before (2015–2019) and after (2021–2022) implementation, using a difference-in-differences approach. We compared municipalities that exceeded the 20% threshold in the baseline period (2015; treated municipalities) with those that already complied (control municipalities). We found that treated municipalities reduced the share of funds allocated to P&UPF by 4.21 percentage points relative to control municipalities; of this, the reduction in ultra-processed foods alone was 3.28 percentage points. Decomposing purchases by food group, we found that the restrictions reduced procurement of sweetened beverages, P&UPF breads, cookies, and other sweets, while procurement of fresh or minimally processed alternatives, particularly meats and eggs, increased. Our findings show that healthy public procurement policies are feasible and effective, as shown by immediate reductions in P&UPF purchases within one of the world’s largest national school feeding programs. Brazil’s experience may serve as a model for designing and implementing large-scale healthy food procurement regulations elsewhere.

detail.abstract: This paper examines what happens when rapid data-centre growth encounters slower-moving electricity infrastructure, using Virginia, Ireland and the Singapore-Johor region as deliberately contrasting cases. The central analytical distinction is between physical infrastructure expenditure, the accounting or legal payer, contractual or regulated cost allocation, and ultimate economic incidence. A second distinction separates requested, forecast, contracted, connected and realised load. The study combines regulator orders, utility and system-operator planning documents, official electricity statistics, government capacityallocation policies, company and investment-agency disclosures, and a focused literature on data-centre energy use and utility rate design. Three findings stand out. First, electricity-system constraints are material in high-growth locations, but the relevant constraint and the credibility of the demand signal are jurisdiction-specific. Second, institutional responses differ sharply: Virginia uses retail tariff commitments while PJM and FERC address separate wholesale and transmission layers; Ireland conditions new connections on complementary supply and locational constraints; Singapore allocates capacity within a managed resource envelope while Johor combines expansion incentives with its own power, water and sustainability conditions. Third, public evidence is much stronger on physical constraints and formal risk allocation than on ultimate incidence. The paper therefore does not estimate a household 'cost of AI' or infer that Singapore's constraints caused Johor's expansion. Instead, it argues that rapid digitalinfrastructure growth creates planning uncertainty and conversion risk between early-stage load signals and realised demand, while tariffs and connection rules allocate some of the resulting underutilisation and stranded-asset risk.

detail.abstract: We show that strengthening creditor rights in the sale and repurchase (repo) market can exacerbate financial instability, particularly under short debt maturities and low collateral volatility. We build a model of financial intermediaries that raise financing by pledging collateral in the repo market. In the short term, increasing collateral pledgeability makes repo creditors safer and reduces debt rollover risk; however, it also expands long-term debt capacity and leverage, ultimately heightening run risk. This instability is a distinct feature of environments with long-term liabilities and lowvolatility assets, where market discipline fails to constrain post-policy leverage. We test our model's predictions by exploiting the 2005 BAPCPA bankruptcy reform, which expanded creditor protections via repo safe harbors. Using hand-collected data on dealer repo collateral, we confirm that while the law enhanced collateral pledgeability, it fueled short-term leverage and precipitated sharper de-leveraging during the downturn.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none

detail.abstract: A Credit Default Swap (CDS) is conceptually simple: the protection buyer pays a premium and receives compensation if the reference entity suffers a defined credit event. Accurate pricing, however, depends on a tightly specified combination of contract dates, accrual conventions, discounting, survival probabilities and credit-curve calibration. This article develops the pricing framework used by the ISDA CDS Standard Model, starting with the standardised contract and its quotation conventions and then building the premium and protection legs from the underlying cash-flow definitions. The treatment is deliberately code-grounded. One of the practical difficulties in implementing CDS pricing independently is that high-level descriptions of the model are considerably easier to find than the precise implementation instructions needed to reproduce it. Small details of date adjustment, survival observation, accrual treatment and value-date handling can matter to the last basis point, yet these details are often distributed across source code, technical notes and market conventions rather than presented as one coherent implementation guide. This article is intended to help fill that gap. It brings the mathematical description and the reference implementation together in one place, so that a practitioner can move from the convention to the equation and from the equation to the corresponding piece of code without having to reconstruct the model from scattered sources. The article follows the path from market dates and the risky timeline through the closed-form valuation of the protection leg and accrual-on-default, the risky annuity and par spread, and finally the calibration procedures used for both internal valuation and the ISDA Standard Model Converter. The aim is practical as well as explanatory: to provide a useful implementation companion for anyone building, validating or reconciling an independent CDS pricer. A central distinction is maintained throughout. A firm's internal valuation system normally requires a multi-pillar credit curve for marking positions and measuring curve risk. The ISDA Converter, by contrast, uses a single-pillar flat hazard rate to convert the market quote for one standard CDS into the exact upfront amount used for execution and settlement. These are different calibration purposes built on the same pricing engine. The objective is not merely to reproduce a CDS price, but to show why each convention exists, where it enters the mathematics, and which implementation details are essential if an independent pricer is to reconcile with the ISDA reference model.

detail.abstract: A central design goal of settlement systems is that security should not degrade when transaction values are high. Using Ethereum's Proof-of-Work era, we show that Proof-of-Work can fail this test: higher transaction fees-the reward for a successful attack-cause miners to deviate from honest behavior and fork the chain, undermining settlement finality when it is most needed. We exploit a unique feature of Ethereum's Proof-of-Work era that records, for each fork, both the winning block and its displaced competitor's timestamp. We jointly instrument hourly mean log fees, hashrate, and block size using a crypto shock indicator constructed from Ethereum hacks, market crises, and regulatory events, together with one-hour lags of hashrate and block size. Higher fees significantly increase canonical blocks arriving exactly one second later than the siblings they displace, which is consistent with deviation from honest behavior. The converse event showing honest behavior-a canonical block arriving before its siblings-is not driven by high fees. This contrast indicates that fees affect equilibrium behavior and settlement finality in Proof-of-Work blockchains.

detail.abstract: The instrument-free endogeneity correction of Park and Gupta (2012) identifies causal effects from distributional dissimilarity rather than from an exclusion restriction. We set out its five identifying assumptions and what Gaussian regressor-error dependence substantively requires, review the evidence on performance, and survey the generalisations to correlated regressors, unknown margins, and panel, spatial, Bayesian, non-continuous and frontier settings. Nearly every assumption has been relaxed except the dependence structure, which carries the identification and admits no direct test. We close with the open questions, arguing that the requirements of the method are requirements on the economic mechanism generating the data.

detail.abstract: Only relative prices matter. New York's taxi market tests the proposition on records that count every cab. A 17 percent uniform fare rise in 2012 raised every hour's return and the driver's outside option alike. Pay rose a third. Hours did not move. A 2022 rush-hour surcharge raised four hours' return relative to the rest and put ten points more fleet into them. The leading structural model reports an elasticity of 1.8 to a uniform rise. detail.abstract: A criminal conviction restricts occupational access through several thousand provisions spread across federal law, state codes, administrative rules, and licensing board practice. None of it is indexed to an occupational classification system. All of it is written in offense class language that does not match how people describe their own records. Much of it expires, and much of the rest can be waived. A job seeker cannot determine which paths are closed, which are conditionally open, and which are unrestricted. Neither can the workforce professionals support them. Practice therefore defaults to one of two failures: blanket avoidance of regulated sectors, or silence until a background check ends a placement after the training has been paid for. This paper describes a system that routes justice impacted individuals to viable careers in seconds rather than weeks and improves as outcomes return. It rests on three components. An eligibility substrate encodes 37 federal and Michigan provisions with statutory authority, offense class key, NAICS and SOC index, temporal horizon, relief path, and per provision verification confidence. A routing layer composes a substrate with occupational transferability, regional labor demand, and a destination tier constraint, narrowing roughly 2,000 verified training programs to a scored shortlist before any generative step runs. A feedback layer closes the loop through declared intent, engagement, and, where available, placement outcome. Three findings are reported. The regulated universe is small: 39 four-digit NAICS industries appear anywhere in the corpus, so most of the economy restricts nothing and reaching it requires no analysis. Foreclosure is bounded even at the extreme; a felony level-controlled substance record leaves 7 of those 39 industries fully open and 16 more open subject to a stated requirement. And offense classification dominates offense category, because residual clauses attach to any felony without regard to conduct. That last finding inverts the emphasis of conventional reentry counseling, which organizes around offense type. We also identify an unwritten barrier that a statute only corpus cannot see. Employers decline candidates on the ground that insurance will not cover them, citing nothing, appealable to no one, and frequently without having read the policy. The mechanism is insurance for employers that hire felons, and the remedy already 2 exists in the Federal Bonding Program, which is built for exactly the population commercial underwriters decline. We argue this makes bonding a routing output rather than a resource listing, and we flag insurance underwriting practice as the most consequential omission in the present dataset. Of the 37 provisions enclosed, 8 are both permanent and without any waiver, consent, or expiry. The other 29 carry a named process or a date. We catalogue those as affirmative pathways and treat surfacing them, rather than cataloguing restrictions, as the operative contribution. The system is governed by three constraints: asymmetric error cost, which requires it to fail open; confidence gating, which stops unverified provisions from driving exclusion; and zero retention screening, under which a sensitive attribute conditions inference and has never persisted.

detail.abstract: In temporal voting, a fixed set of voters makes a collective decision in each of several rounds, and proportionality requires that groups with shared interests be represented across these decisions. Full justified representation (FJR) is among the strongest proportionality axioms known to be satisfiable in this setting, since it allows different members of a group to be satisfied by different selected candidates. However, whether an FJR outcome can be computed in polynomial time has remained open. We resolve this question by introducing temporal FJR+, a strengthening of both FJR and extended justified representation+ (EJR+) that can be computed and verified in polynomial time. The axiom measures a group's agreement in each round by the largest number of its members who approve a common candidate, and requires some member to attain the integer part of the group's proportional share of its best attainable average satisfaction, with a shortfall of at most one unit when this share is an integer. We show that verification reduces to counting approvals among the voters below each satisfaction threshold. For computation, we observe that local search for Proportional Approval Voting (PAV) can stop at an outcome violating FJR. Somewhat counterintuitively, the remedy is to subtract a small multiple of the minimum voter satisfaction from the PAV score: every FJR+ violation then admits a single-round change whose improvement guarantees polynomial running time. We further show that temporal FJR+ is strictly stronger than FJR and EJR+ combined, and coincides with lower quota on party-list preferences. Finally, temporal FJR+ and multiwinner FJR+ are incomparable in general, but coincide when approvals are static and each candidate-round pair is treated as a separate candidate.

detail.abstract: This article examines how economists at Data Resources, Inc. (DRI) incorporated the financial determinants of the business cycle into their analysis of the U.S. economy. DRI was one of the largest private companies providing forecasts based on a large-scale macroeconometric model. The case of DRI illustrates how forecasts were constructed and why they did not rely exclusively on the mechanical use of the model. Instead, DRI economists relied on other tools to determine the state of the economy. They identified a “flow-of-funds” cycle characterized by transformations in balance sheets through historical analysis. They then developed monitors and barometers to assess which stage of this cycle the U.S. economy was in, draw implications for the business cycle, and modify the DRI model of the U.S. economy. This reliance on “judgment” external to the model in the practice of forecasting created a growing gap between forecasting practice and discussions of economic theory.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has brought about considerable progress in scientific, industrial, and social applications, but at the same time its growing need for computing power has led to greater worries regarding energy use and environmental sustainability. The present study looks at the issue of enhancing the energy efficiency of AI by systematically looking at various methods in the areas of algorithmic optimization, model compression, hardware and software co-design, cloud computing, AI-enabled Internet of Things (AIoT), data-center optimization, and carbon-aware deployment. It reviews the available literature, compares the energy-efficiency techniques and results that have been reported, and examines how different technical and deployment factors affect the sustainable performance of AI. On the basis of this review, the study proposes a conceptual framework for the sustainable deployment of AI which incorporates efficiency considerations throughout the entire AI lifecycle rather than considering energy consumption as a problem that only applies at the model level. The results show that energy efficiency is not solely a function of the model's architecture; instead it results from the interactions between the algorithms, the characteristics of the data, the hardware, the software, the workload patterns, the deployment environments, and the sources and times at which energy is used. The analysis also makes a distinction between "green-in AI", which is concerned with reducing the environmental impact of developing and running AI systems, and "green-by AI", which involves using AI to improve sustainability in other fields. The main conclusion is that sustainable AI can only be achieved through coordinated optimization in the areas of computing, infrastructure, operations, and energy.

detail.abstract: Synthetic-control studies interpret the donor weights: a region is called the principal comparator, or two countries are said to supply most of the comparison. We propose a report for such statements. For any claim linear in the weights-a lead, a majority, a margin, or a group share-we compute the smallest deterioration in pretreatment fit under which some admissible weight vector overturns it, and the overturning weights. Deterioration is measured in the RMSPE-ratio units of Ferguson and Ross (2021) on both the outcome and the predictor-loss scale; a three-donor example shows that effectsensitivity curves cannot recover these thresholds. In the Basque study, Catalonia's majority survives a 24% predictor-loss deterioration under the published criterion, yet an outcome-only criterion assigns Catalonia zero weight and needs only 0.64% extra GDP RMSPE to make it lead: the claim is criterion-dependent. In the UK military-spending study, Canada's lead over the USA is overturned by a predictor-loss deterioration below 0.11% under every criterion examined, whereas their joint majority survives at least 19% under every competitively fitting criterion once outcome fit is held within 10% of the reference. Thresholds also vary across nearly equally fitting predictor-weight matrices, so the criterion must be reported with the claim.

detail.abstract: This article formulates the Theory of Dynamic Adaptive Warfare (TDAW) as a post-classical framework for analyzing contemporary conflict. The problem is not that classical strategic theory has become obsolete, but that no single classical vocabulary adequately captures conflicts in which military force, cyber operations, economic coercion, information manipulation, space systems, private actors, and legal constraints interact at the same time. TDAW therefore treats war and strategic coercion as dynamic systems in which force, decision, and normativity are mutually constitutive rather than analytically isolated. The article makes three contributions. First, it develops the force-decision-norm triad as a parsimonious analytical core that preserves Clausewitzian politics while incorporating strategic interaction and legal constraint. Second, it treats international law as an endogenous variable in strategic calculation: law changes costs, legitimacy, coalition behavior, operational options, and escalation pathways before conduct occurs, not merely after the fact. Third, it conceptualizes domain migration as an adaptive mechanism through which actors substitute military, cyber, informational, economic, legal, and orbital instruments when resistance or cost rises in one domain. The framework is qualitative and theorybuilding; it does not claim deterministic prediction or collapse all hostile competition into war. Its purpose is to organize causal reasoning, identify cross-domain substitution, and generate propositions that can be tested in historical and contemporary cases.

detail.abstract: What should a macroeconomically relevant climate index contain? The composition is inherently ambiguous, and aggregation choices affect structural inference. We introduce the Assemblage VAR, which jointly estimates nonnegative aggregation weights and VAR parameters by maximizing the system likelihood-gain criterion, effectively outsourcing aggregation to observed macroeconomic dynamics. Two variants operate in component-space and rank-space, reweighting named subcomponents or emphasizing regions of the cross-sectional distribution. Applied to disaggregated U.S. climate data from the Actuaries Climate Index and NOAA, VARs using the assembled climate measures yield contractionary impulse responses that are substantially larger than those estimated using fixed-weight benchmarks. Weights emphasize high-wind variables and distributional tails over slow-moving components such as sea level.

detail.abstract: Alice and Bob play a symmetric zero-sum coin-flipping game. Conditional on any fixed score for Bob, Alice’s expected payoff from playing is $+1/2$; conditional on any fixed score for Alice, it is $-1/2$.   Each of these conditional gambles has finite support, so the comparisons require only ordinary von Neumann–Morgenstern expected utility theory. Nevertheless, applying a natural countable dominance principle to the two different partitions yields opposite recommendations about whether Alice should play ---  and no form of the principle, strict, weak, or indifference, is consistent with the remaining hypotheses. The unconditional expectation does not exist, and although the game is symmetric and zero-sum, repeated play does not restore the usual expected-value justification for indifference; in fact , the Law of Large Numbers fails so thoroughly that repeated play leaves the distribution of Alice's average winnings essentially unchanged: the average of five million plays is distributed like the average of five. A symmetry principle, by contrast, is consistent, and commands indifference between playing and abstaining. Beyond that, any finite valuation of playing is consistent with the remaining hypotheses, so the surviving theory neither compels nor forbids any attitude toward the game: Alice may do as she prefers. We use the example to explore and illustrate the limits of extending familiar dominance and expected-utility reasoning to unbounded gambles.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how consumers allocate demand across differentiated services in congested markets. I use temporary, withinday attraction closures at Walt Disney World's Magic Kingdom to identify how congestion shifts when one option becomes unavailable. Displaced demand moves disproportionately toward services that were already heavily demanded, and this concentration is stronger when the market is crowded. At the same time, conditional on persistent popularity, unusually high current waits deter additional inflows. The results suggest that in congested markets, consumers favor services with greater revealed appeal, even when doing so entails higher waiting costs.

detail.abstract: This chapter argues that the desertion of aging and marginally producing fossil fuel infrastructural assets is an increasingly visible and costly issue for the province of Alberta. Like many other hydrocarbon-rich geographies, Alberta's landscape is dotted with wells, processing facilities, pipelines, platforms, manifolds and more which are critical to the circulation of fossil oil and gas. But all of this infrastructure has a costly end-of-life price tag stemming from the decommissioning, remediation, and reclamation of it and the land where it operated. Here, I build on the existing literature critiquing the environmental governance of the province's conventional oil and gas fields. I show how fossil and financial firms leverage this poor governance model as a corporate strategy of profit preservation through shifting end-of-life care onto quasi-regulatory institutions. I showcase both the worst case of fossil desertion in the industry to date-Lexin Resources-along with community-led resistance to this dangerous phenomenon.

detail.abstract: The 2002 European Insolvency Regulation (EIR) unexpectedly reassigned the insolvency jurisdiction of fully-owned foreign subsidiaries in the European Union from their own to their parents' host countries, exposing firms in the same environment to different creditor rights regimes. Using triple-difference designs, we provide causal evidence that shifts toward stronger (weaker) creditor rights regimes raise (lower) debt-taking. Notably, most prominent creditor protection dimensions matter for borrowing but often asymmetrically. Further tests suggest that the subsidiaries change their debt levels to adjust their financing mixes but not their real policies, and that the changes survive granular industry-location-time fixed effects, supporting a supply-side effect. Moreover, UK-subsample tests reveal that the changes come from bank but not group or leasing debt and are conditioned by bank fundamentals, supporting a bank-induced effect. Our final tests demonstrate that our results do not arise through creditor rights proxying for enforcement, cultural, religious, and political factors.

title: Temporal Pathway-Regularized Dynamic Graph Learning for Ordinal Stroke Recovery Prediction from Intensive Care Time Series
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Temporal Pathway-Regularized Dynamic Graph Learning for Ordinal Stroke Recovery Prediction from Intensive Care Time Series
detail.abstract: Background: Stroke recovery is heterogeneous, and early identification of patients at risk of poor functional outcome remains challenging. Existing electronic health record models either ignore the acute-phase physiological trajectory or omit biological prior knowledge.Methods: We used 4,858 stroke admissions from MIMIC-IV. Of these, 2,875 had complete 64-step ICU time series covering 14 physiological and neurological channels and 218 static features. We mapped discharge disposition to a six-level ordinal outcome. A temporal pathway atlas from four public transcriptomic stroke cohorts was encoded as monotone-progression and bounded-drift constraints in a dynamic graph gated recurrent unit, DG-GRU+TPR. Models were evaluated under five-fold cross-validation in a stacking ensemble and transferred to eICU-CRD, MIMIC-III, and two independent cohorts with 90-day modified Rankin Scale outcomes.Results:  The stacked ensemble achieved a macro-AUC of 0.830. This exceeded the strongest baseline of 0.826, with a bootstrap 95% CI from +0.0005 to +0.0083. The pathway prior contributed interpretable structure rather than a predictive gain. Negative-control and leakage audits indicated that the results were free of label or temporal leakage. Discrimination was preserved on transfer to eICU-CRD, with macro-AUC 0.809 and mortality AUROC 0.962, and to MIMIC-III, with 0.814 and 0.920. Transfer to a 511-patient cohort with recorded 90-day modified Rankin Scale outcomes reached an AUROC of 0.635 against an internal estimate of 0.739. A 185-patient hospital cohort achieved 0.739 on admission-time transfer, with 0.738 after fine-tuning.Conclusion: The framework provides a transferable template for integrating biological priors with ICU temporal deep learning, positioning the pathway prior as an interpretability mechanism rather than a predictive increment.

title: An Evaluation of Tumor-Type and Cohort Effects in Pan-Cancer Survival Prediction
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, , State University of New York (SUNY) - Department of Systems Science and Industrial Engineering (SSIE) and

detail.title: An Evaluation of Tumor-Type and Cohort Effects in Pan-Cancer Survival Prediction
detail.abstract: Background Pan-cancer survival models trained on TCGA gene expression routinely report areas under the receiver-operating curve (AUC) of 0.80 to 0.85. We investigate the extent to which these apparently strong discrimination values reflect true within-cancer prognostic performance. Methods Using overall-survival labels derived from confirmed clinical endpoints, a leakage-aware pipeline and four model families evaluated out-of-sample, we reproduce the familiar result: logistic regression attains a pooled test AUC of 0.828 and a Cox elastic-net model a concordance index of 0.749. Results We then examine the factors contributing to this predictive performance. A clinical baseline built from routine chart variables reaches AUC 0.801, and tumor type alone reaches 0.779; adding the year of diagnosis, a purely administrative variable, contributes a further 0.014. Expression improves on the clinical chart by a significant but small margin of +0.027 AUC, whereas clinical variables provide no measurable incremental discrimination once expression is included, because the selected components already recover tumor type (95.6% accuracy), patient sex (AUC 0.981), and contributing institution (62.7% accuracy), consistent with a batch effect. Critically, when evaluated within tumor type rather than pooled, the expression AUC falls from 0.828 to 0.693. We further show that the censoring-based exclusion is not random: excluded patients differ from those retained by diagnosis year, stage, and site. We characterize where the transcriptome adds value within diagnosis, report a sparse biomarker panel of which four genes survive correction in held-out data, and show that a common attribution workflow is unstable across analyses. Conclusions The apparent accuracy of pan-cancer survival models is therefore substantially an artefact of tumor-type composition and cohort selection rather than within-cancer prognostic discrimination

detail.abstract: Geopolitical fragmentation, rising electricity demand, and climate risks are intensifying the challenge of reconciling energy security, efficiency, and decarbonization. This study asks whether policy tools based on domestic energy indicators miss a systematic global channel: how a country's productivity co-moves with the relative performance of countries sharing similar energy and carbon characteristics. Using a two-way country and year fixed-effects panel covering 129 to 207 countries over 2009-2023, we combine country-specific labor, capital, energy-use intensity, carbon intensity, and energy-import dependence with corresponding global relative-performance indicators. A global environment favoring energy- and carbon-intensive economies is significantly associated with lower productivity, whereas one favoring energy-importing economies is significantly associated with higher productivity. These relationships remain stable across country-specific controls, sample expansions, alternative rolling windows, additional covariates, exclusion of the COVID-19 shock years, and alternative clustering. We develop two policy applications: a peer-group adjustment factor for climate-risk and carbon-border assessments, and a diagnostic scorecard for identifying exposures across energy security, decarbonization, and competitiveness. Illustrative cases from Japan, China, and the 2022 European energy-price shock show how efficiency, restructuring, diversification, and price exposure can transmit these relationships. The results support treating energy security as a portfolio of domestic capabilities and global relative exposures rather than domestic supply alone.

detail.abstract: Why do countries converge on institutional form but diverge on outcomes? I argue that institutional form-function divergence can arise when external assessment creates stronger and more directly actionable incentives for scoreable formal compliance than for the decentralized implementation required to produce function. I exploit the pre-scheduled timing of FATF mutual evaluations to test this mechanism. Assessment sharply increases technical compliance but produces no improvement in AML functional performance. The divergence is largest among low-capacity countries, which generate the largest formal compliance gains from a lower baseline while showing no functional improvement. Greylisting accelerates formal remediation without improving functional performance during the monitoring period. Exit from greylisting is associated with significant Basel improvement, consistent with positive selection on implementation progress rather than mere completion of the formal action-plan checklist.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a continuous-time forecasting framework for realized volatility using the fractional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (fOU) process. To overcome the computational burden of exact likelihoods and to bridge continuous dynamics with discrete forecasting, we estimate the fOU by approximate Whittle maximum likelihood (AWML) with a modified Paxson spectral kernel and couple the estimates with a truncated causal best linear predictor (fOU-BLUP) for direct multi-step means. We also spell out the out-of-sample map from residual-scale forecasts to level-scale variance, so that MSE and Patton QLIKE can be read jointly while accounting for loss asymmetry and exponential transformation curvature. On a panel of liquid high-frequency equity assets used as a demanding empirical test bed, rolling causal horse races show that fOU-BLUP enters the 90% model confidence set against HAR, freed ARFIMA, and GARCH at the horizons we study, with the clearest MSE gains away from the most heavily mined mega-cap names. The results underscore the value of encoding spectral roughness in a discrete linear predictor for real-time volatility forecasting.

detail.abstract: Gross domestic product (GDP) measures how much an economy produces, not how well its households can live on, or withstand shocks to, what it produces. This paper proposes the revised Financial and Inclusive Development Index (FIDI 2.0), a composite scorecard on a 0-100 scale. Addressing structural design flaws identified in earlier composite formulations-specifically income double-counting and low variance in institutional freedom across OECD economies-the headline FIDI model adopts a clean, three-pillar household architecture: real disposable purchasing power after essential housing costs (40%), income equality (30%), and rescaled institutional freedom (30%). Gross output scale is deliberately kept outside the headline composite to allow clean, unconfounded comparisons with GDP per capita, while a four-pillar companion index (FIDI+Output) is preserved for alternative evaluation. Following OECD-JRC guidelines for composite indicators, we present empirical results across 37 OECD member states, introduce the Output Capture Ratio diagnostic metric, and provide a formal extension for metropolitan-level applications (FIDI-City).

detail.abstract: This paper studies how government demand affects the labor share of income. Winning a procurement contract lowers a firm's labor share. The decline is driven by higher revenue per worker with limited pass-through to wages, and these revenue productivity gains reflect rising firm-level markups rather than improvements in physical efficiency. The effects are strongest for firms winning contracts as the only bidder. Evidence from bids, award prices, and political connections points to limited competition in procurement as the driving force. Government demand thus shapes the division of income between firm owners and workers, with implications for inequality.

title: GlucoFLEX-SSM-CA: Compact Multihorizon Glucose Forecasting with Clinical-Context Residual Adaptation, Conformal Uncertainty, and Dysglycemia Risk Scoring in Type 1 Diabetes

detail.title: GlucoFLEX-SSM-CA: Compact Multihorizon Glucose Forecasting with Clinical-Context Residual Adaptation, Conformal Uncertainty, and Dysglycemia Risk Scoring in Type 1 Diabetes
detail.abstract: Background: Short-horizon glucose forecasting may support earlier recognition of impending dysglycemia, but performanceestimates are sensitive to preprocessing, data splitting, target construction, and the statistical unit used for inference. Methods:We developed GlucoFLEX-SSM-CA, a 14,220-parameter framework combining two learnable exponential state-space blocks, ahistory-only clinical residual adapter, horizon-specific split-conformal intervals, and forecast-derived glycemic-risk scores. The12-participant OhioT1DM benchmark was evaluated at 15-, 30-, and 60-min horizons. Official participant train/test files werepreserved; development windows were partitioned chronologically into training (n = 15,977), validation (n = 2,284), and calibration(n = 4,573), leaving 4,271 official-test forecast origins untouched. Comparators included persistence, ClinicalHGB, compactLSTM/GRU models, a patch-Transformer, and architectural ablations. Participants, not overlapping windows, were the inferentialunits. Results: GlucoFLEX-SSM-CA achieved pooled MAE of 7.39, 13.13, and 22.37 mg/dL and RMSE of 11.21, 18.78, and 31.10mg/dL at 15, 30, and 60 min, respectively. After three-horizon Holm correction, it outperformed persistence, LSTM, and GRUat all horizons; against ClinicalHGB and PatchTransformer, multiplicity-adjusted significance was confined to 15 min. Empiricalcoverage of nominal 90% intervals was 90.85%, 90.68%, and 89.82%. Hypoglycemia risk discrimination yielded AUROC 0.962 andAUPRC 0.623 at 3.39% prevalence; hyperglycemia yielded AUROC 0.958 and AUPRC 0.957. Range-stratified analysis revealedsubstantially larger 60-min errors at observed hypoglycemic and hyperglycemic values than in the 70–180 mg/dL range. Conclusion:GlucoFLEX-SSM-CA is a compact, reproducible, uncertainty-aware forecasting framework with promising within-benchmarkperformance. Its retrospective 12-participant evaluation does not establish clinical effectiveness; external and prospective validation,including alarm-burden and glycemic-extreme analyses, is required.

title: On the Origin of Algebraic Complexity in Games and Resource Allocation

detail.title: On the Origin of Algebraic Complexity in Games and Resource Allocation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author received no funding for this work and declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no funding for this work and declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract:
When the primitives of an economic model are rational numbers, its solution
need not be. We ask which solution concepts manufacture algebraic complexity
and which merely transmit it. Every standard transferable-utility concept --
the core, the Shapley and Banzhaf values, the nucleolus, the kernel, the
bargaining set, the tau-value -- is piecewise rational-affine in the
characteristic function and never leaves the field generated by the coalition
values. The complexity of a cooperative solution is therefore that of the
technology behind it: degree 2187 in a three-trader exchange economy, degree
one for assignment, bankruptcy, flow and linear production games. Nash
equilibrium, by contrast, creates complexity. The sharp boundary runs through
axiomatic bargaining. On polyhedral problems the utilitarian, egalitarian and
Kalai-Smorodinsky solutions are always rational, whereas the weighted Nash
solution -- equivalently, the equilibrium of a Leontief-Fisher market -- has
degree at most (m-1 choose l-1), where m counts distinct input proportions and
l binding resources, and all of its algebraic conjugates are real. With two
resources the allocation is rational at every rational capacity if and only if
m is at most 2; five agents and three resources already produce an allocation
whose Galois group is the symmetric group S6. The relative-price equation that
governs this arithmetic also orders who gains and who loses from capacity
expansion.

detail.abstract: We study how decentralized equity market infrastructure influences local business creation. Leveraging the staggered rollout of China's Regional Trading Centers (RTCs), we find that their launch significantly boosts start-up formation. These effects are concentrated among small firms and the firms supported by industrial policies. Mechanistically, RTC launches expand early-stage equity financing opportunities and stimulate regional interest in entrepreneurial activity. Together, our results suggest that localized and decentralized equity markets can foster business creation, particularly in environments with severe financing and information frictions.

detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) regulation moves from principles towards enforceable obligations, an important institutional question concerns who should supervise compliance and under what conditions. This study examines AI supervision as a problem of supervisory allocation, distinguishing the design of regulatory obligations from the institutional arrangements that monitor and enforce them. Using a qualitative, desk-based comparative case-study design, it analyses five established supervisory regimes: Swiss anti-money-laundering supervision, U.S. securities regulation, EU data protection, EU conformity assessment and market surveillance, and Indian securities-market self-regulation. The cases are compared across institutional dimensions including expertise, information access, independence, enforcement authority, adaptability, accountability, supervisory capacity, and exposure to capture or conflicts of interest. The analysis finds that no single supervisory architecture suits all functions. Delegation suits bounded and technically specialised tasks, while functions requiring coercive authority and heightened public accountability favour direct public involvement. Where technical expertise and statutory authority must operate together, hybrid arrangements become particularly relevant. Delegation also creates a secondary governance requirement: meta-supervision, whereby public authorities oversee delegated supervisors' competence, independence, and performance. Building on these findings, the study develops the AI Supervisory Allocation Framework (ASAF) to assess the institutional fit of direct, delegated, and hybrid arrangements for specific supervisory functions. The study advances a functional approach to AI supervision by focusing on how supervisory responsibilities can be allocated based on a function's requirements and the capabilities and constraints of the institutions involved.

detail.abstract: We study whether religious language in financial contracts influences investor behavior and bond pricing. Using a dataset of 814 Islamic bond (sukuk) prospectuses, we identify religious references and measure their effect on issuance yields. We find that religious statements-although legally non-binding-significantly reduce bond yields, and especially for riskier issuers. The effect is nonlinear: excessive referencing results in higher yields, suggesting a penalty for overuse. The impact is amplified when religious cues are likely to better capture investors' attention-e.g., positioned early, varied in form, or rarer words. Our results are robust to issuer fixed effects, endogeneity controls, and alternative religious signaling. These findings reveal a behavioral pricing channel through which religious cues function as non-financial signals in contract design.

detail.abstract: The Federal Trade Commission alleges that Amazon misled advertisers by describing its auctions as second-price auctions while using undisclosed reserve prices to raise charges above the amounts needed to win. This paper asks when experience can reveal profitable bid reductions and what evidence would establish successful adjustment. Absent competitive ties at value, own-bid payments at initial value bids signal a profitable small cut under a soft reserve. Yet successful adjustment can leave these payments frequent: further cuts lose valuable clicks as well as reduce payments. In a stationary campaign with two known candidate models, positive prior probabilities and arbitrarily small bid changes, exact payment records can identify the pricing rule in one observation. For the current-profit strategy studied here, win-loss records also support bounded cumulative expected profit loss at each fixed positive prior. With winloss feedback alone, however, the strategy's losses under soft reserves can grow as the initial probability assigned to them approaches zero. An assessment of adjustment can combine payment records with experimental changes in win rates and returns to identify remaining profitable bid changes. For bidders maximising gross value subject to a return target, the relevant test instead concerns the highest feasible gross value. The conclusions depend on the advertiser's objective, contemplated alternatives and available feedback.

detail.abstract: This article examines the evolution of equity capital in the U.S. banking industry over the past thirty-five years. Earnings are the major driver of increases in equity capital in the banking industry. While common stock issuance is frequent, amounts issued are generally small and do not contribute meaningfully to equity capital growth in most cases. Common stock dividends and repurchases are significant drains on equity capital. It is not uncommon for banks to pay out more than they earn, reflecting both capital planning motivations and negative shocks to earnings. It is also common for banks to both issue new common stock and make repurchases in the same year, with these offsetting actions related to employee stock-based compensation.

title: Estimating Yield Impacts of Treasury Demand and Supply Changes

detail.title: Estimating Yield Impacts of Treasury Demand and Supply Changes

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: International Finance Discussion Papers (Topic)

detail.abstract: We develop a rich demand system framework to quantify the yield effects of shifts in U.S. Treasury supply and demand. Our model captures time-varying holdings shares and estimates sectoral demand elasticities using instrumental variables. We find that the Treasury market has become increasingly price-sensitive over time, driven by the declining participation of less price-sensitive foreign official investors and the rising role of more price-sensitive hedge funds and other private investors. A $100 billion increase in Treasury supply currently raises five-year yields by approximately 3 basis points. We validate the model by showing that the shifts in investor base explain a significant portion of historical yield changes. Our framework provides a flexible tool for policy analysis and counterfactual scenarios, including the yield effects of foreign official investor sales and Federal Reserve balance sheet policies.

detail.abstract:
Background: Quality control is essential for ensuring consistent standards in fetal ultrasound examination, but conventional peer auditing is labour-intensive and difficult to implement across institutions. We aimed to develop a deep-learning-based quality-control system for second-trimester fetal ultrasound and evaluate its application in regional obstetric ultrasound quality management in Liaoning Province, China.

Methods: We developed a prenatal ultrasound quality-control system (PQCS) for automated standard-view classification and image-quality assessment. Model performance was evaluated against expert assessment. The system was subsequently applied in 30 hospitals for regional quality auditing, and a Plan–Do–Check–Act (PDCA) cycle incorporating automated assessment, feedback, supervision, and targeted training was implemented.

Findings: The algorithm achieved 95.38% accuracy for fetal ultrasound view classification and showed excellent agreement with experts for image-quality scoring (ICC=0.979, p<0.001). Significant differences in image-quality scores were observed among different types of hospitals. Following implementation of the PDCA-based quality-control programme, image quality significantly improved compared to control group (p<0.05), including among practitioners from different institutional and professional backgrounds.

Interpretation: The deep-learning-based system achieved expert-level performance in fetal ultrasound image evaluation and enabled scalable regional quality auditing. Integration of PQCS with a PDCA-based supervision framework may help reduce disparities in prenatal ultrasound quality between institutions and support continuous improvement in practitioners’ examination skills.

title: Mimicry, Endogenous Observability, and Recurrent Cooperation
affiliations: and University of Kassel

detail.title: Mimicry, Endogenous Observability, and Recurrent Cooperation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: When preferences are imperfectly observable, stable cooperation may be impossible. We show that cooperation can nevertheless recur when observability is generated by a signal opportunists can copy. Conditional cooperators use the signal to find one another; opportunists mimic it to exploit them. Mimicry erodes signal precision and reverses the fitness advantage of cooperative preferences; as cooperators decline, mimicry becomes unprofitable, allowing the signal to recover. Whether this feedback produces a stable cycle depends on behavioral adjustment. Under replicator dynamics, no interior periodic orbit exists. By contrast, sufficiently strong responsiveness to rare profitable strategies generates a locally unique attracting periodic orbit when preferences evolve slowly. A rare-response index characterizes this condition, which is satisfied by Smith dynamics and smooth boundary-preserving protocols. The cycle remains attracting in the complete strategy system and requires neither mutation nor a signaling-cost advantage for cooperative types. Thus, endogenous observability can sustain recurrent cooperation without a stationary cooperative state.

detail.abstract:
Background: A falling national average does not establish that gaps between groups have narrowed. We examined whether area deprivation was associated with early-life mortality in South Korea and whether inequality changed across cohorts.

Methods: We linked Statistics Korea birth and death registrations for all 2010–19 live births in this nationwide cohort study, ascertaining mortality to 5 years; 3,549,480 term, normal-birthweight infants were analysed. Deprivation was measured by the district-level area deprivation index (ADI); quartiles and fractional ranks were derived within each cohort. Outcomes were neonatal, infant, and under-5 death. Inequality was quantified as the slope (SII) and relative (RII) indices of inequality, and change tested by a rank-by-cohort interaction.

Findings: The most deprived quartile had higher odds of under-5 death (adjusted odds ratio 1.18, 95% CI 1.09–1.28) and infant death (1.14, 1.03–1.26), but not neonatal death (1.01, 0.81–1.27). Both were significant in each cohort: SII 0.31 per 1,000 births (0.09–0.52) and RII 1.24 (1.07–1.45) in the 2010 cohort; 0.25 (0.02–0.47) and 1.19 (1.01–1.40) in the 2015 cohort.

Interaction: testing showed no evidence of change (RII ratio 0.95, p=0.667; SII difference −0.06, p=0.677).Interpretation Inequality in under-5 mortality by area deprivation persisted in both cohorts under universal health coverage, with no detectable change and none in the neonatal period. In a Western Pacific setting with among the lowest child mortality worldwide, monitoring on both scales and area-based action in deprived districts remain warranted.

detail.title: The Cost of Hurricane Evacuations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no relevant or material financial interests that relate to the research described in this manuscript. declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded in part by the Rasmuson Foundation.

detail.abstract: Climate-driven tropical storms pose physical risks for public safety. Evacuation is a key protective action against hurricanes, but it may be costly for individuals. Despite their importance to emergency management decisions, there is little evidence on the size of these costs. In this paper we estimate the welfare cost of hurricane evacuations and sheltering. We combine spatial data on hurricanes and evacuation orders with billions of records of individuals' cell phone-derived movement activity. These data generate rich insights about evacuation behavior, including differences by physical risk, information provision, and demographics. Using a structural travel cost model we estimate that the welfare costs of evacuation and sheltering can be large when compared to mortality costs, averaging 55 percent as a share of the value of statistical life lost. Our results demonstrate a novel application of the travel cost demand method and document an understudied cost of hurricanes.

detail.title: Credit Rating Agencies' Liabilities

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Corporate Governance Institute - Law Working Paper No. 965/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: European Corporate Governance Institute (ECGI) - Law Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Credit ratings assess the creditworthiness of an issuer or financial instrument. They help overcome information asymmetries and facilitate the functioning of financial markets. Credit ratings also serve a regulatory function, as they are used, inter alia, to determine the regulatory capital requirements of banks. Credit rating agencies thus act as private gatekeepers in financial markets. The global financial crisis of 2008 revealed serious shortcomings in the credit rating industry and led to a significant tightening of regulation and oversight. This paper focuses on the civil liability of credit rating agencies.

The central issue concerns the liability of credit rating agencies towards investors who suffer losses as a result of excessively optimistic ratings. Credit rating agencies have traditionally been considered largely immune from civil liability. While this remains true to some extent, the paper demonstrates that the legal landscape is evolving. Some jurisdictions have adopted specific liability rules (China, the EU). Courts have tested concepts of quasi-contractual liability, as known in civil law jurisdictions (e.g., Austria, Germany, Portugal, and Türkiye), and in mixed legal systems (e.g., Israel). Similarly, courts have adjudicated cases on the basis of the common law tort of negligent misrepresentation (e.g., Australia, Singapore, the United Kingdom, and the United States).

As a general finding, the emerging public regulation of credit rating agencies appears to trigger corresponding civil duties and, in turn, to enhance liability risks. Credit ratings are increasingly treated as professional assessments. It is therefore less likely today that a court will deny liability on the ground that the rating constitutes protected speech.

 The paper presents the key findings of a cross-country study conducted under the auspices of the International Academy of Comparative Law. It examines the  relevant law and policy in 18 jurisdictions, including the European Union.

title: Recursive Portfolio Learning and the Endogenous Riskless Rate
affiliations: Texas Tech University, Kean University, , Texas Tech University and Johns Hopkins University - Carey Business School

detail.title: Recursive Portfolio Learning and the Endogenous Riskless Rate

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: Portfolio optimization almost universally treats the riskless rate as exogenous, typically a short Treasury yield. In incomplete markets, this is an artifact as the rate at which an investor can discharge risk depends on the hedging technology inside her own portfolio, not on a security she may not trade at scale. We formulate portfolio choice as a recursive learning operator on conditional covariance operators by selecting a minimum-risk direction, re-estimating its return law under long-memory, heavy-tailed dynamics, re-injecting it, repeat. The map admits a fixed point whose expected return defines the Adaptive Minimum-Risk Rate, an endogenous, portfolio-specific shadow benchmark. Contraction is governed by the covariance operator's condition number, destabilizing precisely when assets become near-collinear. Empirically, the recursion converges on equity and cryptocurrency universes to a fixed-point invariant to the informational regime, lying orders of magnitude below the raw minimum-variance level-separating reducible risk from the structural residual no hedge removes.

title: Beyond Optimization and Blind Selection: Reflexive Agency in Economic Evolution

detail.title: Beyond Optimization and Blind Selection: Reflexive Agency in Economic Evolution
detail.abstract: Evolutionary economics explains economic change through variation, selection, retention, transmission, innovation, and institutional transformation, whereas much of economics explains outcomes through purposive choice. This article argues that these modes of explanation become recursively connected once economic agents can represent the evolutionary processes in which they participate and intentionally alter their operation. It develops the concept of reflexive economic evolution: agents do not merely choose within given constraints or adapt to existing selection pressures, but can generate new possibilities, modify selection environments, organize transmission, and sometimes revise the criteria and mechanisms by which variants are selected. This latter second-order capacity is termed meta-selection. Reflexive economic evolution does not imply comprehensive control or a predetermined social end-state: guidance changes the distribution of possible trajectories under uncertainty rather than determining a trajectory. The framework shows how intentional and evolutionary explanations can be causally complementary, why effective agency is partly endogenous, and why policy should be understood not only as changing current outcomes but also as reshaping the evolutionary environment in which subsequent adaptation and innovation occur.

title: The Economics of the 351 Exchange: Optimal Seeding of a Tax-Deferred ETF under Concentration Constraints

detail.abstract: A U.S. investor holding a large, low-basis single stock can move into a diversified fund without triggering the embedded capital-gains tax by contributing securities in kind under Internal Revenue Code Section 351, provided the basket she contributes clears a statutory diversification test: no single issuer above 25% of its value, and the five largest issuers together at or below 50%. The regulation tests each contributor's own basket, so the other contributors cannot rescue a concentrated investor. This note formalizes the seeding decision the test creates and quantifies its economics. We write the 25%/50% test as linear constraints on contribution weights, cast the choice of seed basket as a linear program that maximizes deferred gain, and derive three closed-form consequences of the caps. Contributing a position of value C at the 25% ceiling requires at least 3C of eligible ballast from the investor's own holdings, so the share of a concentrated position that can go in is her eligible ballast divided by 3C; a seed that places one issuer at the cap can be no more diversified than sixteen effective names; and deferral loses to an immediate sale only if the capital-gains rate at the horizon exceeds a breakeven set by today's rate, the growth factor and the step-up probability alone. We then compare four ways to handle a $10M low-basis position (351 seed, exchange fund, hold-and-borrow, and sell-and-pay) on after-tax terminal wealth and on a risk-aversion-adjusted certainty equivalent, over horizons of 10 to 30 years and across the probability of a basis step-up at death. In the base calibration the 351 seed has the highest certainty equivalent at every horizon, because it pairs the deferral of a sale with real diversification at a low fee. Hold-and-borrow posts the highest expected wealth and the lowest certainty equivalent, as borrowing against an undiversified position would predict. All figures are reproducible from a single script with a fixed seed.

detail.abstract: This study examines the phenomenon of rebranding and its impact on product competitiveness through strategic, theoretical, and regulatory lenses. Global market dynamics compel corporations to transform their identities to maintain business relevance, optimize cost structures, and respond to shifting consumer behaviors. By synthesizing theories of brand equity, repositioning, brand architecture, and Transaction Cost Economics (TCE), this study analyzes various case categories ranging from the termination of franchise licenses and global alignment to radical overhauls and reputation recovery strategies. The analysis reveals that rebranding success is heavily determined by the alignment of value communication, equity risk management, and adaptation to the government policy landscape and applicable legal compliance. While digital-based regulatory support and international agreements can facilitate the transition process, territorial administrative hurdles and sectoral regulations remain critical challenges that corporate decision-makers must carefully mitigate.

detail.abstract: Hiring and admissions systems routinely collect category data (name, photograph, age, sex, geography, credentials) at the stage where it does the most documented damage: before evaluation. Social-psychological research shows that category salience activates stereotype threat in candidates and population priors in evaluators; audit studies show that identical files receive divergent outcomes when only the category signal changes; and the large-scale French anonymous-CV experiment shows that the intuitive remedy, masking, can worsen outcomes by removing evaluators' ability to read atypical trajectories in context. This paper specifies an open protocol that resolves the tension by relocating rather than deleting category data: evaluation is category-blind but trajectory-rich; assessment is untimed within a bounded window; demographic and credential data are collected only after the evaluation decision, firewalled from evaluators, and used exclusively for audit, compliance and administration. The protocol treats the individual, not the population, as the reference class, and the individual's trajectory, not a credential snapshot, as the primary evidence of capability. It is published as a free and open standard, with a reference implementation, so that any organization (employer, school, HR vendor, public service) can adopt or build upon it. Access to employment is treated here as a matter of basic equity, not as a market to be enclosed.

title: Relative Development and the Intelligence Divide
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Relative Development and the Intelligence Divide
detail.abstract: Will artificial intelligence (AI) help poorer countries catch up? This paper argues that the answer depends less on access to AI than on the capacity to use new knowledge productively. We show that countries have narrowed gaps in capital and schooling more readily than gaps in productivity. Technology can diffuse widely without producing productivity convergence. Measured human capital explains only a modest share of productivity differences in levels, but is associated with sharply different mobility regimes. The estimated transition processes imply an expected time to exit the lowest-productivity state of about 65 years for economies below the estimated human-capital threshold, compared with about 25 years for those above it. This reconciles development accounting with the view of human capital as absorptive capacity. If AI mainly augments skilled workers and capable firms, it may reinforce existing gaps. If it lowers the costs of learning, adaptation, and implementation in weaker-capability economies, it could instead promote convergence. The Intelligence Divide is therefore not simply about access to AI, but about the capacity to turn knowledge into productivity.

detail.abstract: Online reviews shape consumer trust because they are often perceived as authentic records of consumption experiences. Generative AI challenges this trust by producing reviews that appear fluent, persuasive, and humanlike. Drawing on a cue-based account of authenticity judgment, we examine how consumers distinguish AI-generated reviews from human-written reviews and why detection may fail. Across three online studies, we examine how consumers distinguish AI-generated reviews from human-written reviews and why detection fails. Studies 1 and 2 provide initial evidence that paraphrasing-based AI reviews are harder to detect than standard AI-generated reviews. Study 3 extends this evidence by testing a cue-erosion mechanism in a larger review-classification experiment with 168 participants and 13,073 review evaluations. The results show that consumers detected AI-generated reviews above chance but imperfectly. Detection was substantially worse for paraphrasing-based AI reviews than for standard label-based AI reviews, with accuracy falling from 72.4% to 52.3%. A linguistic-distance analysis showed that paraphrasing-based reviews were significantly closer to human-written reviews, indicating cue erosion. Predictive models further showed that consumers used multiple linguistic cues when judging AI authorship, but their cue use only partially aligned with the cues that distinguished actual AI-generated reviews from human-written reviews. Cognitive reflection improved detection and cue alignment, but did not eliminate vulnerability when paraphrasing reduced cue diagnosticity. These findings suggest that platforms should treat paraphrasing-based AI reviews as a distinct provenance risk because they can preserve linguistic markers of authentic experience while obscuring origin.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in improving green marketing strategies to drive sustainable consumer decisions through personalization, transparency, and communication. It bridges the knowledge gap regarding the effects of AI-based systems on consumer trust, perceived usefulness, and purchase intentions, and alleviates technological anxiety, especially in emerging markets such as Pakistan. In a cross-sectional, quantitative design, the data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to investigate the direct, mediating, and moderating relationships among AI-driven marketing constructs. The research assessed reliability, validity, and model fit using SmartPLS 4 with 385 respondents with experience with AI-based marketing tools. The findings showed that transparency and green marketing communication using AI is the most significant predictor (R2 = 0.773) of sustainable consumer choice. Consumer trust and perceived usefulness play significant roles in mediating these relationships, whereas technological anxiety does not. The arguments are supported by the findings that AI is a technological and behavioral attacker of encouraging sustainability. The study is an expansion of the Resource-Based View (RBV) and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), as it frames AI as an ethical strategic asset that can fill the gap between digital innovation and environmental responsibility, providing practical recommendations on how AI can be used to sustain marketing activities and AI policy development.

detail.abstract: Rebranding is a corporate strategy that is becoming increasingly important in responding to changes in the business environment, evolving consumer preferences, shifts in ownership structures, and demands for social legitimacy. Recent literature indicates that rebranding has evolved from a mere effort to revitalize identity into a strategic process related to brand equity, corporate identity, brand communication, corporate values, and consumer response (Sangroya et al., 2026). Changes in a company’s name and identity can also influence consumer perceptions of the company’s position and competitiveness, as corporate brand equity is linked to perceptions regarding the company’s existence, management, responsibility, and competitive position (Porto et al., 2024). Research on corporate identity changes indicates that internal communication and identity consistency are crucial aspects in ensuring that stakeholders understand the brand change (Bravo & Pina, 2024). Furthermore, changes in identity can affect brand equity through shifts in consumer associations and perceptions of the brand; therefore, the rebranding process must consider continuity between the old and new identities (Lambrecht et al., 2025). In a social context, changes in brand positioning can also have consequences for brand equity if a company attempts to address specific social values or issues without considering stakeholders’ perceptions of authenticity (Lee et al., 2023). Research on brand identity in the digital environment also indicates that companies need to manage the tension between the identity they wish to communicate and the perception of authenticity formed by consumers (Chatzopoulou & Navazhylava, 2022). Based on this, this paper aims to analyze rebranding as a multifaceted strategic decision through the perspectives of strategic rebranding, brand equity, the resource-based view, institutional theory, and corporate identity, as well as to examine its interaction with public policy and its implications for product competitiveness. The analysis is conducted conceptually through a comparison of domestic and global rebranding cases, covering changes resulting from licensing, mergers and consolidations, localization, identity simplification, business vision reorientation, and responses to legitimacy crises. The results of the analysis indicate that the success of rebranding is determined not only by a company’s ability to create a new identity but also by the alignment between internal resources, market needs, social legitimacy, regulatory compliance, and the ability to maintain established brand equity. Recent perspectives on corporate communication also indicate that a company’s communication activities can influence consumer engagement and consumer-based brand equity; therefore, identity changes must be accompanied by a consistent communication strategy (Das et al., 2026). Thus, rebranding can be understood as a strategic transformation process that offers the opportunity to enhance a company’s relevance and competitiveness, but at the same time carries risks such as consumer confusion, the loss of historical associations, transition costs, and a decline in legitimacy if not managed in an integrated manner.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the strategic, theoretical, and regulatory implications of corporate rebranding on product competitiveness within dynamic market environments. Adapting brand identity evidenced by commercial transitions such as BreadTalk to MAKO, Cheetos to Chiki Twist, and Dunkin's global naming adjustments serves as an adaptive response to shifting consumer behavior, licensing constraints, and market disruption. Utilizing foundational frameworks including Customer-Based Brand Equity (CBBE), Brand Repositioning, Brand Architecture, and Transaction Cost Economics (TCE), this study analyzes how structural and cosmetic identity modifications influence long-term corporate performance. Through case synthesis across contractual restructurings, global alignments, radical ecosystem shifts, and defensive reputation recoveries, the paper demonstrates that successful rebranding depends on preserving historical brand equity and minimizing consumer friction. Furthermore, the analysis integrates the government policy landscape, evaluating facilitating mechanisms such as the Madrid Protocol and First-to-File registration systems alongside restrictive administrative hurdles including BPOM recertification, halal compliance, and territorial legal constraints. A conceptual model is proposed positioning government policy as a moderating variable between rebranding execution and product competitiveness. Ultimately, disciplined managerial execution, transparent communication, and alignment with regulatory frameworks are identified as essential.
