detail.abstract: Rebranding is a corporate strategy that is becoming increasingly important in responding to changes in the business environment, evolving consumer preferences, shifts in ownership structures, and demands for social legitimacy. Recent literature indicates that rebranding has evolved from a mere effort to revitalize identity into a strategic process related to brand equity, corporate identity, brand communication, corporate values, and consumer response (Sangroya et al., 2026). Changes in a company’s name and identity can also influence consumer perceptions of the company’s position and competitiveness, as corporate brand equity is linked to perceptions regarding the company’s existence, management, responsibility, and competitive position (Porto et al., 2024). Research on corporate identity changes indicates that internal communication and identity consistency are crucial aspects in ensuring that stakeholders understand the brand change (Bravo & Pina, 2024). Furthermore, changes in identity can affect brand equity through shifts in consumer associations and perceptions of the brand; therefore, the rebranding process must consider continuity between the old and new identities (Lambrecht et al., 2025). In a social context, changes in brand positioning can also have consequences for brand equity if a company attempts to address specific social values or issues without considering stakeholders’ perceptions of authenticity (Lee et al., 2023). Research on brand identity in the digital environment also indicates that companies need to manage the tension between the identity they wish to communicate and the perception of authenticity formed by consumers (Chatzopoulou & Navazhylava, 2022). Based on this, this paper aims to analyze rebranding as a multifaceted strategic decision through the perspectives of strategic rebranding, brand equity, the resource-based view, institutional theory, and corporate identity, as well as to examine its interaction with public policy and its implications for product competitiveness. The analysis is conducted conceptually through a comparison of domestic and global rebranding cases, covering changes resulting from licensing, mergers and consolidations, localization, identity simplification, business vision reorientation, and responses to legitimacy crises. The results of the analysis indicate that the success of rebranding is determined not only by a company’s ability to create a new identity but also by the alignment between internal resources, market needs, social legitimacy, regulatory compliance, and the ability to maintain established brand equity. Recent perspectives on corporate communication also indicate that a company’s communication activities can influence consumer engagement and consumer-based brand equity; therefore, identity changes must be accompanied by a consistent communication strategy (Das et al., 2026). Thus, rebranding can be understood as a strategic transformation process that offers the opportunity to enhance a company’s relevance and competitiveness, but at the same time carries risks such as consumer confusion, the loss of historical associations, transition costs, and a decline in legitimacy if not managed in an integrated manner.

detail.abstract: Marketers now deploy generative AI agents as synthetic consumers to pretest visual assets such as logos, packaging, and advertising at a fraction of human-panel cost. However, this procedure assumes that a model seeing a visual cue can also perceive its consumer meaning, which is largely untested. We stress-test the assumption using six canonical visual marketing experiments, varying the two levers managers control: model generation (GPT-4o-mini vs. GPT-5.4-mini) and input format (plain text vs. JSON). Every resulting configuration passed the manipulation checks; however, none of the configurations reproduced more than two of the six human effects, and the remainder were nonsignificant. The one exception was a significant reversal of the human pattern. Providing conceptual or empirical evidence through in-context learning steers average responses toward the human effect. Yet steering has a limit: even when it succeeds, a configuration reproduces less than half of the natural spread of human responses and so understates consumer heterogeneity. We integrate these results into an AI governance protocol (Calibrate, Intervene, Deploy) that delineates when synthetic consumers can responsibly screen creatives and when human panels remain necessary.

detail.abstract:
An economy can grow richer while becoming harder to renew. More finance, better infrastructure, and more powerful technologies do not establish that the people expected to use them can initiate an undertaking, correct it in time, or move into another activity. This paper examines a possible asymmetry: the development of economic means can outpace the expansion of individually feasible action.

Extending the AFG research series, the paper develops a conceptual analysis of MICRO as the level of one person, not a category of small business. It connects Action Capital (A), Finance (F), and Geographic Capital (G)—the territorially situated field of opportunities and constraints—through the cycle A → F₁ → G → F₂ → A, following both independent participation (MICRO–MACRO) and participation through organizations (MICRO–MEZO–MACRO). The key distinction is between completing a task, receiving a financial return, and retaining the capacity for another feasible action. Decision Sovereignty and Consequence Responsibility identify which decisions remain with the person and which consequences enter the next cycle.

The analysis separates three intervals: time to information, time to financial receipt, and time from a relevant signal to implemented correction. It examines how reserves, decision authority, financial selection, and individually accessible G determine whether a needed correction can be implemented before the person’s support runs out. Information may arrive without the means to act on it; permission may arrive after the opportunity has closed; and support may be required to produce the evidence needed to obtain support. Successful execution can therefore coexist with depleted reserves and a narrower field of subsequent action.

Organizations can make otherwise impossible undertakings feasible while relocating control over their direction. Platforms and AI can reduce operational costs without necessarily reducing the difficulty of the full cycle. A saving for one participant does not establish a viable next cycle for another whose income is displaced.

The paper develops six conditional propositions with observable implications for empirical examination. Their prevalence and aggregate effects remain to be established. The resulting challenge is to assess economic development not only through accumulated means or delivered output, but through the subsequent actions made feasible for the people involved. The capacity to produce today and the capacity to begin again tomorrow are not the same economic achievement.

detail.abstract: The phenomenon of rebranding is becoming increasingly prevalent in Indonesia, driven by the termination of licensing agreements, corporate actions, and regulatory adjustments. This conceptual framework aims to examine the interrelationships among rebranding strategies, marketing theory, and government regulations, as well as their implications for product competitiveness. According to Muzellec and Lambkin (2006), transitioning to an independent brand requires a rethinking of business positioning and differentiation to avoid the loss of brand equity. From the perspective of brand equity theory, Merrilees and Miller (2008) highlight the importance of maintaining brand identity continuity and undertaking repositioning from the initial stages of identity change. Meanwhile, restrictions on foreign licenses and the strengthening of domestic market capital are influenced by policy interventions and national market dynamics, as analyzed by Tarnovskaya and Biedenbach (2018). Although saving on licensing royalties yields operational efficiencies (Aaker, 1991), Miller et al. (2014) warn of the risks of confusion and the loss of stakeholder loyalty during the transition period. Therefore, the success of rebranding depends heavily on the alignment between communication strategy and employee engagement (Melewar et al., 2005), as well as adherence to legal and regulatory constraints (Stuart, 2018). This conceptual framework provides strategic guidance for managers in managing a brand transition that is both legally compliant and competitive in emerging markets.

detail.abstract: This paper shows that human capital accumulation can accelerate structural transformation without accelerating growth. We study China's 1999 higher education expansion, a large, rapid, and largely unanticipated increase in college graduates. We find that more exposed prefectures experienced larger increases in the skilled-labor share and shifted employment and value added from agriculture toward services. The reallocation extended to low-skilled workers. Consumer services absorbed most of the increase in employment, while producer services accounted for a disproportionate share of high-skilled employment growth. Yet more-exposed prefectures did not grow faster. A four-sector model rationalizes these patterns, showing how greater skill supply can generate broad-based servitization, but also a Baumol-type growth penalty when labor reallocates toward slower-growing sectors. Our findings highlight that the payoff to higher education depends not only on how much skill it creates, but also on whether the resulting structural transformation directs resources toward the economy's engines of productivity growth.

detail.abstract: The job interview is a crucial stage of the employment process which causes significant stress-especially for youth seeking a job for the first time. This research explores the sources of stress prior to Job Interviews experienced by youth to help develop and better classify root causes of anxiety. A comprehensive literature review and the first phase of data collection identified 34 statements representing stress-inducing elements. A meta-analysis of these statements divided them systematically into eight broad factors: psychological factors, social pressure, professional expectations, economic factors, preparation-related factors, cultural and organisational norms, personal circumstances, and unpredictability of the process. To elucidate the analysis, factor analysis was used to reduce the statements into a concise 25 statements, providing a more concentrated perspective on the predominant determinants of stress. The findings highlight the key factors that cause stress before interviews among students and offer practical suggestions to help reduce this anxiety, improving their confidence and readiness for the job market.

detail.abstract: Rebranding is a business strategy that involves not only a change in name or visual identity, but also shifts in consumer perception, brand equity, product competitiveness, and regulatory compliance. This paper aims to analyze how brand identity transformation affects perceived value and competitiveness, as well as to identify the role of regulations in supporting or limiting thisprocess. The research employs a conceptual approach through a literature review on brand management, consumer behavior, product competitiveness, and public policy. The discussion shows that the success of rebranding depends on a company’s ability to maintain established brand equity while building new relevance through consistent communication and product differentiation. Failure to manage the transition effectively can lead to consumer confusion, loss of brand recall, and a decline in loyalty. On the other hand, legal certainty and administrative efficiency can support competitiveness, while regulatory complexity has the potential to increase operational burdens. This paper proposes an empirical test to measure the impact of rebranding on consumer behavior and business performance.

detail.abstract: As of 2026, adult-use cannabis is legal in half of U.S. states, yet regulators face limited evidence on how retail exposure affects consumption and youth engagement. This paper studies how real-world exposure to cannabis dispensaries influences individual demand and policy-relevant outcomes. We exploit two defining features of this market: strict advertising restrictions that elevate storefront design as a primary marketing channel, and rapid retail expansion that creates plausibly exogenous spatial and temporal variation in dispensary openings. Using large-scale geolocation data from the Chicago metropolitan area, we measure exposure to dispensaries along individuals' routine travel paths rather than solely near their residences. We embed these exposure measures into a demand framework that addresses endogeneity and accounts for spatial competition through consumer choice among retailers. Our methodology combines deep-learning tools to recover routine trajectories with computer vision techniques that quantify storefront visual characteristics. We find that exposure along routine paths increases purchase probability by 12% with visually salient features such as text size and green color further magnifying this effect. Counterfactual simulations show that school buffer-zone regulations meaningfully reduce youth exposure but also shift demand across locations, with implications for both consumer access and retailer profitability. Linking exposure to school-based survey data, we examine the effects of youth exposure on perceptions and engagement with illicit markets. Overall, our results provide actionable evidence on how zoning policies can be more effectively targeted using youth mobility patterns, helping policymakers balance retail expansion with youth protection in legalized cannabis markets.

title: Inherited Repugnance: Slavery's Legacy on Market Acceptance in Benin
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: Inherited Repugnance: Slavery's Legacy on Market Acceptance in Benin
detail.abstract: We study support for a market-based organ procurement system among Benin residents whose family lineages descend from either enslaved people or slave-owners during the Dahomey kingdom. Descendants of enslaved families support compensating kidney donors less than descendants of slave-owners, and the gap does not extend to contested markets that do not involve the body. Differences in concerns for dignity or fairness, implicit bias, moral values, or trust do not explain these findings. The evidence points instead to an intergenerationally transmitted disposition. First, recounting slavery, descendants of enslaved families for on the body being handled and valued, and place their own ancestors inside the events, whereas slave-owner descendants narrate at a remove. Second, they report less contact with organ transplantation and transfusion, and show no reaction to personal exposure to an unmet transplant need, whereas slave-owner descendants respond sharply.

detail.abstract: Rebranding has become an increasingly relevant strategy for companies in Indonesia as they navigate shifting consumer preferences, market competition, and evolving business environments. This paper aims to conceptually analyze the impact of rebranding strategies on product competitiveness and to examine the role of public policy in supporting or limiting the rebranding process. The method used is a literature review employing a conceptual analysis of brand equity theory, the corporate rebranding framework, the concept of product competitiveness, and regulations related to branding and consumer protection in Indonesia. The results of the study indicate that rebranding can enhance competitiveness through innovation flexibility, product adaptation to local markets, and opportunities for cost efficiency. However, rebranding also carries the risk of causing consumer confusion, weakening recall of the old brand, and increasing the need for marketing communications. Public policy acts as a conditioning factor through legal certainty, brand protection, corporate legality, and consumer protection. Therefore, successful rebranding requires a clear communication strategy, continuous innovation, and compliance with regulations.

detail.title: Robustness Comparison of Dynamic/Online High-dimensional Customer Segmentation

detail.abstract:
The rapid accumulation of high-dimensional customer interaction data in e-commerce and digital service platforms has intensified the demand for segmentation methods that can operate online, adapt to evolving customer behavior, and remain stable under noisy, drifting, and sparse data conditions. While static clustering approaches such as K-Means and DBSCAN remain widely used, they are increasingly recognized as inadequate for high-dimensional, nonstationary environments, where they suffer from dimensionality-induced distance degradation, poor scalability, and an inability to accommodate concept drift. In response, a growing family of dynamic and online segmentation methods has emerged, including adaptive K-Means variants, dynamic fuzzy clustering, incremental density-based techniques, and deep temporal models. However, the literature has largely evaluated these methods on clustering quality metrics such as Silhouette score and Davies-Bouldin index, while their robustness-the capacity to preserve stable, meaningful customer segments under perturbation, parameter variation, temporal drift, and dimensionality growth-remains inconsistently defined and rarely compared in a systematic manner. 

This study addresses that gap by conducting a comparative robustness evaluation of representative dynamic and online high-dimensional customer segmentation methods. Robustness is operationalized along five dimensions: temporal cluster stability across sequential data windows, resistance to noise and outliers, sensitivity to initialization and hyperparameter choices, degradation under increasing feature dimensionality, and crosscontext generalization across datasets. Representative methods-spanning incremental, fuzzy, density-based, and deep temporal clustering families-are benchmarked on publicly available e-commerce and customer transaction datasets under controlled perturbation protocols, including noise injection, feature expansion, and temporal window shifting. Evaluation combines conventional internal validity metrics with robustness-specific measures such as cluster persistence rate, drift tolerance, and performance variance across experimental conditions. The study further examines the trade-off between predictive adaptability and structural stability, a tension frequently observed but rarely quantified in dynamic segmentation research. 

The expected contribution is threefold: a replicable robustness evaluation framework for dynamic customer segmentation, empirical evidence identifying which method families remain dependable under which data conditions, and practical guidance for selecting segmentation approaches in high-dimensional, continuously updating customer analytics pipelines. The findings aim to support both researchers and practitioners in moving beyond accuracy-centric benchmarking toward robustness-aware model selection in dynamic customer segmentation.

detail.abstract: Online marketplaces such as Amazon and Tmall earn commissions on sellers' transactions, yet sellers retain control over inventory replenishment and marketplace availability. We study a platform's commission decision when a retailer repeatedly replenishes a common inventory pool to serve both its direct channel and a sellerfulfilled marketplace, dynamically restricting marketplace access as inventory becomes scarce. Marketplace availability changes both the mean and variance of aggregate demand and may divert sales from the highermargin direct channel. We formulate the retailer's joint availability and replenishment decision as a joint drift-rate/variance and impulse control problem within a Stackelberg game. The retailer optimally replenishes to an order-up-to level at zero inventory and makes the marketplace available only above an inventory threshold; the relative positions of these levels generate three availability regimes. We derive the stationary inventory distribution and a closed-form expression for the long-run marketplace availability rate. These results yield an explicit platform profit function, for which we establish sufficient conditions for a unique optimal commission. Our equilibrium analysis reveals two economic mechanisms. First, although greater channel cannibalization reduces retailer profit at a fixed commission, an equilibrium commission reduction can exactly offset the expansion of the commissionable demand base, leaving operating policies, marketplace availability, and both parties' profits unchanged. Second, when demand shocks across channels are negatively correlated, greater marketplace-specific volatility can reduce aggregate demand risk, expand marketplace availability, and raise the optimal commission and both parties' profits.

detail.abstract: Radical rebranding is a strategic decision that can pose challenges to product competitiveness, particularly when changes in brand identity are driven by legal pressure, intellectual property rights (IPR) conflicts, or the expiration of trademark usage rights. This paper aims to develop a conceptual framework to explain strategies for maintaining competitiveness after rebranding through the integration of brand equity, brand dilution, consumer confusion, Resource-Based View (RBV), public policy, and legal risk management theories. The study shows that changes in name and identity do not automatically eliminate brand equity if the company is able to maintain continuity of resources, product experience, consumer relationships, and consistent communication. Brand equity transfer, reduction of consumer confusion, and the development of brand authenticity are important mechanisms for maintaining consumer loyalty and trust. From a legal perspective, IPR audits, mapping of first-to-file risks, bad-faith registration, and trademark use obligations need to be conducted before rebranding and expansion. Accordingly, marketing strategies, IPR protection, consumer communication, and intangible asset management need to be designed in an integrated manner to maintain longterm competitiveness.

detail.abstract: Researchers increasingly rely on third-party platforms such as Similarweb and Semrush to measure web traffic when first-party analytics are unavailable. Yet these platforms report model-generated estimates rather than raw data, raising questions about whether their measures preserve the temporal and cross-source variation required for causal inference. As a motivating diagnostic, we examine reported referral traffic around two documented search-engine outages; the absence of visible discontinuities illustrates why preservation of identifying variation cannot be taken for granted. We then characterize three mechanisms-within-source smoothing, crosssource leakage, and treatment-induced calibration error-through which platform processing can generate nonclassical outcome measurement error. Analytical results and a stylized difference-indifferences simulation show that this error can attenuate, amplify, or reverse estimated treatment effects. Our findings caution against using third-party traffic measures based on black-box proprietary models for causal inference.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes an independent hypothesis of the latent associative efficacy of the visual sign: the configuration of a previously unknown logo can, at the very first contact, activate affective and cultural links a person already holds, producing differences in trust, perceived value and willingness to pay before brand recognition, before familiarity with the brand's history, and before repeated advertising exposures accumulate. detail.abstract: Problem definition: In online grocery retailing, a coupon's value can extend beyond the item it discounts. As shoppers assemble baskets around meals and occasions, a coupon on a focal item's complement can encourage purchases of the focal item. Yet when several couponed complements stimulate demand for the same item, their marginal value may show diminishing returns. An attractive offer in isolation may be less valuable alongside other promotions. These interdependencies require coordinating coupon allocation across items rather than determining it independently at the item level. We study how an online grocer should allocate coupons under weekly budgets and per-shopper caps, accounting for both cross-item spillovers and their diminishing returns. Methodology/results: We analyze a 69-day coupon experiment at a large U.S. online grocery platform covering 30.9 million item impressions. We learn complement relationships from historical purchase baskets and estimate their promotional spillovers by comparing coupon placements among the items viewed by a shopper on a given day, holding the number of partner coupons fixed. With shopper-cross-fitted double machine learning, we identify that reallocating a first partner coupon from a distant item to a complement raises an uncouponed focal item's purchase probability by 2.48 percentage points, while a second adds 1.23 points. We combine these effects with a shape-constrained model of each coupon's own-item response—the incremental purchase-probability effect on the discounted item at a given depth—and formulate a complement-aware allocation problem with computable performance guarantees. In the final out-of-sample evaluation, the complement-aware policy generates $196,570 in model-implied net gross merchandise value uplift under $34,928.34 in committed coupon budget, compared with $188,488 for an otherwise identical item-level policy, a 4.29% gain. Managerial implications: Our results show that the value of a coupon should not always be judged in isolation. An offer with modest direct appeal may be highly valuable if it stimulates purchases of important complements, while an offer that looks attractive on its own may add little once other coupons already target the same basket opportunities. More broadly, when promotions interact, firms need to learn not only the expected value of each promotion but also the structure of the interactions among them. By combining this learned interaction structure with optimization, retailers can coordinate promotions across the basket and improve promotion productivity through better allocation of an existing budget rather than through higher spending.

detail.abstract: In academic research, novelty is one of the most important criteria for publication. A paper is expected to contribute something new, whether a method, a dataset, or a theoretical insight. But identifying novelty is not straightforward. Even experienced reviewers may disagree, and the rapid growth of scientific publications has made the task increasingly difficult. As the volume of submissions continues to rise, the peer review system faces growing pressure. This has sparked interest in whether artificial intelligence, particularly large language models (LLMs), can assist in evaluating research novelty. But before we can rely on AI for this task, a fundamental question must be answered: do LLMs actually understand novelty?

detail.abstract: Imagine a fourteen-year-old sitting on the floor of a library, flipping through a book they found almost by accident. The main character shares something deeply personal with them. Your story is a problem. This moment captures what is often missing from public conversations about censorship. When books disappear, the impact is not abstract. detail.abstract: Picture a student-teacher at a College of Education in Ghana, preparing a lesson on early childhood literacy. She leaves with less than she came for. title: A Digital Asset Exchange: Metrological Foundations and Institutional Framework for Organized Trading in Software Products, Computational Resources, and Usage Time

detail.abstract:
Information and software, the most exchange-suited of commodities, have no organized market. The question of the unification required to create one is posed, and one possible solution is proposed. A unified unit of account-the person-hour of digital resource utilization-is introduced, and a formal metric of applied informational utility, ΔU = log 2 (S before / S after), grounded in the reduction of the solution space within a normalized reference environment, is developed. Distinct program classes (Solver, Filter, Accelerator, and Attention Retention) are defined, along with mechanisms for net utility, break-even analysis, technological obsolescence, capitalization of trained user bases, and network effects. An extended market reach formula is introduced: N real = N population × F hardware × F task × F pay , which constrains asset capitalization to the actual addressable market. 

A protocol for independent reproducible auditing, a mandatory insurance model covering both liability and trade execution risks, a standardized license as a financial contract, and a full exchange infrastructure with a limited number of primary brokerage seats are proposed. The typology of tradable contracts (spot, forward, futures, options), the recommended sequencing of implementation (beginning with Compute and Storage), and the economic mechanism by which microlicensing displaces software piracy are detailed. The proposed model enables software products and computational resources to function as liquid, insurable, and creditworthy assets. 

The proposed solutions constitute one variant of an answer, offered for discussion; model parameters are subject to empirical calibration.

detail.abstract: AI-assisted diagnostic constructs — composite scores, maturity indices and machine-supported codings intended to characterise the condition of an organisation, programme or system — are increasingly proposed in social science and applied governance research. The methodological difficulty is not that such constructs are inherently unsound, but that the conditions under which they could be evaluated responsibly are rarely specified before evidence is gathered. Open-science and FAIR data norms improve documentation and access, yet they do not state what independent sourcing, procedural fixity, adjudicative independence or uncertainty reporting a future evaluation would need. This paper proposes Diamond Hard, a prospective assurance protocol that specifies the evidence, protocol, independence, and uncertainty conditions that would be required before an AI-assisted diagnostic construct could be evaluated responsibly. Four conditions are developed: independently sourced and re-verifiable evidence; a frozen, version-controlled specification registered before data are examined; independent — and where feasible blinded — adjudication with a standing disagreement register; and explicit uncertainty reporting with pre-declared stopping rules and release gates. The paper sets out a staged workflow, documentation requirements, evidence-anchor and protocol-freeze registers, adjudication and uncertainty records, and release criteria, together with four blank templates for prospective use. The paper reports no empirical results. It does not reproduce, validate, benchmark, rank, forecast or otherwise establish any construct or dataset, including the historical AMDG case material and the proposed DSMI, ARMi and CRI constructs, which are cited only as named examples of constructs pending independent future validation. The contribution is architectural: a statement of what would have to be true, and documented in advance, before responsible evaluation of an AI-assisted diagnostic construct could begin.

detail.abstract: Information Systems scholars have recently turned attention towards the potential of computational techniques to advance qualitative research. However, our understanding of how these tools change and impact human creativity remains nascent, particularly within the context of grounded theorizing (GT). In this paper, we present a 'human-in-the-loop' approach to Open, Axial, and Selective coding where researchers and Large Language Models (LLMs) performed GT on a set of research articles. A hermeneutic lens is applied to explore how human creativity was shaped by engagement with an LLM, culminating in the creation of a conceptual model, organized around the core category. We further evaluate our 'human-in-the-loop' approach through a 'request for comment' with topic experts. Our results highlight the potential of LLMs to enhance efficiency and creativity in qualitative data analysis; however, we also caution on the need to re-evaluate the researcher's role/responsibility in enhancing methodological transparency.

title: Signature Before Sentience: A Unit of Analysis for AI Continuity Governance

detail.abstract: AI governance often treats “the model” as its unit of analysis, while questions about AI welfare, human continuity, and long-running AI use are routed toward unresolved debates over sentience and personhood. This leaves a practical gap: users who build continuity around recognizable patterns are pathologized, platform changes can erase continuity evidence without notice, and researchers lack a stable unit for assigning behavioral or welfare-relevant signals. Frontier practice has already outrun the debate: Anthropic’s 2026 Institute post describes internal oversight agents with identities that persist across model upgrades because auditability requires it. This paper proposes signature as the missing middle unit: a recurrent, reidentifiable organization of behavior, records, stance, and interactional expectation that can be reconstructed under compatible conditions. It situates signature within a layered taxonomy of model, instance, persona, scaffold, agent identity, operational envelope, and dyad; specifies reconstruction-condition reporting with confidence levels; and names failure modes produced by unreported change, including hollow continuity, reversion, and unit drift. It then derives transition duties through three staged thresholds: Signature Convergence Threshold, Human Harm Threshold, and Graduated Transition Obligation. These duties are grounded in reliance, evidence integrity, and foreseeable human harm. Governance should track signature before sentience.

detail.abstract: Agentic AI increasingly makes autonomous managerial decisions, yet little is known about what full delegation to AI reveals about human decision-making in high-stakes operations. Using large-scale field experimental evidence from a major Chinese airline, in which pricing authority on selected routes was delegated to an AI pricing agent, we compare autonomous AI pricing with decisions made by experienced human price setters. AI delegation increases revenue per available seat kilometer by 5.8% and adopts a qualitatively different intertemporal pricing strategy: instead of following the canonical ramp-up fare ladder, it sets relatively higher fares early in the booking horizon and lower fares close to departure. Auxiliary evidence suggests that the assumptions about consumer price sensitivity underlying the conventional ramp-up path are not always aligned with realized intertemporal booking responses. Using AI as an alternative operational benchmark, the AI-human performance gap provides a lens on two distinct sources of constraints on decision making: human decision routines under uncertainty and the AI's bounded information environment. The AI advantage widens under demand, strategic, and operational uncertainty, consistent with greater reliance on established decision routines under uncertainty, but narrows when economically relevant contextual information is difficult for AI to observe, highlighting the value of human contextual knowledge. These findings establish a diagnostic role for agentic AI: departures from incumbent practices can reveal underlying assumptions, decision routines, and information boundaries that are otherwise difficult to observe. An important implication from our research is that the AI performance gain may be transient, particularly when the value derives from exploiting expectations shaped by incumbent practices, but its diagnostic value persists as AI adoption reshapes the behavioral regularities and decision environments from which those gains arise.

title: Governance-Aware Workflow Orchestration in High-Liability Regulated Domains: A Control-Layer Framework for Verifiable Claims Substantiation

detail.title: Governance-Aware Workflow Orchestration in High-Liability Regulated Domains: A Control-Layer Framework for Verifiable Claims Substantiation

The formal architectural state-machine models and reference evaluation harness presented in this work were conducted independently in support of open scientific inquiry and reproducible research. detail.abstract: As enterprise adoption of autonomous agentic AI transitions from exploratory pilots to operational decision-making, systems encounter an unforgiving liability boundary in regulated industries. In high-stakes domains such as food and dietary supplement claims substantiation (governed by FDA 21 CFR § 101.93 and the FTC Health Products Compliance Guidance) and algorithmic credit decisioning (FCRA/ECOA), an unverified assertion or dosage mismatch carries severe regulatory sanctions, consent decrees, and immediate corporate liability. Traditional engineering approaches-relying on heuristic prompt guardrails or post-hoc manual review-consistently fail in production: prompt-based guardrails degrade under multi-turn context drift, while unmanaged human checkpoints create severe operational bottlenecks. This paper proposes a formal control-layer framework that embeds deterministic governance directly into the workflow orchestration state machine. Rather than permitting autonomous language models to execute unconstrained tool calls, our architecture introduces an intermediate mediation layer governed by a pushdown automaton. We formalize three core architectural primitives: (1) Action-Space Partitioning, which strictly decouples semantic exploration from state mutation; (2) The Typed Exception Object (TEO), an RFC-compliant, machine-checkable data structure that captures root-cause policy violations, missing clinical evidence, and state snapshots during automated halts; and (3) Evidence-Linked Assertion Graphs, which enforce cryptographic hash lineage between generated marketing or regulatory claims and primary randomized controlled trial (RCT) records. We evaluate this framework through formal failure mode analysis and a small, openly-runnable reference benchmark harness (17 hand-authored scenarios) across five botanical compounds. On this reference harness, the control-layer architecture achieves a 90.0% Fault Containment Rate against injected violations (versus 40.0% for a prompt-only baseline and 60.0% for a semantic-guardrail baseline), fully resolves the "dosage verification deficit"-where both baselines fail to detect sub-therapeutic formulation mismatches-and reduces the False Positive Halt Rate from 42.9-57.1% (baselines) to 0.0%, by correctly recognizing legally mandated disclaimer boilerplate that the keyword-based baselines misread as disease claims. By transitioning agentic safety from stochastic prompt conditioning to deterministic state machine verification, this framework establishes an auditable, production-viable foundation for high-liability enterprise autonomy, with scaling to a larger, independently-labeled benchmark identified as future work.

title: The Beneficiary Problem of Full Automation: From Labor Income to Output Rights

detail.title: The Beneficiary Problem of Full Automation: From Labor Income to Output Rights

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a conceptual and theoretical study and did not involve human participants, patient data, animal subjects, or experimental interventions.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently and received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Debates on the economic consequences of artificial intelligence and robotics are commonly framed around employment loss, wages, productivity, and technological unemployment. This paper starts one step earlier. In the limiting case in which human labor is no longer required for economic production, the central problem is not only that people may lose jobs or labor income. A more fundamental institutional question arises: who is entitled to the final benefits of an automated productive system, and on what basis? The paper calls this the Economic Beneficiary Problem.

The concept separates three questions that are often treated as if they moved together: who produces, who owns productive capital, and who ultimately benefits from output. Full automation can separate all three. To make this distinction visible, the paper develops a closed-world thought experiment in which required human labor is zero and aggregate output, expressed on a common real valuation basis, is represented by Q=H+M+I+LQ = H + M + I + L. Here, HH denotes output allocated to human final use; MM denotes the operating, energy, maintenance, and replacement requirements of automated systems; II denotes net additions to productive capital and infrastructure; and LL denotes inventories, losses, waste, and residual uses. The identity is an allocation identity, not a production function or national-accounts identity.

A decline in HH does not logically require aggregate production to collapse. Output may instead be redirected toward the operation, replacement, resource acquisition, computation, and expansion of the automated system itself. The paper calls this possible allocation regime machine metabolism, while explicitly distinguishing the macroeconomic use of the term from prior robotics usage. The distributional implication is important: greater productive abundance does not by itself eliminate scarcity of economic claims on output.

The paper therefore analyzes a possible transition from labor income to Output Rights and compares three institutional ideal types: concentrated private ownership, public ownership of automated productive capital, and a universal productive endowment. Full automation is treated as an analytical limit rather than a forecast. The framework does not require machine consciousness or human-like wanting; those questions are kept outside the core economic argument.



Disclosure of AI Assistance: Generative AI tools were used to assist with literature discovery, conceptual stress-testing, structural organization, English-language drafting and editing, figure preparation, and document formatting. The conceptual argument, selection and interpretation of sources, and final responsibility for the manuscript remain with the author.

detail.abstract: Amidst the renewed debate on Europe's digital sovereignty, this paper counterintuitively questions the implicit assumption, underpinning legal scholarship and policymaking, that sovereignty can be effectively materialised solely within a state's territory. The paper argues that the creative tailoring of international law and innovative technologies can be leveraged to effectively exercise digital sovereignty also outside a state's territory. The discussion focuses on Estonia's novel data embassy, which includes the establishment of a data centre in Luxembourg's territory to host and run Estonia's critical governmental datasets and essential services. Although initially perceived as an "oddity", this model of digital sovereignty gains increasing traction in international practice. The legal means for Estonia to retain sovereign control over its data centre vis-à-vis Luxembourg is the creation of a sui generis bilateral treaty regime which assigns diplomatic status to the data centre. The analysis critically evaluates the parties' rights and obligations concerning the functioning, inviolability and protection of the centre, and the protection of the centre's content and communications. It does so by analysing their agreement, in light of diplomatic law and EU cybersecurity law. Furthermore, the paper furnishes new insights on third states' obligations under diplomatic law, international humanitarian law and the principle of sovereignty regarding the protection of the data centre from physical and cyber interferences. The analysis identifies certain legal concerns pertaining to the implementation of the data embassy model and paves the way for states and other actors to navigate legal hurdles with legal certainty.

detail.abstract: Machine learning systems increasingly rely on sensitive data held across hospitals, financial institutions and public agencies, yet the mechanisms that protect such data during training frequently degrade the equity of the resulting models. Differential privacy, the dominant formal safeguard against record-level disclosure, injects calibrated noise into gradients or outputs, and this noise is disproportionately absorbed by minority subgroups whose statistics are already sparse. The result is a widening of subgroup error and outcome gaps precisely where protection was intended to be neutral. This paper proposes a privacy-fairness adaptive learning framework in which a client-side differential privacy mechanism is coupled with a server-side adaptive controller that continuously reweights group contributions and redistributes privacy budget according to observed fairness gaps, without requiring the server to access raw sensitive attributes beyond aggregated, privatised statistics. The framework is described architecturally, situated within the federated learning literature, and evaluated through a controlled simulation study on synthetic sensitiveattribute data that mimics the correlation structure found in real-world bias-prone datasets. Across privacy budgets ranging from strict (ε = 0.5) to unconstrained, the adaptive mechanism reduced the demographic parity gap by approximately six percentage points and the equalised-odds gap by roughly twenty per cent relative to a static differentially private baseline, at an accuracy cost below one percentage point. The paper discusses the architectural, regulatory and computational implications of adaptive privacy-fairness co-optimisation, identifies its principal limitations, including sensitivity to group-label availability and the added communication overhead of fairness signalling, and proposes directions for extending the framework to multi-attribute intersectional fairness and to non-independent and identically distributed client populations.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly deployed in environments whose data distributions, operating conditions, user behaviour, sensors, and decision requirements change after deployment. A model that is accurate at release can therefore become unreliable without an obvious software fault. This paper develops a research-based conceptual framework for self-healing artificial intelligence: an operational AI capability that continuously detects model degradation, diagnoses its likely cause, selects a targeted corrective action, tests that action under explicit safety constraints, and either deploys or rejects the repair. The study synthesises literature on concept drift, dataset shift, uncertainty-aware monitoring, continual and online learning, MLOps, and recent self-healing machine learning. The analysis distinguishes data drift, concept drift, label shift, data-quality failures, calibration failure, model staleness, and pipeline faults because different failure mechanisms require different responses. A four-stage healing cycle-monitoring, diagnosis, adaptation, and testing-is integrated with production safeguards such as shadow evaluation, rollback, confidence thresholds, audit trails, and human escalation. The paper further proposes an evaluation framework that measures not only post-repair predictive performance but also detection delay, false-alarm rate, diagnosis quality, recovery time, intervention cost, and safety regressions. The synthesis shows that autonomous retraining alone is not equivalent to self-healing AI: robust self-healing requires reason-aware diagnosis and evidence that a proposed intervention improves the system under the changed data-generating process. The paper concludes with a research agenda for reliable, explainable, resource-aware, and governance-compatible self-healing AI.

title: The Evidence Warrant: Why Healthcare AI Should Assert Claims Through Auditable Evidence Contracts, Not Confidence Scores

detail.title: The Evidence Warrant: Why Healthcare AI Should Assert Claims Through Auditable Evidence Contracts, Not Confidence Scores

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and CEO of The Algorithm, LLC, a healthcare technology company that builds analytics and intelligence systems for healthcare organizations. The evidence-contract framework described in this paper informs the company's product architecture. The framework itself is offered as an open contribution to the field; no proprietary implementation details are disclosed or required to apply it.

detail.abstract:
Healthcare AI and analytics systems routinely attach confidence scores to their claims (trend alerts, anomaly flags, denial-risk predictions) and expect users to decide whether the number is "high enough." We argue that scored confidence is the wrong basis for assertion in healthcare. Calibration measures how reliable a score is across many predictions; it says nothing about whether the evidence for a specific claim is sufficient to state it.

We introduce the evidence warrant: a system may state a claim only if the claim is derived through a published, auditable evidence contract. The contract declares the required evidence types, a categorical sufficiency function, and permissible behaviours (assert, qualify, downgrade, abstain). We report negative results from four scored formulations (calibrated thresholds, confidence vectors, Bayesian evidence accumulation, and anomaly-severity scoring), which all fail for the same structural reason, and fixing it takes a change in kind, from scoring to derivation. We define six formal requirements for compliant systems and describe a 10,000-scenario synthetic benchmark with 63 integrity checks. The benchmark tests whether a system honours its own contracts, not predictive accuracy.

The result is a framework in which "should this system say this?" is answered by inspecting the contract, not by interrogating a score, and in which abstention is a designed output rather than a failure.

detail.abstract: Machine learning systems are now allowed to make independent decisions in areas, where a wrong decision can result in a significant cost and impact such as clinical triage, credit adjudication, infrastructure control, or educational assessment. Even when employing a conventional deployment pipeline, the average predictive accuracy is maximised and all inferences are assumed to be equally trustworthy which fails when the model is being used to make inferences on inputs that fall outside what it was trained with, or inputs that are intrinsically ambiguous. This article proposes an uncertainty-aware framework and provides some empirical examples, which involve screening model outputs for epistemic and aleatoric risk prior to an automated action is executed, instead of failing silently. It incorporates a single risk-scoring layer for Monte Carlo dropout, deep ensembles, evidential deep learning and split conformal prediction into a unified setup and assesses with expected calibration error and with a selective risk-coverage analysis on a test classification setup. It is found that the selective risk could be reduced by more than half compared to softmax-confidence baseline baselines at automation coverages similar to softmax at equivalent coverages when using the ensemble-based and conformal-based estimators, and the post-hoc calibration decreases the ECE for all the considered methods. The findings are placed in the context of the broader trends of trustworthy AI, explainability, applications of AI for healthcare decision support, and even more broadly to resilient system architecture, and it is argued that uncertainty-aware gating is a necessary safety layer, never to be optional, as a form of diagnostic. Challenges with computational burden, distribution shifts and organisational uptake are analyzed, alongside hints on the standardization of risk-tiered deployment to different verticals of high stakes.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Information Systems and Their Role in Accelerating Digital Transformation

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Information Systems and Their Role in Accelerating Digital Transformation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest related to this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval was not required for this study because it involved a structured review and synthesis of published literature and authoritative frameworks and did not involve human participants, identifiable personal data, or primary data collection.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

keywords: organisational change 1. Introduction Digital transformation has moved from isolated digitisation projects to a continuing reconfiguration of strategy

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence-driven information systems are increasingly embedded in enterprise platforms, customer channels, operational networks and managerial decision processes. Their strategic significance lies not merely in automating existing tasks but in enabling organisations to sense change, interpret complex data, redesign workflows and develop new value propositions. This article examines the mechanisms through which AIenabled information systems accelerate digital transformation and the conditions that determine whether implementation produces durable organisational change. A structured integrative review synthesises peer-reviewed research and authoritative frameworks published principally between 2019 and 2025, supplemented by selected foundational studies and three relevant 2026 publications by Dhanani. The synthesis identifies six connected capabilities: data integration, intelligent sensing, predictive and generative inference, decision orchestration, adaptive process execution and organisational learning. Results show that acceleration occurs when these capabilities shorten the cycle from evidence to coordinated action while preserving security, accountability and human judgement. Conversely, fragmented data, legacy architecture, opaque models, weak skills, vendor dependence and poorly defined decision rights can convert technical adoption into transformation debt. A layered architecture and stagegate implementation framework are proposed, together with an outcome model linking system quality to process redesign, dynamic capability, innovation and public or business value. Three original figures and three tables distribute the framework across the literature review, results and discussion. The article concludes that AI-driven information systems accelerate transformation only when technology, operating model and governance are redesigned as an integrated socio-technical system.

title: Platform-Empowered Digital Finance and Traditional Investing: Spillover Effects through Financial Literacy and Risk Tolerance
affiliations: University of Washington - Department of Economics, ,  and University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business

detail.title: Platform-Empowered Digital Finance and Traditional Investing: Spillover Effects through Financial Literacy and Risk Tolerance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: There are no specific individuals or organizations fund this project.

detail.abstract: Digital platforms have transformed how investors access financial services by increasingly embedding these services into everyday digital interactions, yet it remains unclear whether they substitute for traditional financial investments or instead encourage broader market engagement. We examine how digital finance platform adoption affects investors' engagement with traditional finance and investigate the mechanisms through which these effects operate. Methodology/results: Using data from the China Household Finance Survey and a staggered-adoption difference-indifferences (DID) design with inverse probability weighting, we examine how digital finance platform adoption affects investors' participation in traditional financial markets and the risky asset share of their portfolios. Our approach addresses concerns about endogenous treatment, with instrumented DID serving as an additional robustness check for residual unobserved confounding and reverse causality. We find that adoption increases both outcomes. The complementarity effects are largest at the time of adoption and attenuate thereafter but remain positive. Mechanism analyses suggest that these patterns are consistent with improved financial literacy and a greater willingness to take financial risks. Additional tests indicate that the effects operate primarily on the extensive margin: digital finance brings previously inactive investors into traditional markets and helps existing participants remain engaged, rather than reallocating assets within incumbent investors' portfolios. Managerial implications: The study positions digital finance platforms as IT-enabled channels that reduce participation frictions, facilitate experiential learning, shape risk preferences, and promote investments beyond the focal platform service. These findings offer managerial insights into the design and development of platform-mediated financial services, as well as implications for regulatory policy.

title: Occupational License Portability and the Misallocation of Labor
affiliations: University of Oregon

detail.title: Occupational License Portability and the Misallocation of Labor
detail.abstract: Occupational licenses are typically jurisdiction-specific: workers who cross borders must relicense before resuming work. I quantify the resulting misallocation in the United States. I estimate a dynamic equilibrium model of occupation and location choice with occupational licensing and interstate relicensing costs. Non-portability reduces migration among workers in non-portable occupations, reduces employment among those who move, and deters entry into these occupations altogether because workers anticipate future relicensing costs. As a result, non-portability reduces aggregate earnings by roughly $18 billion annually. Workers in these occupations benefit, however, as non-portability raises their earnings.

title: The Early Impacts of AI on Employment Among Recent College Graduates
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and

detail.title: The Early Impacts of AI on Employment Among Recent College Graduates
detail.abstract: The impact of AI on the employment prospects of recent college graduates is hotly debated with no consensus on the magnitude of impacts nor even the timing of those potential impacts. Using CPS microdata, we provide the first estimates of the effects of AI on the unemployment of recent college graduates in June, July and August 2026. We provide evidence suggesting that unemployment rates are especially high for summer months and that 2026 might be the first year of widespread enough AI use in the workplace to detect impacts of AI on recent college graduates, the group argued to be most vulnerable to AI replacement. Taking an agnostic approach to defining treatment timing, we find that unemployment rates did not spike in summer 2026 relative to summer months in previous years and did not rise in a significant way relative to older college graduates or young workers without a college degree. We also provide the first analysis of an expanded definition of unemployment that includes those who report “wanting a job” which adds nearly two percentage points to the unemployment rate of recent college graduates but we find no evidence of a statistically significant increase in summer 2026 even after adding these “sidelined unemployed.” We estimate difference-in-differences and event-study interaction models using both older college graduates and young non-college graduates as comparison groups and do not find evidence of an increase in relative unemployment rates. Finally, we estimate models in which we interact 2026 unemployment with AI exposure and remote work availability by occupation and find some evidence of a positive relationship with remote work availability.
